abstracts.title: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Physical Complaints and Preventive Conditioning Practices Among Japanese Esports Athletes Certified by the National Federation
abstracts.by: Hyo Kitamura, Takeru Onishi and Jun Kubota, High Performance Sport Center, Japan
abstracts.aus: Hyo Kitamura, Takeru Onishi and Jun Kubota

sec.t: As esports evolves as a competitive sport, increasing attention has been towards the conditioning of esports athletes from the perspectives of health, well-being, and performance (DiFrancisco-Donoghue et al., 2019; Emara et al., 2020). Previous studies have reported the esports athletes have experience physical complaints such as musculoskeletal pain, injuries, and spinal function problems (Lindberg et al., 2020; Clements et al., 2022; Lam et al., 2022). These symptoms have been associated with factors including posture, distance from the screen, device usage, prolonged sitting, and playing hours. However, evidence regarding the physical condition and preventive conditioning behaviors of Japanese esports athletes remains limited.

This study aimed to investigate pain and discomfort, weekly esports play time, and warm-up and cool-down practices among esports athletes certified by Japan’s national esports federation, the Japan Esports Union (JESU).

This web-based cross-sectional survey targeted 350 JESU-certified athletes. A total of 83 athletes who provided complete responses were included in the analysis (mean age, 31.0 ± 7.5 years; 80 males, 3 females). Participants held licenses across 14 JESU-recognized titles, including Street Fighter 6, Tekken 8, and eFootball. The questionnaire collected information regarding esports title, pain or discomfort and affected regions, weekly play time, and warm-up and cool-down practices. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data.

Among the 83 participants analyzed, 51 (61.4%) reported pain or discomfort in at least one area. The most frequently reported area was the lower back (29, 34.9%), followed by the shoulders (27, 32.5%), neck (23, 27.7%), and eyes (21, 25.3%). Additionally, 33 (39.8%) reported symptoms in multiple areas. Regarding esports play time, 22 (26.5%) reported playing for 35 hours or more per week, based on a cut-off value used in a previous study (Ekejärd et al., 2024). Among participants who reported symptoms, 17 (33.3%) played for 35 hours or more per week, whereas this proportion was 15.6% among without symptoms. And among participants with symptoms, 37 of 51 (72.5%) did not perform warm-up exercises, while 22 of 32 participants without symptoms (68.8%) also did not. Similarly, 44 of 51 participants with symptoms (86.3%) and 28 of 32 without symptoms (87.5%) did not perform cool-down exercises.

The prevalence of symptoms observed in this study was comparable to findings from previous study involving the 62.5% prevalence of physical symptoms among Swedish professional esports gamers. Although the proportion of athletes playing 35 hours or more per week was lower than that reported in earlier study, longer playing time tended to be more common among athletes with symptoms. In contrast, the lack of warm-up and cool-down routines was consistently high regardless of symptom. The conditioning support should address prolonged play time and promote preventive conditioning for all athletes, and support staff should monitor these symptoms and consider title- and device-specific strategies.

This study found that complaints involving the lower back, shoulders, neck, and eyes were more common. Future support systems should incorporate title- and device-specific approaches while enabling continuous monitoring of athletes’ physical condition and preventive conditioning practices.

abstracts.title: A framework for identifying healthy displays of masculinity in online gaming communities
abstracts.by: David Micallef, Taylor Hardwick, Lauren Gurrieri, Melissa Wheeler, Lukas Parker and Lisa Given, RMIT University, Australia
abstracts.aus: David Micallef, Taylor Hardwick, Lauren Gurrieri, Melissa Wheeler, Lukas Parker and Lisa Given

sec.t: Online gaming, streaming, and esports are influential social environments for boys and young men. Gaming influencers do more than model gameplay; they also model ways of communicating, competing, relations with peers and the management of emotions (Gurrieri et al, 2024). Existing research has examined harmful or restrictive masculine practices in gaming, including hegemonic masculinity, toxic gamer culture, geek/gamer masculinity, harassment, and gendered exclusion (Meriläinen et al., 2026). Meriläinen et al.’s review found limited connection with broader men’s studies, and comparatively little research on men’s lived gendered experiences in gaming. Less attention has been paid to healthy masculine displays in gaming environments, particularly in content targeted at tween boys aged 9–12, an important developmental stage for developing social and emotional norms (Agirre & Fernández, 2024).

This study forms part of a broader project examining the influence of gaming influencers on tween boys. It focuses on an early phase of that work, identifying how healthy masculinities is constructed and performed by gaming influencers within content aimed at tween boys. Based on this mapping, the study aims to publish a conceptual framework for identifying healthy displays of masculinity in online gaming content.

A synthesis of literature on healthy masculinities was conducted to identify performances of healthy masculinities. This included non-gaming-based masculinity frameworks such as the relational-cultural framework (Di Bianca & Mahalik, 2022) and reviews of masculinity theorisations and programs (Flood et al., 2024; Exner-Cortens et al., 2021; Wilson et al., 2022). These literatures informed the development of theoretical codes used to analyse healthy displays of masculinities by content creators in videos featuring gameplay, commentary and audience interaction. A qualitative content analysis was conducted on gaming content likely to be viewed by tween boys, using a purposive sample of gaming influencers and their content on YouTube. Investigators view the content and record observations using the coding frame.

The study will present a draft conceptual framework with examples identified through a content analysis of gaming influencer content. The framework will identify how performances of healthy masculinities, such as emotional expression, are being modelled by gaming influencers who create content for tween gamers. The framework will identify if, and how, these healthy performances manifest in gaming communities.

This paper contributes a theoretically grounded framework for identifying healthy masculine displays in gaming content. While prior gaming research has richly documented harmful masculine norms, this framework shifts attention toward how healthy masculinities are communicated in online gaming communities. It also provides a foundation for future research into how gaming influencers may support healthier gender norms among boys and young men. By identifying and analysing healthy masculine displays, the framework may support researchers, educators, public health communicators, and industry stakeholders seeking to engage male gamers in more respectful and prosocial online behaviour.

The framework offers an early conceptual and methodological tool for examining healthy masculinities in gaming influencer content. Rather than positioning gaming communities only as sites of harm, the framework enables researchers to identify moments where content creators model care, respect, inclusion, emotional regulation, and accountability. In doing so, it creates a basis for future work exploring how healthier masculine norms can be recognised, supported, and amplified in gaming cultures.

abstracts.title: Accelerating the performance level of first-person shooter game beginners: Using the biofeedback training focused on gaze movement
abstracts.by: Inhyeok Jeong, Daisuke Shimane, Akinori Takeda and Masaki Takeda, Kochi University of Technology, Japan
abstracts.aus: Inhyeok Jeong, Daisuke Shimane, Akinori Takeda and Masaki Takeda

sec.t: First-Person Shooter (FPS) games are an esports genre where players battle with opponent players using guns, knives, and throwing weapons. During FPS gameplay, superior gaze (absolute position of the eyes in space, Schmid & Zambarbieri, 1991) control abilities are essential for achieving high performance (Jeong et al., 2025; Koposov et al., 2020), and gaze-based training can reduce the reaction time of FPS game players (Jeong et al., 2026). Nevertheless, three important gaps remain to be addressed in the current research: 1) it is unknown whether training based on the gaze control abilities of high-skilled esports players can lead to improvements in actual competitive performance, 2) the training methods developed in the esports field often only target esports players who already have sufficient esports playing experience, and 3) the previous studies only investigated the acute effect (10 minutes) of gaze-based training.
We aimed to investigate whether long-term gaze-based training (peripheral vision training; PVT) could accelerate in-game performance improvement for individuals new to FPS games.

Twelve male participants with no prior esports experience were recruited. Participants were randomly assigned to either a training group (six participants), which performed PVT alongside FPS gameplay (Valorant), or a control group (six participants), which played only the FPS game. During the PVT, participants received audio feedback when their gaze was off-center from the monitor. The experimental period consisted of 12 testing sessions (2−3 sessions per week, a total of 5 weeks). During PVT and playing the AimLab, reaction time, accuracy, and gaze distribution (recorded using Tobii 5) were collected. The Kill/Death/Assist (KDA) score was measured after each match of Valorant. The KDA score from tests 1 through 3 was set as the baseline. All data from 12 tests were analyzed across four periods (3 tests per period: Early, Early-Mid, Mid, and Late; interval between each period: one week).

First, gaze distribution was significantly decreased in the training group compared to that of the control group in the Early-Mid period (p <.05). Second, the reaction time of the training group was significantly decreased compared to the control group in the Early-Mid, Mid, and Late periods (all p <.05), but not in accuracy. Third, the KDA score of the training group increased significantly in the Late period compared to the baseline, relative to the control group (p <.05).

The results of this study suggest that gaze-based training might be useful for individuals with no prior esports experience who wish to improve their cognitive functions through esports. Specifically, improvement of cognitive functions related to peripheral vision, thereby accelerating improvements in reaction time and gaming performance. Esports is well known for improving cognitive function (Boot et al., 2011), but adapting to the gaming environment requires substantial effort and time. Therefore, combining gaze training with gameplay might help newbie esports players adapt more efficiently while gaining cognitive benefits.

Five weeks of gaze-based training can accelerate the reaction performance improvement of those new to playing esports. Furthermore, PVT not only improves reaction performance but also enhances in-game performance. Finally, results highlight the necessity of science-based training in esports and suggest potential applications in esports coaching and cognitive rehabilitation.

abstracts.title: Advertising Returns in Esports: Media Attention, Media Sentiment, and Financial Performance of Chinese A-Share Firms
abstracts.by: Huawei Sun, Seoul National University, South Korea

sec.t: Advertising can attract stakeholder attention and support firm value, but its financial returns are context dependent (Joshi & Hanssens, 2010). In esports, this issue is important because firms operate in a digital-native sport market shaped by young audiences, platform communities, and interactive spectatorship (Hamari & Sjöblom, 2017). Media coverage may therefore do more than amplify advertising exposure: marketing levers can attract investor attention and shape how corporate activity is interpreted by audiences (Borah et al., 2022).

This study examines whether advertising investment is associated with improved financial performance among esports-related firms and investigates two media-based mechanisms: the mediating role of media attention and the moderating role of media sentiment.

Using an unbalanced panel of 69 Chinese A-share listed firms engaged in esports-related businesses from 2010 to 2023, the study estimates firm and year fixed-effects regression models. Financial performance is measured by return on assets, advertising investment by annual advertising expenditure, and media attention and sentiment by firm-level news coverage. Mediation and moderation analyses test the indirect role of media attention and the conditional roles of online and print media sentiment. Robustness checks include alternative performance measures and instrumental-variable estimations.

Advertising investment is positively associated with financial performance. Media attention partially mediates this relationship, suggesting that advertising is linked to firm outcomes partly by increasing media visibility. Media sentiment shows asymmetric moderating effects: favorable print media sentiment strengthens the advertising-performance relationship, whereas online media sentiment does not significantly moderate it. Additional analyses show that advertising returns are stronger among firms with more focused esports portfolios, non-state-owned enterprises, eastern-region firms, and game development firms.

The findings suggest that esports firms should treat advertising not only as consumer-facing promotion but also as a strategic communication signal directed toward media and capital-market audiences. Managers should coordinate advertising investment with credible media exposure, especially through institutionalized print media channels, to improve the financial returns of advertising.

This study extends advertising effectiveness research to the esports industry by showing that advertising investment is linked to financial performance through media-based mechanisms. It highlights media attention and media sentiment as important conditions shaping how advertising translates into organizational outcomes in emerging digital sport markets.

abstracts.title: Being an Esports Fan Across Borders: An IPA Exploration of Transnational LCK Fandom
abstracts.by: Yaewon Jin, Ewha Womans University, South Korea

sec.t: As esports has scaled globally, its fandom has become increasingly heterogeneous and transnational — shaped by diverse motivations, attachments, gaming experience, and platformed participation across languages and regions (Hamari & Sjöblom, 2017; Macey et al., 2025; Rietz & Hallmann, 2023; Yu et al., 2022; Jin, 2010). League of Legends Champions Korea (LCK) represents a particularly instructive site for examining this shift. As one of the popular esports leagues, LCK is broadcast in six languages and draws approximately 67% of its viewership from overseas, with global AMA reaching 255,000 in 2023 — a 22% increase from 2022 (Kim, 2023). Yet existing research has struggled to account for this complexity, remaining largely quantitative and examined in disciplinary isolation from broader cultural and transnational contexts. Recent scholarship calls for more nuanced understandings of esports fan diversity, recognising that no single model can fully capture the complexity of esports communities (Jarrett, 2024). While work has expanded to address fan motivations, points of attachment, and gendered practices (Rietz & Hallmann, 2023; Yu et al., 2022; Yin & Xu, 2023), transnational dimensions remain underexplored. LCK fandom further raises questions for Korean Wave scholarship: despite esports’ positioning as a key vehicle of the New Korean Wave in South Korea’s 2020 national cultural policy, it has received far less attention than other Hallyu sectors — K-pop, K-drama, K-beauty — where global fandom has been examined across diverse regional contexts. Lived-experience accounts of global fans of Korean esports remain particularly scarce.

This study aims to explore the lived experiences of transnational LCK fans. Specifically, it asks how fans interpret their entry into LCK fandom, what meanings they attach to everyday fandom practices, and how transnational contexts of nationality and culture shape their experience of LCK fandom.

Methodologically, the study employs Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA), suited to detailed, idiographic examination of personal lived experience in complex and emotionally laden phenomena (Smith & Osborn, 2015). As part of the qualitative component of a larger ongoing mixed-methods study on global esports fandom, this paper presents an exploratory IPA case series selected from semi-structured interviews with transnational LCK fans. Following IPA’s idiographic commitment to small, purposively, and carefully situated samples (Smith et al., 2022), the analysis focuses on three to five information-rich cases.

As an ongoing study, the anticipated findings will illuminate three dimensions of transnational LCK fandom through IPA’s idiographic analysis: fans’ pathways into fandom and identity formation; the meanings fandom holds in everyday life; and esports participation as a transnational cultural practice. By foregrounding lived experience, the study offers conceptual groundwork for understanding esports fandom beyond disciplinary isolation and contributes to the theorisation of transnational esports fandom. For leagues, industry stakeholders, and policymakers, the findings invite a reframing of esports fans as culturally situated participants in transnational fandom spaces, with implications for sustainable and culturally responsive global audience development. The study also contributes to broader conversations in esports research on fan engagement, cross-regional audience dynamics, and qualitative methodologies for studying fandom across cultural contexts.

abstracts.title: Between Olympic Values and Esports Culture: Community Perceptions of the Olympic Esports Games
abstracts.by: Leon Janßen, University of Bayreuth, Germany; Felix Wachholz and Sophie Kreller, University of Innsbruck, Austria; Heiko Heidenreich, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Germany
abstracts.aus: Leon Janßen, Felix Wachholz, Sophie Kreller and Heiko Heidenreich

sec.t: Following the announcement of the Olympic Esports Games (OEG) by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) in 2024, Riyadh was initially selected as the host city for the event planned for 2027. However, subsequent organizational developments and the resulting indefinite postponement of the initiative have contributed to ongoing uncertainty surrounding the future implementation of the OEG (International Olympic Committee, 2025). Despite these developments, the OEG represent a significant attempt to integrate esports into established Olympic structures, a process that remains constrained by structural barriers such as the absence of a recognized international esports governing body and contested game title selections (Jenny et al., 2024). While the initiative may contribute to the institutional recognition of esports, it has also sparked controversial discussions within gaming and esports communities. Public debates revolve around legitimacy, authenticity, commercialization, game selection and the role of traditional sport organizations in shaping esports culture. The compatibility of Olympic values and esports culture also remains contested in academic literature (Postma et al., 2022). As the value creation of Olympic esports initiatives depends on the interplay of multiple stakeholder groups (Lefebvre et al., 2024) and online communities represent a central stakeholder group (Wachholz et al., 2025) as well as a key audience of the OEG, understanding their perceptions is critical for evaluating the initiative’s potential acceptance and legitimacy (Heidenreich et al., 2022).

While initial research has explored esports fans’ perceptions of the IOC’s esports strategy through focus groups (Lefebvre et al., 2023), naturally occurring online discourse surrounding the OEG remains largely unexamined. Therefore, this study aims to examine how the OEG are perceived within online gaming and esports communities. Specifically, the study investigates i) prevalent community perspectives on the OEG including expectations, support and concerns, ii) perceptions of the compatibility between Olympic values and esports culture and iii) how community members negotiate tensions between esports culture and traditional Olympic structures in online discourse.

The study follows an exploratory qualitative research design. A qualitative content analysis using an inductive-deductive category-building approach will be conducted on publicly accessible online posts and comments (e.g. Reddit, X, YouTube). Data will be systematically sampled from forums and social media discussions within defined timeframes surrounding major OEG-related announcements.

Data collection and analysis are currently in preparation. The analysis is expected to identify recurring discursive patterns related to legitimacy, authenticity, commercialization and the perceived compatibility between Olympic values and esports culture. In addition, the study aims to outline different stakeholder expectations regarding the role of Olympic institutions within esports ecosystems.

The study is expected to provide relevant insights for organizers, governing bodies and esports stakeholders involved in the development of the OEG. Understanding how online communities perceive the OEG could support more community-sensitive communication and governance strategies. Notably, community criticism of earlier Olympic esports events has already prompted the IOC to revise its game title selections (Jenny et al., 2024). Furthermore, monitoring online discourse may help identify stakeholder expectations, potential sources of resistance and opportunities for increasing community acceptance as well as credibility.

The OEG represent a significant step in the ongoing institutionalization of esports within traditional sport structures. At the same time, the initiative raises questions regarding legitimacy, authenticity and the compatibility between the Olympics and esports, with the study aiming to contribute to a deeper understanding of how Olympic involvement in the esports context is perceived. In addition, the findings may provide a valuable baseline for future pre-, mid- and post-event analyses examining how community perceptions evolve throughout the implementation and potential realization of the OEG.

abstracts.title: Beyond Competition: Esports as a Tool for Inclusion and Growth
abstracts.by: Ole Martin Pedersen Gjestad, KRED Norge, Norway

sec.t: Esports and gaming culture are increasingly recognized as more than entertainment alone. Around the world, municipalities, educational institutions, tourism actors, and grassroots organizations are exploring how gaming communities can contribute to social inclusion, learning, innovation, local development, and destination-building (Taylor, 2012; Hamari & Sjöblom, 2017; Becka et al., 2024). However, there is still limited research and practical documentation on how esports can function as long-term civic infrastructure within smaller cities and public-sector frameworks. KRED Norge is a Norwegian competence and resource centre for digital culture, based in Sarpsborg, working with esports, gaming culture, inclusion, education, public-sector development, and community-based digital participation.

This presentation explores how esports and gaming culture can be used as tools for social inclusion, workforce participation, urban development, and destination-building through the case of KRED Norge in Sarpsborg, Norway. The objective is to examine how grassroots gaming initiatives can evolve into broader community and development platforms when they are systematically aligned with municipal planning, public-sector priorities, local communities, and international networks. While existing research on esports hospitality and tourism has highlighted major international esports destinations and the role of event hosting in city branding and destination development, this case examines how a smaller city can use esports and gaming culture as long-term civic infrastructure connected to inclusion, participation, local identity, and municipal development.

The presentation is based on a qualitative, practice-led case study of KRED Norge’s development between 2021 and 2026. The case sample consists of selected initiatives developed or facilitated by KRED Norge during this period, including national grassroots esports tournaments, senior esports activities, open gaming spaces, alternative education arenas, inclusive gaming programmes, event development, public-private partnerships, and international collaborations connected to esports and gaming culture. Data were collected through organizational documentation, project reports, programme descriptions, internal planning material, event records, partnership processes, practitioner observations, and reflections from practical implementation. The case also draws on experiences from ecosystem-building within a municipal context, including collaboration with public-sector actors, civil-society organizations, education providers, local communities, and international esports networks. A central methodological element is the systematic use of Sarpsborg municipality’s Community Plan 2018–2030 as an analytical framework. The community plan’s vision, “Together we create the city”, and its three strategic areas — “The good home place”, “Jobs for the future”, and “Experiences for life” — are used to examine how esports and gaming culture can contribute to broader municipal priorities. This includes analysing how esports initiatives may strengthen social inclusion, learning and mastery, workforce participation, innovation, local identity, civic participation, and destination development. The data are analysed through practitioner reflection and thematic interpretation. The analysis focuses on how esports initiatives are designed, implemented, adapted, and embedded within a municipal and community-based context. Rather than treating KRED Norge as a single event or project, the presentation examines it as an evolving civic ecosystem in which public-sector goals, grassroots legitimacy, physical meeting places, cross-sector partnerships, and international networks interact over time.

The case demonstrates how gaming culture can contribute to several municipal development priorities. In relation to “The good home place”, KRED Norge has helped create inclusive social environments, open gaming spaces, senior esports initiatives, and alternative learning arenas that support belonging, mastery, and participation across generations. In relation to “Jobs for the future”, the case shows how gaming culture can connect young people, public actors, education providers, and local partners around digital competence, innovation, entrepreneurship, and new pathways into work and education. In relation to “Experiences for life”, KRED Norge has contributed to event development, civic pride, international partnerships, and increased visibility for Sarpsborg as a place connected to esports, digital culture, and community-driven innovation. The findings indicate that esports ecosystems can support broader goals connected to community development, youth engagement, local identity formation, destination-building, and public-sector innovation.

Findings offer practical insight into how municipalities and smaller cities can integrate esports and gaming culture into broader strategies for inclusion, urban development, workforce participation, and sport tourism destination-building. The case highlights the importance of physical meeting spaces, cross-sector collaboration, grassroots legitimacy, and hospitable environments when developing sustainable esports ecosystems. It also suggests that smaller cities can use esports not only as an event format, but as a platform for participation, belonging, learning, innovation, and local growth.

The KRED Norge case suggests that esports can function as more than competitive entertainment. When supported through long-term collaboration, municipal alignment, and local infrastructure, gaming culture can become a platform for social innovation, community-building, and regional development. The presentation argues that smaller cities may have unique opportunities to position themselves nationally and internationally through community-driven esports ecosystems rooted in inclusion, participation, and cultural innovation.

abstracts.title: Beyond Screentime: Differential Associations of Active and Passive Activities in Front of Screens with Mental Health in Generation Z – A Systematic Review
abstracts.by: Felix Wachholz, Stefanie Freimann and Lion Ramoser, University of Innsbruck, Austria; Tobias Scholz, University of Agder, Norway
abstracts.aus: Felix Wachholz, Stefanie Freimann, Lion Ramoser and Tobias Scholz

sec.t: Digital media have become a defining element of everyday life for Generation Z, shaping leisure and social interaction (Cheng et al., 2025). Within this landscape, gaming and esports represent central forms of active digital engagement (Nicholson et al., 2024). However, research on the relationship between screen time and mental health remains inconclusive, partly due to the aggregation of heterogeneous media activities into a single construct (Ferguson, 2017). Differentiating between active (gaming, esports) and passive (social media, TV) forms of engagement is therefore essential to understand how digital practices shape mental health trajectories in youth.

This study aimed to systematically compare the associations of active and passive screen time with mental health outcomes in adolescents of Generation Z, with a particular focus on gaming and esports as key forms of interactive digital participation.

A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Searches were performed in Web of Science, PubMed, and EBSCO. Inclusion criteria comprised peer-reviewed empirical studies examining active and/or passive screen time in relation to mental health among Generation Z populations. A total of 30 studies (N = 1.410.176 participants) were included and analyzed using a structured comparative approach.

Passive screen time was consistently associated with negative mental health outcomes, including depressive symptoms, anxiety, psychosomatic complaints, reduced life satisfaction, and impaired sleep. These associations were frequently dose-dependent, emerging at thresholds of approximately 2-4 hours per day. In contrast, active screen time demonstrated a heterogeneous pattern. Several studies reported no significant associations, while others identified context-dependent positive effects, such as enhanced social connectedness, emotional regulation, and well-being. However, high-intensity use - particularly in esports contexts - was linked to negative outcomes, including sleep disturbances and increased psychological strain.

The findings challenge reductionist “screen time minimization” approaches. Instead, interventions might prioritize reducing excessive passive consumption while promoting active, socially embedded, and purposeful digital engagement. Media literacy, context-sensitive guidelines, and the integration of digital environments into health promotion strategies are critical. In esports contexts, attention should be given to workload management, sleep, and psychosocial support structures.

Screen time is not a monolithic construct. While passive media consumption is consistently linked to adverse mental health outcomes, active engagement - particularly gaming and esports - represents a complex, context-dependent practice situated between risk and opportunity. Future research and policy should move beyond quantity-based metrics toward a differentiated understanding of digital behavior that reflects the evolving role of gaming as part of nowadays youth culture.

abstracts.title: Beyond the Arena: Esports Tournaments as Research Instruments
abstracts.by: Arjun Madhusudan, North Carolina State University, United States of America; Josef Spjut, Ben Boudaoud and Joohwan Kim, NVIDIA, United States of America; Benjamin Watson, North Carolina State University, United States of America
abstracts.aus: Arjun Madhusudan, Josef Spjut, Ben Boudaoud, Joohwan Kim and Benjamin Watson

sec.t: Esports research has grown around competitive games, players, spectators, teams, and events. Much of this work already recognizes esports as a rich cultural, social, and competitive domain. However, tournaments are often treated as objects to observe: events where players compete, spectators gather, organizations operate, and communities form. We argue that esports tournaments can also be treated as research instruments: structured competitive environments intentionally designed to support data collection, intervention, and experimentation.

This framing is important for research on skill, expertise, performance, pressure, fairness, player experience, and their relationships to game systems and design choices. Laboratory studies can isolate variables with high experimental control, but often remove the competitive dynamics that make esports distinctive. Conversely, observational tournament research preserves authenticity, but usually provides limited control over the conditions studied. Building on calls for more rigorous experimental esports research (Campbell et al., 2024), field experiments (Harrison & List, 2004), and prior tournament-based intervention work in sport (Rowsell et al., 2009), tournament-based methods offer a similar middle ground for esports: preserving meaningful competition while allowing researchers to vary, structure, and measure aspects of play.

We ground this argument in our ongoing work on tournament-experiments: live esports tournaments in which experimental manipulations are embedded into the tournament structure itself (Madhusudan et al., 2026). Across two Rocket League pilots, we introduced controlled visual and temporal conditions while preserving bracket progression, player motivation, and match stakes. These pilots serve as methodological case studies for examining how experimental control can be introduced into competitive settings without fully removing the social and structural conditions of tournament play.

Our pilots suggest that tournaments can support experimental research without disrupting player experience, but also reveal challenges for esports research. Our contribution is to treat tournament structure itself as part of the research design, rather than only as a setting for observation or intervention. Similar to field-based sport research, these methods trade some control for ecological validity, participant motivation, and competitive authenticity. Expertise, seeding, advancement, fairness, and player trust are not peripheral complications; they are fundamental components of esports competition, shaping both the tournament and the data it produces. For example, a tournament-experiment might alternate conditions within a best-of-three match and use a balanced third game to protect advancement fairness. Alternatively, all matches could use balanced conditions while experimental contrasts are distributed across matches, preserving perceived fairness but reducing within-match comparison.

Researchers should treat tournament structure as part of research design. They must ask not only what to measure, but also what to vary, what to preserve, and what kinds of fairness matter for a given study. Conditions might be assigned dynamically across rounds, stratified by seed or expertise, or adjusted to prioritize experimental balance, bracket integrity, player trust, or logistics. These choices are not simply implementation details; they shape what claims the study can support. Game developers and platform holders can support tournament-based research through administration modes, scripted condition changes, replay APIs, telemetry exports, and privacy-aware data access.

Our goal is to situate tournaments within the methodological toolkit of esports research. Rather than replacing laboratory, survey, or observational approaches, tournament-experiments offer a complementary method for studying competition in context. For observational studies, tournaments can support richer collection of gameplay data, player characteristics, audience behavior, and competitive context. For experimental studies, they raise questions about introducing manipulations without compromising competitive legitimacy. With better tournament-aware methods and developer support, esports scholars can build methods appropriate to the domain itself.

abstracts.title: Beyond Title-Based Classification: Developing a Functional Framework for Esports Disciplines and Transnational Governance
abstracts.by: Eunkyoung Choi, Hanshin University, South Korea

sec.t: Esports has developed across heterogeneous gaming ecosystems, yet competitive disciplines continue to be identified primarily by proprietary game titles or broad genre labels. Scholarship has examined esports against established conceptions of sport (Jenny et al., 2017), demonstrated persistent heterogeneity in how esports is defined (Formosa et al., 2022), and conceptualized the field as a complex ecosystem of stakeholders and governing principles (Scholz, 2020). Despite these advances, the esports discipline as an institutional unit of organized competition remains insufficiently theorized and structurally classified. If esports is treated as a distinct, sport-level domain of organized competition, a fundamental question therefore arises: how should its disciplines be distinguished beyond individual game titles? This study asks firstly, what structural principles can be derived from established sport classification systems, and secondly, whether these principles can be reformulated into a functional framework capable of classifying esports disciplines across different gaming and national ecosystems.

The study conceptualizes esports as organized human competition mediated by video games. It therefore distinguishes esports as the overarching competitive domain from proprietary game titles and treats classification as institutional ordering rather than genre labelling. It borrows the layered logic of organized sport without reproducing its categories, adapting that logic to publishers, platforms, technologies, rule changes, and culturally differentiated competition practices.

Methodologically, classification structures used by the International Olympic Committee, international federations, ASOIF, WOF, and the Olympic Council of Asia were comparatively analyzed. Recurrent features were synthesized into four layers: discipline/sub-discipline, form, rule set, and gender/age category. The analysis identified variable activation of these layers across traditional sports. Four cross-cutting criteria, functional, technological, competitive-format, and genre-related characteristic were then specified for esports. The framework was applied to 72 titles contested in official esports competitions held during 2024 across Korea, China, Japan, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, the USA, Canada, and Europe.

The findings show that title-based classification obscures structural comparability across games and regions. MOBA and FPS titles clustered around functional and competitive format characteristics, hybrid titles required combinations of layers, and VR/AR formats were differentiated primarily through technological criteria. Variable layer activation accommodated heterogeneous competition forms without making publisher ownership or individual titles the basis of discipline recognition.

This study argues that esports classification requires both a common functional framework and an institutional process of coordination. The architecture provides a shared basis through which national discipline organizations and relevant stakeholders can compare, negotiate, and recognize esports disciplines. Transnational governance is therefore required to coordinate these deliberative processes while accommodating social, technological, and cultural differences among national ecosystems. Such a framework can create the institutional conditions for diversity, inclusion, cross-regional recognition, and the sustainable expansion of emerging esports formats.

abstracts.title: Bridging Collegiate Values: Understanding the Global Positioning of Collegiate Esports Teams, Degrees, and Schools
abstracts.by: Andrew Wilson, University of Rhode Island, United States of America; Amanda Cote, Michigan State University, United States of America; Maxwell Foxman, University of Oregon, United States of America; Brandon Harris, University of Alabama, United States of America
abstracts.aus: Andrew Wilson, Amanda Cote, Maxwell Foxman and Brandon Harris

sec.t: As esports becomes increasingly visible across university campuses (Parshakov & Barajas, 2024), university-supported varsity programs are giving way to esports-forward institutions like the University Campus of Esports (London, UK) and Tokyo College of Anime and E-Sports (Tokyo, Japan). Collegiate esports clearly enjoys widespread interest among diverse stakeholders: student-athletes, academics, investors, and more. However, institutions are still trying to understand esports’ place on campus, especially amid more well-entrenched financial and cultural power stemming from traditional sports (Zhong et al., 2024), regardless of specific national peculiarities (e.g., Foxman et al., 2024). Scholarship points to positive student or institutional outcomes when esports programs are cultivated—for example, a greater sense of belonging within one’s campus community or enhanced university branding—but such literature tends to concentrate on North American experiences (Buzzelli & Draper, 2021; Cote et al., 2024).

This study investigates and compares how an array of esports-focused institutions worldwide present and promote their esports degrees (e.g., production, business, medicine), varsity programs, or esports clubs. We aim to uncover how institutions situate esports within their unique cultures, how they position it to potential players, students, and other stakeholders, and how these patterns vary globally. This work is a deliberate effort to redirect academic attention toward collegiate esports’ ongoing growth and institutionalization beyond North America.

This research takes a case study approach, first identifying key institutions (e.g., esports-specific schools and academic programs, highly promoted competitive collegiate teams), then analyzing their esports-related webpages. Using inductive thematic analysis (Clarke & Braun, 2017), we identify general descriptive information (e.g., majors and degrees offered, number of teams/players, games played, etc.) and assess descriptions of esports’ role in student life, testimonials from student-athletes or staff, and other relevant information. Collectively, we will show how value statements that universities employ to justify their esports investments shape esports’ broader cultural status and positioning.

Collegiate esports provide an exciting opportunity to engage students, alumni, fans, and even potential investors (Lee & Lee, 2026; Jenny et al., 2025). Our initial analyses suggest that universities also frame esports degree programs as essential to preparing students for future-facing careers in the creative and media industries, such as broadcasting and event management. However, much of collegiate esports’ growth occurred during an overall gaming boom fueled by the COVID-19 pandemic, a period now tempered by an industry-wide contraction (colloquially, the “esports winter”; see Levine et al., 2026). As such, how collegiate esports significance is framed during this challenging moment may be a bellwether for the field’s long-term success.

Understanding how universities frame the value of esports will allow us to evaluate its potential resilience and enable meaningful cross-cultural comparisons. This work will also help program directors, fans, and players to identify additional value propositions to promote their own work. Finally, academics will be able to critically assess esports’ wider institutionalization, structures, and the symbolic capital (Bourdieu, 1989) it provides to different participants.

abstracts.title: Bridging Esports Futures: Panel on Worldwide University Esports Competition Structures
abstracts.by: Nikita Bair, Syracuse University, United States of America; Seth E. Jenny, Slippery Rock University of Pennsylvania, United States of America; Joey Gawrysiak, Syracuse University, United States of America; Charlie Smith, University of Suffolk, United Kingdom
abstracts.aus: Nikita Bair, Seth E. Jenny, Joey Gawrysiak and Charlie Smith

sec.t: While the professional-level esports ecosystem continues to mature and adopt best practices, competitive structures of collegiate/university esports vary widely across educational institutions, leagues, and game titles internationally.

The primary objective of this panel is to compare university esports competition structures from North America, Europe, and Asia, focusing on multi- and single-game title structures, varying organizational models of university esports programs, and challenges and opportunities within university esports globally.

This is a moderated panel discussion incorporating existing research on the worldwide university esports ecosystem. University academic and industry esports practitioners from North America, Europe, and Asia will discuss shared and contrasting experiences. Published descriptive and correlational statistical research on university esports will also be shared and discussed.

University-specific tournaments, leagues, or conferences exist in the United States, Canada, Mexico, Netherlands, France, Croatia, Germany, United Kingdon, South Korea, Australia, among others (Jenny, 2025). Worldwide there is a lack of standardization as competitive structure varies widely across regions and within single countries. In North America alone, it is estimated there are over 2,000 collegiate/university esports programs, with over 70 entities of athletic conferences, esports leagues, and game-specific tournaments that compete to organize and govern competitions across fragmented and overlapping structures (Jenny & Sharpe, 2025). Despite being the most established region, North American universities differ in their purpose for supporting esports and the benefits institutions receive (Jenny et al., 2025). Factors for why the North American university esports ecosystem is significantly larger vary, but the school-sports model compared to the club-based sports model outside North America is likely the greatest factor. Another reason, for example, is that some universities tend to favor supporting esports education academic curriculum rather than university-sponsored competitive teams, such as the case in South Korea (Chang, 2022). Research from university students on perceptions of esports differ globally; Italian students were found to believe participation in esports negatively impacted other aspects of their lives while American students did not perceive esports as taking away time from other activities (Delello et al., 2023).

Panel discussion points will emphasize how fragmented and confusing collegiate/university esports competition structures worldwide hinder growth and adoption, underscoring the need for organizers and publishers to consolidate and create a more sustainable ecosystem. Practical suggestions surrounding utilizing the School-based Esports Model to help solve the Esports Pipeline Problem relating to Esports Pathways to Pro (Jenny, 2024) will also be discussed.

Much like its professional counterpart, university esports competition is being supported globally. Due to key cultural differences, university esports competition thrives in the United States and Canada and is less supported in locations such as Italy or South Korea, but is trending upwards in countries like the United Kingdom. More research is still needed to note growth rates in other global regions, but it is expected that the number of universities supporting esports competition worldwide will increase, particularly in Asia.

abstracts.title: Bridging Gaming Hardware and Hospitality Experience in Esports Hotels: An Empirical Investigation
abstracts.by: Wenxuan Liao, Hong Kong Shue Yun University, China; Gangli Tan, University of Hamburg, Germany; Xiaobo Ke, The Education University of Hong Kong, China
abstracts.aus: Wenxuan Liao, Gangli Tan and Xiaobo Ke

sec.t: As esports culture rapidly diffuses across Asia, esports hotels have emerged as a technology-enabled lodging format that integrates high-performance gaming hardware (notably GPUs) into guest rooms. Prior research has emphasized their emotional and symbolic appeal (Babar & Zhao, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), yet it remains unclear whether high-end hardware configurations create value equally across different guest needs.

Drawing on Task-Technology Fit theory, which posits that user outcomes hinge on the alignment between technology features and task demands (Goodhue & Thompson, 1995), this study examines how GPU performance shapes customer satisfaction in esports hotels and whether this effect is contingent on travel purpose, conceptualized as the underlying task.

We collected 5,241 consumer reviews of esports hotels across 10 major Chinese cities from Ctrip.com. SnowNLP and an AI-agent (DeepSeek and ChatGPT combined) re-scoring procedure were used to generated sentiment-based evaluations for five review-derived dimensions: service, hygiene, location, facilities, price–experience value. GPU configurations extracted from room descriptions were coded on a 15-point performance scale. Linear and quadratic regressions, controlling for city, room capacity, and hotel rating, were estimated for the pooled sample and across travel-purpose subsamples.

In the pooled model, hygiene (β = 0.170), facilities (β = 0.167), service (β = 0.071), and GPU configuration (β = 0.060) positively predicted satisfaction at p < 0.01 or better. Subsample analyses uncovered marked heterogeneity: GPU configuration exhibited an inverted U-shaped effect for couple travelers (linear β = 0.164, p < 0.01; quadratic β = –0.126, p < 0.05), a positive linear effect for business travelers (β = 0.100, p < 0.05), and no significant effect for solo or friend-group travelers. Hygiene and facilities continued to drive satisfaction across subsamples, except among business travelers.

Hardware upgrading is not universally value-adding: esports hoteliers should align GPU tiers with the dominant task profiles of their guest segments. Couple-oriented properties stand to benefit more from mid-range GPUs paired with ambience investment, whereas business-segment hotels gain from sustained GPU escalation. Hygiene and facilities remain consistent drivers of satisfaction across most traveler groups, underscoring the continued importance of core hospitality fundamentals.

Hardware contributes to esports hotel satisfaction, but its marginal value depends on the fit between hardware capability and travelers’ tasks. The inverted-U effect among couples implies that excessive digital immersion may erode the physical co-presence central to relational travel. This study extends esports research into everyday hospitality settings, showing that more technology does not always create more value.

abstracts.title: Bridging Generations Through Play: Exploring Older Adults’ Experiences with Esports
abstracts.by: Sarah Standridge, East Tennessee State University, United States of America; Kevin Mast, Johnson City Parks and Rec, United States of America

sec.t: The last few years, esports have started becoming popular among older individuals (Onishi et al., 2022). Gaming has been associated with stress relief (Yeh, 2021), skill-building (Sardi et al., 2017), improved attention and focus (Yu & Chan, 2021), and fostering more social connectedness (Soares et al., 2022). A better understanding of how esports function as a leisure-based platform may offer the potential to foster intergenerational interaction, build confidence with emerging technologies, and reduce barriers to participation among older adults.

The purpose of this study was to explore how participation in a structured esports program effected older adults’ perceptions of gaming, confidence with technology, and opportunities for intergenerational social engagement.

Grounded in leisure theory, this mixed-method study was conducted with five older adults. The group consisted of three men and two women with an average age of 68. Participants engaged in a six-week workshop developed in partnership with a local senior center. The workshop introduced participants to Rocket League through structured gameplay sessions, spectator experiences, and guided group discussions. Data collection included pre and post workshop surveys, participant observation, and a focus group. Qualitative data were transcribed, member-checked, and thematically analyzed to better understand participants’ lived experiences and meaning-making processes related to esports participation (Charmaz, 2014; Saldana, 2012). Data analysis examined changes in attitudes, knowledge, and social confidence regarding gaming and esports using paired-samples t-tests on seven Likert-scale survey items. Due to the exploratory nature of the study and limited sample size (n = 5), statistical power was constrained and no findings reached conventional significance levels (α =.05). Cohen’s d effect sizes were used as indicators of practical meaningfulness.

Findings supported the idea that esports functioned primarily as a relational and cultural bridge rather than solely as a competitive activity. Participants expressed motivation not only to improve gameplay skills but also to better understand and communicate with children and grandchildren. Initially, the group experienced some barriers. Confidence in gaming and comfort increased throughout the workshop due to repeated exposure, structured instruction, and the maintenance of a supportive, low stakes learning environment.

This study highlights the importance of intentional program design when implementing esports programming for older adults. Psychological safety, accessibility, structured facilitation, and opportunities for social interaction were critical components for supporting participant engagement and retention. Findings show esports programming could potentially provide recreation professionals, senior centers, and community organizations a tool for promoting digital inclusion, intergenerational engagement, and social well-being among aging populations.

Positioned within the growing global esports and gaming landscape, these findings point towards the possibility that esports may serve as a platform for intergenerational connection, social engagement, and meaningful participation among older adults. This contributes to the emerging insight into the role of esports in supporting well-being, digital inclusion, and community development for aging populations.

abstracts.title: Bridging Silver GAKU Games to the Nordic North: Cultural Translation of an Asian Esports-for-Elderly Programme
abstracts.by: Rune Andersen, University of Agder, Norway; Sayo Okamoto and Dawn Beasley, Gaku, Japan; Tobias Scholz, University of Agder, Norway
abstracts.aus: Rune Andersen, Sayo Okamoto, Dawn Beasley and Tobias Scholz

sec.t: Demographic ageing is reshaping Nordic societies, and with it the demands placed on welfare systems, communities, and the digital lives of older adults. Loneliness, sedentary behaviour, and digital exclusion among seniors are well-documented public-health concerns. Esports and digital gaming have emerged as plausible, but unevenly tested, instruments for cognitive engagement, learning, and social connection in later life. Asian initiatives such as Silver GAKU Games in Japan and Singapore illustrate a coherent format: structured esports days that combine programming-based cognitive titles such as Puyo Puyo Programming with intergenerational play and community building. These initiatives operate, however, in cultural settings where seniors are comparatively tech-curious and embedded in long-standing console and arcade ecosystems.

This conceptual contribution proposes the cultural translation of Silver GAKU Games to the Nordic elderly context. The guiding question is straightforward: how do culturally specific attitudes toward technology, ageing, and competition reshape engagement with structured esports interventions when an Asian senior programme is transplanted to a Nordic welfare-state setting?

The paper is conceptual and design-stage. Drawing on Hofstede’s cultural dimensions and established frameworks of technology acceptance among older adults, the Silver GAKU Games architecture is mapped onto Nordic socio-cultural conditions: individualism, low power distance, an egalitarian welfare model, and historically modest senior gaming uptake. A planned quasi-experimental pilot at the University of Agder will use pre-/post-intervention measures of digital self-efficacy, loneliness, and well-being, alongside semi-structured interviews and observational ethnography. The adapted programme centres on programming-based esports formats, scaffolded learning, and intergenerational play.

As the study is in design, findings are anticipated rather than observed. The expectation is lower baseline engagement and higher technology anxiety than reported in Asian pilots, with adoption gains concentrated in cognitive-learning and intergenerational modules. Competitive tournament framing is likely to require recalibration; cooperative, narrative, and reminiscence-based formats are anticipated to outperform bracket-style structures. The programming-as-play angle is hypothesised to function as a culturally acceptable bridge between scepticism and engagement among Nordic seniors.

The work is intended to deliver a culturally sensitive blueprint for transferring Asian esports-for-elderly programmes into Nordic welfare-state contexts. Municipalities, care providers, and esports organisations developing silver-gaming offers stand to benefit, as do publishers and platforms looking beyond their established Asian core. Programming-driven titles, in particular, are identified as an underexplored entry point for hesitant senior audiences.

Transferring esports-for-ageing programmes across cultural contexts is not a question of replication but of cultural translation. The Silver GAKU Games case offers a productive lens through which to examine how gaming heritage, infrastructure, and senior attitudes co-shape esports futures. Thereby, extending the ERN 2026 theme from inter-regional dialogue to inter-generational practice.

abstracts.title: Can gaming content creators support good health? Lessons from an Australian anti-vaping campaign
abstracts.by: David Micallef, Juan Feng and Edward Hurcombe, RMIT University, Australia
abstracts.aus: David Micallef, Juan Feng and Edward Hurcombe

sec.t: Gaming cultures are often broadly examined through a deficit perspective in health research and policy. Online gaming has been associated with sedentary behaviour, problematic use, and exposure to unhealthy commercial marketing (Chan et al., 2022; Pontes et al., 2022). This framing, however, can obscure the complexity of game-streaming and esports communities, which can include multiple influences on health (Micallef et al., 2022). Gaming streamers, content creators who build communities through live gameplay, do not only mediate game-related discussion. Previous research has shown that streaming communities also host organic conversations about everyday practices, including food, drink, and health (Micallef et al., 2024). While these spaces remain important targets for unhealthy commercial marketing (Roscoe et al., 2023), they may also provide opportunities to promote good health.

This study examines that possibility through an Australian case study of an influencer-led anti-vaping campaign, run by the Australian Government (Department of Health and Aged Care, 2024). Within the broader campaign, this case study focuses on the role of two gaming content creators, Jack Buzza and HeyImZed, to engage their audiences via Twitch, Instagram and TikTok, with content created for the campaign. Through this analysis, this study aims to understand the role that gaming content creators can play in engaging young gamers in health messages.

The study draws on a qualitative analysis of comments posted in response to the campaign content created by both gaming creators, analysis of audience comments from livestreams and semi-structured interviews with the content creators. Data was analysed using thematic coding. Audience comments were also analysed using the Uses and Gratifications Theory (UGT) to understand the gratifications being performed by audiences in engaging with the content.

Findings suggest that gaming content creators have the potential to act as health champions when public health messages are adapted to the norms, humour, language, relational and content expectations of their communities. Through a process of vernacular authentication, content creators translate institutional health messages into culturally recognisable forms that engender trust, credibility and engagement. In this case, anti-vaping messages were not simply repeated verbatim by creators, but were reframed through gaming references. This led to direct audience engagement with the content, the creator and the anti-vaping messages.

The case study also suggests that gaming content creators can be seen as socio-ecological interventions, rather than simple influencer marketing. It suggests that gaming content creators’ embedded role within their communities, their repeat interactions, peer discussions and shared cultural codes, allows them to engage deeply with their communities. This creates opportunities for targeted public health interventions in spaces that reach young audiences, but needs careful management to preserve creator and community authenticity.

Our study contributes to broader debates about health and wellbeing in gaming, and responsibility in gaming and esports cultures. It also opens up opportunities for established gaming structures, such as esports, to engage with governments, public health institutions and their communities to coordinate responses to both local and global health issues.

abstracts.title: Cardiovascular reactivity and body movement patterns during CS:GO gameplay: A secondary analysis of the CEPAV dataset
abstracts.by: Nicholas Lerma, Grand Valley State University, United States of America

sec.t: Organized competitive video gaming, or esports, typically occurs in a sedentary behavior (seated position with low energy expenditure) even in the presence of elevated event heart rate (HR) (Zimmer et al., 2022). There is elevated cardiovascular risk from prolonged sitting exposure during psychological stress (Yamagata et al., 2022).
This study aims to explore the relationship between accelerometer-derived human movement patterns and cardiovascular reactivity during competitive video gaming.

Baseline data from the Competitive Esports Physiological, Affective, and Video (CEPAV) dataset (Behnke et al., 2025) from the Open Science Framework website included three phases with 2-minute summaries: 1) pre-match, 2) Counter Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) gameplay, and 3) recovery. Accelerometers (Actigraph) were used to determine wrist (WM) and thigh (TM) vector magnitude counts per minute. HR beats per minute (bpm) and heart rate variability (HRV; root mean square of successive differences in milliseconds) were collected with the Vrije Universiteit Ambulatory Monitoring System. Players self-reported rank and competition experience. Mixed model ANOVA were performed with Bonferroni correction in pairwise comparisons for phase and experience.

This secondary analysis included 299 male CS:GO players with rank spanning across 18 levels and four categories of competition experience (none=200, local=76, national=17, international=6). Player WM significantly increased by 19% during gameplay (η²p=.024, p=.007) with no differences between pre-match and recovery, and no significant relationship in TM across phases (p=.884). There was a significant phase by experience interaction for HR (η²p=.026, p=.019). On average, gameplay HR increased 4.1 bpm and 7.4 bpm relative to pre-match (81.0 bpm) and recovery (77.6 bpm), respectively. Interestingly, there was a significant reduction in HR and an increase in HRV between pre-match and recovery with no differences in body movement.

Elevated WM during gameplay remained below thresholds for a light-physical activity classification (Montoye et al., 2020). Elevated HR during gameplay and HR/HRV rebound patterns during recovery are consistent with parasympathetic reactivation following psychological arousal of gameplay.
Even brief competitive video gameplay sessions outside of tournament settings are subject to measurable sympathetic and parasympathetic reactivity during the relatively sedentary behavior.

abstracts.title: Changing Narratives of Gamers in Quebec Newspapers Before, During, and After the COVID-19 Pandemic
abstracts.by: Emy Chapleau, University of Quebec in Three-River, Canada

sec.t: Media framing is defined as the way media structure issues and influence public perception by how they represent social groups (Entman, 1993; Guo et al., 2025). Media portrayals of video game players fluctuate between stigma and cultural recognition (Brunborg et al., 2013; Barr & Copeland-Stewart, 2022), influencing public perceptions of gamers (Kümpel & Haas, 2016). Media representation therefore contribute to the creation of stigma (Sallabank et al., 2022).

COVID-19 amplified some media narratives surrounding video games (Brückner, 2024). During the pandemic, video games experienced a surge, sparking both concerns and positive reassessment (Barr & Copeland-Stewart, 2022). However, the media representation of gamers in Quebec has not been studied yet. An earlier version of this project presented preliminary findings based solely on article titles. The current study analyzes the final dataset using full-text articles and comprehensive statistical analyses to examine how gamers were portrayed before, during, and after the pandemic in Quebec.

The corpus consisted of 289 print media articles selected from an initial sample of 446 published in major Quebec newspapers. Two periods were examined: pre-pandemic (n = 161; December 23, 2017–March 12, 2020) and pandemic/post-pandemic (n = 128; March 13, 2020–August 20, 2024). Sentiment analysis assessed changes in emotional polarity, while correspondence analysis identified characteristic lexical associations across periods to understand the evolution of media representation.

The final statistical analyses revealed an evolution in lexical associations across the different periods examined. During the pandemic period, the vocabulary was more strongly centered on esports and cyberaddiction-related concepts (χ² = 3292.3, p <.001; inertia = 0.158; Cramer’s V = 0.141). In contrast, the pandemic and post-pandemic periods were characterized by lexical associations that shifted toward business-oriented and social-related terminology (χ² = 2846.6, p <.001; inertia = 0.143; Cramer’s V = 0.143). Finally, sentiment analyses also revealed an overall shift in the emotional valence of the terms used, including changes in both positive and negative sentiment.

Combining sentiment and correspondence analyses provides a comprehensive framework for understanding how media discourse evolves over time and influences public perceptions, the stigmatization of gamers, and the social legitimacy of video games and esports.
The findings demonstrate significant lexical and emotional shifts in media representations of gamers across the pandemic period.

abstracts.title: Classifying E-Doping in Esports: A Scoping Review of Competitive Integrity Risks
abstracts.by: Salvador Jr. Reyes, University of Lausanne / KU Leuven; Frank Ressat and Thomas Souvignet, University of Lausanne, Switzerland
abstracts.aus: Salvador Jr. Reyes, Frank Ressat and Thomas Souvignet

sec.t: Esports has grown rapidly and is now considered one of the most popular forms of digital entertainment (Cranmer et al., 2021), with competitive video gaming attracting mainstream broadcasting attention (Holden et al., 2017). This rapid professionalisation has surfaced distinctive integrity and regulatory challenges, including the absence of a unified governance framework (Kelly et al., 2022; Martinelli, 2019). Among these challenges is e-doping, defined by Hwang (2022) as “the use of hacks and cheats during e-sports games” (p. 1283)—a phenomenon that existing regulatory frameworks remain ill-equipped to address (Rana & Parsai, 2023). A systematic mapping is needed to support coherent scholarly and governance responses.

This scoping review asks: (1) how documented forms of e-doping can be systematically structured; (2) what patterns emerge across platforms, genres, and technical layers; and (3) what research gaps remain for esports integrity governance.

A systematic search across multiple databases covering 2000-2024 returned 4,158 records. After duplicate removal, title-and-abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment, 61 peer-reviewed studies were included. Data were extracted and synthesised using Webb and Soh’s (2007) four-level technical taxonomy—Game, Application, Protocol, and Infrastructure—alongside sport-ethics concepts of intentional rule violation, deception, and fair play.

The review identified 82 e-doping codings. Application-Level methods dominated (n = 59), including aimbots, wallhacks, bots, macros, recoil scripts, memory manipulation, and speed-hacks. Protocol-Level methods followed (n = 12), including DDoS, packet tampering, interception, and lag switching. Infrastructure-Level threats (n = 6) included modified peripherals, NFC/object-based manipulation, mobile hardware exploits, and mechanical robo-doping. Game-Level e-doping was least represented (n = 5), consisting mainly of bug, glitch, and infinite-combo exploitation. Publication output accelerated from 2021 onward, with 44.3% of the corpus published between 2021 and 2024. The literature also showed a pronounced PC bias (86.9%) and methodological concentration in technical and experimental studies (57.4%), leaving mobile, console, and specialised-hardware esports underexamined.

The taxonomy gives tournament organisers, publishers, anti-cheat developers, integrity bodies, federations, and policy actors a shared map for locating e-doping risks and matching countermeasures to the affected technical layer. It also shows that detection alone is insufficient; governance, ethical education, and forensic capability must develop alongside technical safeguards.

E-doping is a significant integrity challenge for organised digital competition. This review establishes a conceptual and taxonomic foundation for interdisciplinary work across computer science, sport ethics, governance, and digital forensic science. Future research should prioritise mobile and console platforms, longitudinal analysis of cheat persistence, qualitative work on motivation, and forensic interpretation of digital traces.

abstracts.title: Complexity in Control: Evaluating FPS-Performance using Mouse-Movement Sample Entropy
abstracts.by: Inhyeok Jeong, Kochi University of Technology, Japan; Felix Wachholz, Leopold-Franzens-University Innsbruck, Austria

sec.t: Esports performance depends on precise and adaptable sensorimotor control (Jeong et al., 2026), yet objective assessment is often limited to task-specific performance scores. While such scores indicate success within a given task, they may not fully capture the structure of underlying motor control processes. Sample Entropy (SaEn) provides a nonlinear measure of movement regularity and has been used to detect subtle changes in sensorimotor and coordinative control across motor tasks (Gao et al., 2026; Wachholz et al., 2019). Therefore, SaEn might be used to evaluate the sensorimotor and coordinative control of high-and low-skilled esports players.

This study examined whether SaEn derived from mouse-movement time series differs between high- and low-skilled FPS players and whether SaEn is sensitive to task-specific demands such as difficulty and duration. We expected expertise-related differences in mouse-movement complexity and higher SaEn under more demanding task conditions.

Fifteen FPS players were categorized as high-skilled (top 20%; n = 8) or low-skilled (below top 50%; n = 7). Participants completed four randomized AimBooster conditions: 1-min moderate, 2-min moderate, 1-min hard, and 2-min hard. Each condition was repeated five times. Moderate trials spawned 2.5 targets/s, whereas hard trials spawned 3.0 targets/s. Continuous mouse-position data were recorded in MATLAB. For each trial, mouse-movement data were segmented using start and end markers, resampled to 15 Hz, and the final 20 seconds of each trial were extracted. SaEn was calculated for horizontal movement, vertical movement, movement speed, and combined x-y movement using m = 2, r = 0.20 × SD, and τ = 1. Linear mixed models were used to test effects of skill group, situation, trial order, and the Group × Situation interaction, with random intercepts for participants.

Across all SaEn outcomes, there was a consistent main effect of situation (all variables p <.001). Hard conditions showed higher entropy than moderate conditions, indicating more complex or less regular mouse-movement dynamics under increased task difficulty. This pattern was especially clear for combined x-y movement entropy, where post-hoc comparisons showed significantly higher SaEn in hard to moderate comparisons (p <.001), independent of time. In contrast, no significant main effect of skill group emerged, and the Group × Situation interaction was not significant. High-skilled players descriptively showed higher SaEn in several conditions, these differences were not statistically reliable.

SaEn appears to be more sensitive to task-specific demands than to skill group differences in this sample. In light of these points, SaEn has the potential to be used as a metric for evaluating and adjusting the difficulty in esports (e.g., balancing). In esports, the standardized indicators for evaluating difficulty have yet to be established; SaEn may provide useful information about balancing in esports. Furthermore, since SaEn has been widely used to evaluate the complexity of human movement (Wachholz et al., 2019), it has the potential to understand the complex movements of esports players. Furthermore, it may be useful to evaluate both the mouse and keyboard movements to provide a better understanding of coordinative control across motor tasks in esports.

Mouse-movement entropy reflects changes in task difficulty during FPS aiming tasks, but did not reliably distinguish high- from low-skilled players. SaEn may therefore be valuable as an indicator of situational movement complexity rather than as an isolated marker of player expertise.

abstracts.title: Daily Adherence and Barriers to Physical Exercise in Esports Athletes: A 30-Day Diary Study
abstracts.by: Felix Wachholz, Benedikt Hösl and Thomas Astner, University of Innsbruck, Austria; Aleksander Groth, MCI - The Entrepreneurial School, Austria
abstracts.aus: Felix Wachholz, Benedikt Hösl, Thomas Astner and Aleksander Groth

sec.t: Balancing structured positive effects of physical exercise (PE) (Warburton & Bredin, 2017) with intensive esports practice, could play a central role to the future sustainability of competitive gaming (McNulty et al., 2021). Translating intentions into action might hinge on dynamic self-regulation rather than static traits (Schwarzer et al., 2011), underscoring the need for within-person designs and process-oriented approaches in esports contexts.

This study examined i) the extent to which semi-professional esports athletes adhere to planned PE sessions over 30 days, ii) how situational barriers influence execution, and iii) how daily confidence and barriers predict within-person fluctuations in adherence.

Eighteen semi-professional players completed a 30-day diary while following a structured high-intensity interval training (HIIT) program (≥3 sessions/week, self-regulated intensity). Daily entries captured planned PE, completion (full/partial vs. none), barriers (multiple selections), prospective confidence (1–10), and other physical activity. Analyses focused on days with planned sessions. Generalized linear mixed models with random intercepts for participants tested daily adherence, decomposing confidence into within- and between-person components to isolate day-level from person-level effects.

Participants planned 239 sessions and completed 114, yielding 47.7% adherence with substantial within- and between-person variability. The final model showed that both within-person and between-person confidence predicted a higher likelihood of session completion. Adding situational barriers significantly improved fit. Time constraints markedly reduced adherence odds (OR = 0.27) as well as illness (OR = 0.19) Work/study obligations showed a negative trend. Sensitivity analyses with lagged adherence corroborated the robustness of confidence and time constraints as primary predictors.

To strengthen daily self-regulatory capacity, building task-specific self-efficacy and developing concrete barrier-coping strategies during the volitional phase of behavior change should be focused, to translate intentions into action. At the same time structural frictions should be reduced by offering flexible, short sessions and aligning PE with existing esports routines to ease time constraints and competing obligations. PE was in general rated positively by the participants.

Adherence to structured PE in semi-professional esports is driven primarily by day-level confidence and situational barriers rather than stable person-level characteristics. Within-person approaches reveal that enhancing prospective confidence and reducing time-related obstacles are high-yield levers for consistent PE engagement. These insights inform how clubs and practitioners can bridge tradition (intense in-game practice) with tomorrow’s integrated performance models by embedding adaptable, self-regulation–oriented PE within esports training ecosystems.
