abstracts.by: Felix Wachholz, Lukas Graiff, Julia Staudegger and Elisabeth Happ, University of Innsbruck, Austria
abstracts.aus: Felix Wachholz, Lukas Graiff, Julia Staudegger and Elisabeth Happ

sec.t: Generation Alpha is growing up in a highly digitalized environment in which gaming, artificial intelligence, interactive media, and esports are increasingly embedded in everyday leisure experiences (Stylos & Bellou, 2025; Thompson et al., 2022). At the same time, traditional winter tourism destinations face the challenge of remaining attractive to young future guests. Understanding how children imagine a future ski holiday can provide valuable insights for the development of child-centered, innovative, and digitally enhanced tourism products (Poria & Timothy, 2014; Rhoden et al., 2016).

This exploratory study investigates how children of Generation Alpha envision future ski holidays, focusing on the role of digital assets, digital activities, and gaming- and esports-related elements. The aim is to identify which types of experiences are perceived as attractive by children and how these preferences can inform the design of future ski tourism offerings.

A child-friendly pre-study questionnaire was developed in which children evaluated AI-generated images using a five-point smiley scale. The images represented four categories: ski world, ski school, hotel, and youth room. Within these categories, the images included traditional ski-related settings, digital assets and activities as well as elements with gaming and esports reference. After data cleaning, the final sample consisted of 963 valid responses. For analysis and subsequent game design, two age groups were formed: children aged 6-10 and children aged 11-16. Based on age-specific preferences and asset rankings by mean values, a mobile game is being developed as a fully gamified questionnaire. The selectable assets differ slightly between the two age versions to match children’s expressed interests.

The pre-study provides initial evidence that Generation Alpha does not perceive ski holidays solely as traditional winter sport experiences, but as hybrid leisure environments combining skiing, play, digital interaction, and social spaces. Preliminary factor-analytical approaches suggest the emergence of different ski holiday types among children. For example, “Adventurers” show a strong interest in skiing-related experiences such as ski cross, forest trails, and fun parks, while “Gamers” are attracted by gaming and esports-related assets such as gaming gondolas, ski game apps, or ski goggles with live performance data.

The findings offer practical guidance for ski resorts, hotels, ski schools, and destination managers seeking to develop future-oriented products for young guests. Digital assets should not simply be added as isolated entertainment features, but should be meaningfully connected to the physical ski holiday experience. The identified preference patterns can support more targeted product development, such as adventure-based ski areas, digitally enhanced learning tools, interactive youth rooms, and gaming and esports-inspired social spaces. Furthermore, the gamified survey approach demonstrates how research with children could be designed in a playful, engaging, and methodologically appropriate way.

This study contributes to a better understanding of Generation Alpha’s expectations of future ski holidays. The results indicate that digitalization may play an important role in shaping attractive winter tourism experiences for children. By combining survey-based insights with a gamified research design, the study provides both theoretical and practical foundations for developing more childcentered, innovative, and future-ready ski tourism offerings.

abstracts.title: Distinct Health Profiles Among Esports Players: A Latent Profile Analysis of Health Indicators and Health-Related Behaviors
abstracts.by: Alexandra Ziegeldorf, Friedrich Schiller University Jena, Germany; Nina Hottenrott and Lara Wunsch, Leipzig University, Germany; Vasileios Barkoukis, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece; Leonidas Karaiskos, KEA Fair Play Code, Greece; Tobias Scholz, University of Agder, Norway; Matthew Watson, German Sport University Cologne, Germany; Oliver Leis, Leipzig University, Germany
abstracts.aus: Alexandra Ziegeldorf, Nina Hottenrott, Lara Wunsch, Vasileios Barkoukis, Leonidas Karaiskos, Tobias Scholz, Matthew Watson and Oliver Leis

sec.t: Esports has become a major competitive and recreational activity worldwide, making players’ health an increasingly important research topic. Previous studies have typically focused on isolated health indicators such as physical activity, sleep, or mental health, providing only a fragmented understanding of esports players’ health.
The present study aimed to identify distinct health profiles among esports players by simultaneously considering multiple health indicators and health-related behaviors.

A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 413 esports players (83.5% male; M_age = 24.0 years, SD = 7.3) from 48 countries. Variables included body mass index (BMI), physical activity (Godin Leisure-Time Exercise Questionnaire), smoking behavior, alcohol consumption, depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-9), sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index), and perceived social support (Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support). These indicators were selected to represent multiple dimensions of physical, mental, behavioral, and social health. Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) was applied to identify subgroups of players with similar health characteristics. Subsequently, profiles were compared with regard to demographic and esports-related characteristics, including age, gender, competition level, geographical region (Europe vs. non-Europe), and esports genre.

A four-profile solution provided the best balance of statistical fit, interpretability, and profile size. The identified profiles were labeled as (1) Psychologically vulnerable (19.6%), (2) Average health (37.8%), (3) Healthy and active (28.6%), and (4) Behavioral risk (14.0%). Profiles differed significantly across all health indicators and health-related behaviors (all p <.01). The largest between-profile differences were observed for smoking behavior (η² =.869), depressive symptoms (η² =.287), alcohol consumption (η² =.169), and perceived social support (η² =.138). Compared with all other profiles, the Healthy and active profile reported the lowest depressive symptoms (M = 2.74, SD = 2.33), the lowest alcohol consumption (M = 0.07, SD = 0.25), the highest perceived social support (M = 6.02, SD = 0.71), and the lowest BMI (M = 23.0, SD = 3.04). In contrast, the Behavioral risk profile was characterized by substantially elevated smoking behavior (M = 5.64, SD = 1.88). Notably, the Psychologically vulnerable and Healthy and active profiles reported similarly high levels of physical activity but differed markedly in depressive symptoms, sleep quality, social support, alcohol consumption, and BMI. Furthermore, profile membership differed significantly according to age, gender, and esports genre, but not by competition level.

Health promotion in esports should be guided by multidimensional screening that captures combined physical, mental, behavioral, and social health patterns. Such screening may help practitioners, teams, and esports organizations identify distinct support needs and tailor interventions more effectively. This is particularly important because players with similar physical activity levels may still differ substantially in depressive symptoms, sleep quality, social support, BMI, and substance-related behaviors.

The findings indicate that esports players are not a homogeneous population regarding health and health-related behaviors. The identified profiles highlight the coexistence of both protective and risk-related health patterns and suggest that single indicators, such as physical activity, provide only a limited understanding of players’ broader health status.

abstracts.title: Do Generative AI and Esports Mix: A Look at the Student-Athlete Perspective
abstracts.by: Michael Cassens, University of Montana, United States of America

sec.t: Generative AI (gen AI) has become increasingly ubiquitous in everyday culture, permeating students’ academic and professional lives. It has emerged as a lightning rod issue, with public perception shifting notably in recent years. The 2025 Stanford HAI AI Index Report notes a particularly pronounced divergence in the United States, where a majority of the public perceives AI as posing high societal risk, while far fewer recognize its potential benefits (Maslej et al., 2025). Growing negative sentiment, amplified by social media, network television, and mainstream news outlets, continues to shape public opinion and may also influence student-athletes (Ryazanov, Öhman, and Björklund, 2025). Esports, as a rapidly evolving discipline at the intersection of technology and competition, is not immune to this phenomenon. Esports athletes are aware of generative AI, especially for game analysis and skill training, which has led to competing viewpoints. (Lancaster, et al., 2025). However, there is a gap in understanding how genAI has been used in game design and how that has affected player experiences and sentiment.
This study examined whether esports student-athletes’ perceptions of Generative AI shifted depending on their combined knowledge of their game and Generative AI.

An anonymous Qualtrics survey, which took approximately 5-10 minutes to complete, was distributed. The quantitative questions were presented across three domains: their knowledge of and comfort with their esports title; their knowledge, comfort level, and understanding of the ethical use of Generative AI; and their awareness of the integration of Generative AI within their specific title, using a 5-point Likert-style choice spanning from strongly disagree to agree strongly. Qualitative responses were aggregated and analyzed for any common themes.

The results of this small study were compelling among the 26 competitive and non-competitive participants in the esports program at the University of Montana. All major titles were represented, including Fortnite, League of Legends, Marvel Rivals, Rocket League, Overwatch 2, and Valorant, with Overwatch 2 having the highest response rate. Over 83% of student-athletes felt confident explaining what Generative AI is; over 80% felt they could explain it to others; 73% felt confident assessing its ethical use; and over 73% had personally used it. However, knowledge of the implementation of Generative AI in their specific games was far more evenly distributed between those who knew what had been integrated into their title and those who did not. This result revealed an awareness gap among the student-athletes. This gap is notable given that many esports titles have integrated AI and Generative AI over the past several years for bot generation, asset creation, and concept development (Lai, 2023). Despite strong general AI literacy, a majority of respondents expressed negative or strongly negative views toward the use of Generative AI in their titles, contradicting the study’s initial hypothesis that greater knowledge would be associated with a more favorable outlook. The central trend became fairly distinct upon analysis. Awareness of Generative AI use in their game correlated with a negative reaction to it. Qualitative responses reinforced this trend. Students cited environmental impact and copyright concerns related to training datasets as primary drivers of skepticism, mirroring broader public discourse and validating the study’s connection to population-level sentiment.

This research aims to inform developers, publishers, and industry leaders, such as Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, who predicts that AI will be used in nearly all video games in the future (Thibaut, 2025), that end-users, particularly competitive student-athletes, may not view continued Generative AI integration favorably. There should be more discussions and continued awareness as esports titles are developed and evolve. Improved communication could help connect more deeply with esports athletes, fostering greater affinity and loyalty.

As the industry accelerates adoption of these tools, understanding the perspective of collegiate competitors is both timely and essential. Student-athletes can be some of the strongest advocates for a title, especially given the sport’s growth, and this early study could reveal indicators that could help shape the direction of a company, making it more consumer-focused.

abstracts.title: Equality Work in Esports: Between Inclusion, Tokenism, and Structural Change
abstracts.by: Finja Walsdorff, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Germany

sec.t: Despite its rapid growth and increasing professionalization, esports remains a heavily male-dominated field. Research on gender in competitive gaming has consistently highlighted the underrepresentation of women and traced it to structural barriers including exclusionary cultures, gendered harassment, and restricted access to professional networks (Taylor 2012; Ruotsalainen and Friman 2018; Darvin et al. 2021). In response, a range of actors within the esports ecosystem—including publishers, organizations, leagues, and grassroots initiatives—have introduced measures intended to improve gender equality and participation. These include female-only tournaments, targeted development programs, diversity policies, and awareness campaigns aimed at creating safer and more inclusive environments. Existing research suggests that equality initiatives in esports often remain limited in scope and fail to address the structural conditions that reproduce gender inequality (Friman et al. 2023; Piggott 2025).

While gender inequality in esports has been widely studied, far less attention has been paid to how equality work itself is framed, implemented, and experienced in practice. In this presentation, equality work refers to the institutional practices, policies, and interventions through which organizations seek to reduce structural inequalities and improve the participation of marginalized groups. Following Ahmed (2012), it is understood as an ongoing institutional process in which formal commitments to equality must be translated into organizational practice through continuous reflection, negotiation, and adaptation, rather than being treated as problems solved by formal policies alone. The presentation examines how equality work is articulated within contemporary esports cultures and how female players are positioned within these dynamics. It asks how esports organizations and equality initiatives attempt to address gender inequality, and to what extent these efforts challenge—or reproduce—existing power relations within the field.

The presentation draws on a qualitative study of the German esports scenes surrounding Counter-Strike, League of Legends, and Valorant. The study combines ethnographic fieldwork with semi-structured, in-depth interviews conducted with 18 female esports players and 5 industry experts. Ethnographic data were collected through participant observation at esports events as well as observations of digital community spaces. Interview transcripts and field materials were analyzed using a qualitative, inductive coding approach to identify recurring themes and patterns across the data.

The empirical findings indicate that equality work frequently operates in an ambivalent space between inclusion and symbolic representation. In some cases, female players become visible representatives of diversity within organizations while continuing to face unequal competitive conditions. Such dynamics may produce tokenistic forms of inclusion that primarily serve the reputational interests of organizations and sponsors rather than transforming underlying power relations (Blanco, 2024).

Understanding the ambivalent effects of equality work is crucial for developing more effective strategies to promote gender equality in esports. By identifying tensions, blind spots, and unintended consequences of existing initiatives, the study highlights areas where equality measures could move beyond symbolic inclusion toward more substantive structural change.

This study argues that equality work in esports is characterized by a fundamental ambivalence: while such initiatives may create new opportunities for participation, visibility, and support, they often remain symbolic and struggle to transform the structural hierarchies that marginalize women. Beyond the German context, the findings offer insights for equality efforts in other emerging esports ecosystems. As regions with developing professional infrastructures explore ways of building more inclusive competitive environments, the experiences of more established scenes may provide valuable points of reference for identifying both effective practices and persistent challenges.

abstracts.title: Esports and Mental Health: A Critical Realist Account
abstracts.by: Tom Brock, Manchester Metropolitan University, United Kingdom

sec.t: What is it about the social configuration of esports that generates positive and negative experiences of mental health? Research on esports and mental health continues to count the symptoms of psychological distress whilst prescribing clinical interventions on players’ behaviour (Kegelaers et al., 2025; Poulus & Sharpe, 2025; Poulus et al., 2026; Poulus & Rice, 2026). Yet, this research has not asked how the social configurations of competitive gaming - the norms, roles and relationships - generate distress in the first place. Rates of stress, anxiety, depression and burnout are properties of social relations, not of the individuals that report them, and so require a sociological account (also see Brock, 2017; Brock, 2021). This requires a meta-theoretical framework treating competitive gaming as a setting that affords players autonomy, recognition, even escapism whilst generating harms that undermine them.

Bhaskar’s (1998 [1978], 2008 [1975]) critical realism and Archer and Donati’s (2015) relational sociology provide the groundwork for developing a new meta-theoretical framework for examining esports and mental health.

Examining the theoretical foundations of the social science of esports means asking what social reality is and what counts as explaining it (Brock, 2025). This paper turns that ontology toward a different problem. Drawing on Archer and Donati’s (2015) relational sociology, it asks why psychological accounts of esports mental health treat individual experience as separable from the relational contexts that produce it. It argues for two concepts from Archer and Donati (2015): ‘relational goods’ and ‘relational evils’. These are qualities emerging from social interactions that cannot be reduced to individual characteristics. Through a focus on men’s mental health and masculinity within games (Connell and Messerschmidt, 2005; also Meriläinen et al., 2026), the paper applies this framework to ask how esports shapes wellbeing.

The social relations that deliver belonging, recognition, mastery - psychological wellbeing - in esports also produce exploitation, exclusion, and burnout. This paradox, also identified by Kegelaers et al. (2025), is made intelligible by the ‘relational goods’ and ‘evils’ framework. Research must map how these ‘goods’ and ‘evils’ emerge from the interplay of players’ concerns, reflexive tendencies, and the structural and cultural conditions of competitive gaming. The result is an understanding of esports players’ mental health as relationally generated. As a case study, the paper considers what happens when relational evils dominate, and the implications for player mental health.

Mental health in esports is a structural-relational problem that requires a better understanding of the ‘goods’ and ‘evils’ within social configurations, whether these be team cultures, organisational practices, game architectures, or just competitive norms. The extent to which they generate harm (or not) requires a careful understanding of structure, culture and agency. This holistic approach has implications for how esports organisations, governing bodies and mental health practitioners conceptualise and respond to player wellbeing.

This paper demonstrates the value of meta-theoretical work for a research field that has, thus far, proceeded without it - namely, the need to situate claims about mental health within broader social and cultural conditions.

abstracts.title: Esports and the State: Media Framing of Government Involvement Across Economic, Nationalist, and Soft Power Rhetoric
abstracts.by: Claudia Loomis, University of California, Davis, United States of America

sec.t: Governments worldwide have increasingly engaged with esports through legislation, development initiatives, and public sponsorship. While political scientists have examined state investment in traditional sports as a vehicle for soft power, nationalism, and economic development, similar dynamics in esports remain understudied. As esports has grown into a multi-billion-dollar global industry, states are deploying it as a site of public investment, sportswashing, censorship, and cultural diplomacy. Yet the public discourse legitimating this engagement has not been systematically analyzed.

This study investigates how government involvement in esports is publicly framed and legitimated across media sources, and which rationales dominate across different political regimes, regions, and time periods.

This project uses a corpus of newsletters, newswires and press releases, newspapers, web-based publications, and news transcripts sourced from Nexis Uni (2018–2025). The corpus includes 894 documents, assembled using a Boolean search, which systematically aims to identify texts that address the intersection of esports-specific terms (such as “esport”, “electronic sport”, “competitive gaming”, etc.) with government involvement in policy, regulation, and strategic initiatives. The objective of this search is to capture comprehensive coverage where esports is framed within the context of formal government engagement, encompassing both regulatory oversight and proactive support measures. Three complementary quantitative text analysis approaches were applied: raw token frequency using a validated custom dictionary of economic, nationalist, and image-based justification frames; tf-idf weighted analysis to assess document-level framing salience; and keyword-in-context (KWIC) filtering to isolate esports-proximate language. Cross-national comparisons drew on the IMD 2024 World Digital Competitiveness Ranking, the V-Dem Political Regime Index, and the 2025 Global Soft Power Index.

Economic rationales dominate esports policy discourse across all three analytical approaches, comprising approximately 2.5–3% of corpus tokens versus under 1% each for image-based and nationalist frames. This dominance is statistically robust and persists over time, with regression models explaining 64–93% of variance. Contrary to expectations, neither national digital strategy status nor political regime type significantly predicts framing variation. Counterintuitively, countries without strong cultural agendas exhibited significantly higher nationalist framing than those with established nation-branding strategies, a finding likely attributable to country classification limitations.

For esports industry stakeholders and policymakers, these findings suggest that economic justifications are the primary mode of government legitimation in this sector globally, regardless of regime type. This has implications for how esports organizations engage with public funding actors and how researchers should interpret media discourse around government esports development initiatives.

This study positions esports as a legitimate arena of political power and public investment, demonstrating that the framing strategies through which state engagement with traditional sports is publicly legitimated extend meaningfully into esports. Economic rationales consistently dominate, while nationalist and soft power framing play secondary roles. Future research should examine official legislative texts and governmental statements to more precisely capture state-level esports rhetoric

abstracts.title: Esports athletes’ experiences and perceptions of the menstrual cycle in training and competition: an international interview study
abstracts.by: Riley Dunn and Selen Türkay, Queensland University of Technology, Australia; Rebecca Wong, University of Putra Malaysia, Malaysia; Mitchell Nicholson, Geoffrey Minett, Daniel Johnson and Craig McNulty, Queensland University of Technology, Australia
abstracts.aus: Riley Dunn, Selen Türkay, Rebecca Wong, Mitchell Nicholson, Geoffrey Minett, Daniel Johnson and Craig McNulty

sec.t: Across sports athletes, the menstrual cycle is demonstrated to impact training quality, absenteeism, and competitive preparedness due to physical and psychological symptoms (Brown et al., 2021; Bruinvels et al., 2021; Chica-Latorre et al., 2025). Female athletes also report varied comfort in discussing their menstrual health with male coaches, despite the acknowledged impact to training. (Brown et al., 2021; van den Berg & Doyle-Baker, 2024) Given parallels in training environments between sports and esports (e.g. Bonnar et al. (2019) and Jenny et al. (2017)), the menstrual cycle may similarly impact women/female esports athletes. To date, the menstrual cycle has not been empirically investigated amongst esports populations. As such, this work seeks to provide an initial insight to women/female esports athletes’ experiences regarding their menstrual health across international perspectives.
To explore esports athletes’ experiences, opinions, and knowledge regarding their menstrual cycle in formal training and competitive environments across international contexts.

Semi-structured interviews were conducted over Discord with 20 participants (median age [years] = 23) across Malaysia (n=11), Australia (n=2), New Zealand (n=2), Germany (n=2), North America (n=2), and Indonesia (n=1). Convenience and targeted sampling were used to recruit esports athletes with competitive experience in international (n=10), national (n=9), and local (n=1) tournaments of mostly MOBA (n=18) titles (n=2 FPS). All participants were naturally menstruating, except one who was using long-acting contraception with regular withdrawal bleeds. Interviews were conducted in either English language (by one author: RD, n=12) or Bahasa Malay (by one author: RW, n=8). RW also transcribed and translated interviews from Bahasa Malay to English for analysis. Reflexive thematic analysis was undertaken according to Braun and Clarke’s (2021) guidance using inductive coding informed by a social constructivist paradigm.

Preliminary coding identified three candidate themes: 1. Menstrual symptoms shaped perceived readiness and engagement for training and competition, with participants describing pain, headaches, fatigue, and changes in emotional regulation associated with the pre-menstrual and menstrual phases. Participants also described positive changes that supported performance, such as assertiveness and aggression. 2. Disclosure was shaped by team culture and coach gender, with participants more comfortable discussing menstrual timing in women’s teams than with men/male coaches. The perceived maturity and knowledge of men/male coaches may moderate players’ openness to discuss menstrual health in training and competition contexts. 3. Menstrual tracking was seen as potentially useful but ethically sensitive, with concerns about coach knowledge, privacy, stigma, and possible misuse of cycle-related information.

Esports athletes may require support in managing the impact of their menstrual cycle on training engagement and competition. Targeted training to increase coaches’ awareness of the menstrual cycle may facilitate discussion to support and adapt women’s training environments. Input from interdisciplinary stakeholders, including players, is needed to explore the ethical and useful implementation of menstrual tracking in esports. Players may benefit from personal cycle and symptom tracking to understand how their menstrual patterns may shape training readiness, effectiveness, and competition preparedness in the absence of evidence-based guidance.

Our findings will be the first to explore esports athletes’ perceptions of the impact of the menstrual cycle in training and competitive environments. Further empirical attention is needed to equitably promote women’s esports performance development through targeted, culturally sensitive health initiatives.

abstracts.title: Esports Hit the Big Time: What organisational and reputational problems face Esports in the emerging context of authoritarian capitalism and sporting mega-events?
abstracts.by: Rory Summerley, London South Bank University, United Kingdom

sec.t: This paper answers several questions initially raised by the (now-cancelled) Olympic Esports Games 2027. The Games were, arguably, an opportunity to forward the global reputation of esports broadly, but its cancellation, this paper argues, highlights two possible approaches to global esports that are already emerging: their incorporation into sporting mega-events, and their colonisation by authoritarian capitalist investment.

The situation presents various problems and risks that result in several questions that this paper explores including: •What considerations behind the choice of games played (IOC Media, 2024); at sporting mega events are there and what do they reveal? •How will the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s authoritarian capitalist economic policy (Ettinger, 2023) and investment in esports affect the global participation, motivations, and decisions of esports stakeholders regarding upcoming events? •How will esports’ presence in authoritarian capitalist investment portfolios and at sporting mega-events affect the global reputation of esports with respect to the values of different stakeholders?

The problems these questions raise have both organisational and ultimately reputational dimensions and so the paper aims to provide a commentary by case study analysis and literature review of the relevant stakeholders, culture, and history of esports’ integration into larger non-esports bodies; using reputation theory to guide the discussion.

The result so far is that the IOC are considered out of touch with contemporary esports practice and communities, at its worst has been outright corrupt (Fudge, 2023). Like other Olympic inclusions such as extreme sports or the Youth Olympic Games, both intended to attract a younger audience (Prüschenk and Kurscheidt, 2017), the trade-off for esports organisations and the IOC would seem to be mutually beneficial. However, the IOC are perceived as incompetent, if comparatively palatable in comparison to KSA. KSA’s capital investment can support esports very well and its experience running esports events at scale is comparatively competent. However, KSA’s problem stems from the authoritarian nature of its capital driven by national policy which seeks ownership and limited negotiation of the use of its funds, alongside the problematic nature of its human rights history; it is less palatable.

Unresolved questions about the structure and governance of esports at both the national level and for individual games and their communities currently face esports communities everywhere. Authoritarian capitalist investment and sporting mega-events complicate this further. The criteria for deciding what games might be played or supported become bound up in problems relating to corruption, ownership, and exclusion and the tolerance of esports communities for these problems.

The paper addresses the issues noted above, highlighting potential benefits and risks along the way. Conclusions about the future of the global representation of esports outside of ‘native’ esports events veer pessimistic in the short term as esports communities have little bargaining power. The power of these external groups magnifies risks toward esports groups moving forward. In the face of the investment of such large, interested parties, there is no choice but to consider how they will shape esports.

abstracts.title: Establishing a Legal Framework for Esports Between Sport Law and Hybrid Governance: The Lithuanian Case
abstracts.by: Vilius Lapis, Mykolas Romeris University, Lithuania

sec.t: Lithuania has national sport regulation governing organised sport, but esports is not clearly situated within it. Esports-related issues are therefore addressed through scattered rules of private and public law, including contract, intellectual property, consumer protection, gambling and digital regulation. This creates a practical regulatory question: should esports remain governed mainly by general law, be incorporated into existing sport regulation, be regulated through a separate esports-specific act, or be addressed through hybrid governance? Answering it requires distinguishing sports law as a broader legal field, lex sportiva as private and transnational sporting norms, and national sport regulation as the state-based framework governing organised sport.

This paper assesses which regulatory approach would be most suitable for Lithuania. It examines three models: a separate esports-specific act, amendment of existing Lithuanian sport regulation to include esports fully or partially within the national sport framework, and a hybrid model combining general legal rules, limited sector-specific provisions, soft law, co-regulation and private governance. Rather than treating a separate esports act as lex specialis in the strict doctrinal sense, the paper examines whether Lithuania needs a targeted regulatory layer that would complement existing general and special legal rules without displacing them.

The research is based on doctrinal, comparative and regulatory model analysis. It examines Lithuanian legal sources, selected foreign approaches, European Union frameworks and literature on esports law, sports law, lex sportiva and esports governance. It is also informed by the author’s teaching, prior research on Lithuanian sport legislation and ongoing doctoral research on esports legal regulation.

The preliminary findings suggest that a separate esports act could provide visibility, definitions and institutional clarity, but may create risks of rigidity, duplication and rapid obsolescence. Incorporation into national sport regulation could strengthen recognition and institutional coordination, but may not fully reflect the private, commercial and digital structure of esports, including publisher control, intellectual property dependence and platform-based competition. A hybrid model appears more suitable because it allows public authorities to set minimum safeguards while leaving technical rules, competition formats and industry practices to private governance, co-regulation and transnational standards.

The Lithuanian case may assist jurisdictions seeking to regulate esports without rigid legislation. A layered approach could support legal certainty and institutional coherence while recognising public authorities, publishers, organisers, teams, players and platforms.

The paper argues that Lithuanian esports regulation should not depend solely on a separate esports law or direct incorporation into national sport regulation. A hybrid model offers a balanced approach combining minimum legal safeguards with regulatory flexibility and sensitivity to sports law, lex sportiva, national sport regulation and digital platform-based governance.

abstracts.title: Establishing the World Esports Artificial Intelligence (AI) Ethics Guidelines
abstracts.by: Seth E. Jenny, Slippery Rock University of Pennsylvania, United States of America

sec.t: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into esports training and competition has created significant opportunities for performance optimization, player development, accessibility, and operational efficiency. However, these advancements also introduce complex ethical risks related to fairness, competitive integrity, privacy, and safety. As AI systems increasingly influence gameplay preparation, in-game decision-making, and event management, concerns have emerged regarding the potential erosion of core human elements in esports, including skill, teamwork, and strategic thinking. In response to these challenges, the World Esports AI Ethics Guidelines (Jenny & Pastore, 2025) were developed to provide a structured, globally relevant framework for responsible AI use.

The purpose of this research was to establish World Esports AI Guidelines through critical stakeholder input. The primary research question guiding the project was: What are ethical and unethical uses of AI in esports training and competition?

A two-phase mixed-method, cross-sectional design was employed. Phase 1 involved an online survey of 161 esports, gaming, and AI professionals from 28 countries, recruited through purposive and snowball sampling. The survey collected both quantitative and qualitative data on perceptions of ethical and unethical AI use in esports, forming the basis of a preliminary guidelines draft. Phase 2 utilized a modified Delphi method with a panel of 18 international esports experts from 9 countries to refine and validate the guidelines. Across both phases, quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative responses underwent iterative thematic analysis, including open, axial, and selective coding (Lune & Berg, 2017). Final guidelines were produced through structured consensus-building, integrating empirical findings, expert insights, and alignment with relevant literature and legal frameworks.

The final framework consists of 27 guidelines, including 10 general guidelines applicable to both training and competition, 6 training-specific guidelines, and 11 competition-specific guidelines. Key findings highlight the importance of transparency, informed consent, equitable access, and privacy protection in AI use. The guidelines also emphasize preventing unfair competitive advantages, maintaining human oversight, and ensuring compliance with competition rules and legal standards. Context-specific considerations address issues such as cheating prevention, access to analytics tools, broadcasting enhancements, accessibility features, and event management systems. Supporting materials, including illustrative use cases, an implementation checklist, and an enforcement matrix, were developed to facilitate practical application.

The guidelines provide actionable, flexible recommendations for esports stakeholders, including players, teams, organizers, and governing bodies. By offering clear examples of acceptable and unacceptable AI use, along with implementation tools, the framework supports informed decision-making and ethical governance. The proposed establishment of a World Esports AI Ethics Officer Consortium further underscores the need for coordinated oversight and ongoing dialogue across the global esports ecosystem.

The World Esports AI Ethics Guidelines establish a foundational framework for ethical AI integration in esports. They reinforce the principle that AI should augment, not undermine, human agency, fairness, and competitive integrity. As AI technologies and esports evolve, ongoing evaluation and refinement of these guidelines will be essential to maintaining trust, protecting competitive integrity, and ensuring sustainable growth within the esports industry.

abstracts.title: From Esport to Educated?: Describing Esports Participants’ Academic Areas of Focus and Directions for Professional Development
abstracts.by: Amanda Cote, Michigan State University, United States of America; Shane Burrell, Chestnut Health Systems, United States of America; Maxwell Foxman, University of Oregon, United States of America; Brandon Harris, University of Alabama, United States of America; Jeffrey Fricke-Waters, Michigan State University, United States of America
abstracts.aus: Amanda Cote, Shane Burrell, Maxwell Foxman, Brandon Harris and Jeffrey Fricke-Waters

sec.t: As collegiate esports become a mainstay on campuses, advocates suggest that program participation can benefit students’ academic and professional development. Anecdotally, collegiate esports programs synergize with STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math), but only some introductory work (Jenny et al., 2025) has addressed this link empirically. This relationship needs to be investigated further, as there is a pressing need for greater student support in STEM. Despite high student interest, STEM education features low graduation rates, slow or costly paths to graduation, and ongoing disparities for women, unrepresented minorities, students with disabilities, and first-gen students (Hatfield et al., 2022; National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine, 2016; National Center for Education Statistics, 2024). Many universities are turning to esports programs to help, as extracurricular activities can improve students’ sense of belonging, social support, and other factors that predict graduation likelihood (Hansen et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025; Slovacek et al., 2019). Additionally, students perceive esports as related to learning (Zhong et al., 2024) and researchers have illuminated this connection theoretically (Andersen et al., 2024), but empirical connections between esports participation and STEM success remain underexplored.

This project therefore aims to 1) describe the state of STEM education at schools with collegiate esports programs and 2) empirically investigate connections between esports participation and STEM interest/enrollment.

First, we combined publicly available data from the IPEDS (2022- 2023) and College Score Card (2022- 2023) with collegiate esports census data (Sonner et al., 2024) to create a visual dashboard comparing student educational outcomes. Second, we are conducting a short survey of program directors to determine which academic programs their esports players are enrolled in.

Our initial data visualization provides statistical representation of STEM graduation rates among schools with esports programs. It highlights the clear need for greater STEM support. Schools’ STEM completion rates remain low overall, with some in single digit percentages. Further investigation of the visualization will determine which schools have the lowest graduation rates and help tailor interventions based on their needs. Additionally, we expect survey data to identify connections between esports and STEM interest. If students are predominantly majoring in STEM areas, as anticipated, esports programs can effectively engage in field-specific forms of support; if findings point instead to a wider range of majors, community- or support-oriented interventions may be more effective.

This research will lay the foundation for future explorations of esports’ effects on student academic achievement and career trajectories. It will also help program directors build professional development initiatives that support students’ real interests and needs. Given the anecdotal connections between esports and STEM, program directors are likely tailoring resources towards these areas. If, however, students are enrolled in a wider array of degrees, such as arts and humanities, programs should focus more on community-building, sense of belonging, and other factors that relate to academic persistence, rather than providing narrower student support.
We anticipate completing data visualization and the initial survey by mid-summer and look forward to presenting detailed findings at ERNC2026.

abstracts.title: From Ping to Proximity: Measuring and Improving Discord Community Connection with the Zero Latency Framework
abstracts.by: Jorrel Batac, SXNGA / Project Moonlight, United States of America; Bethany Pyles, ctrlPause / Project Moonlight, United States of America; Rachel Lehrer, Community Advocates / Project Moonlight, United States of America; Caroline Hayes, Equimundo / Project Moonlight, United States of America
abstracts.aus: Jorrel Batac, Bethany Pyles, Rachel Lehrer and Caroline Hayes

sec.t: Online communities—especially those organized around esports—rely on volunteer and semi-professional moderators to maintain trust, a sense of belonging, and safety. Yet most moderation systems are oriented toward enforcing rules, managing toxicity detection, or incidents, rather than the relational work through which communities become healthier over time (Kowert & Noel, 2025). Building on research on online masculinities, healthier digital connection, and moderator archetypes, Project Moonlight proposes that community health should be understood not only as the absence of harm, but as the presence of measurable connection (Equimundo, 2021; Equimundo, 2024; Equimundo, 2025; Kowert & Noel, 2025; Lomanowska & Guitton, 2016).

We introduce Zero Latency, a measurement-and-intervention framework for Discord communities that translates observable relational behaviors into a single, longitudinal “ping-like” score (0–999ms; lower is better) intended for within-community tracking. The framework asks: (1) Can prosocial and repair-oriented behaviors in chat be operationalized as indicators of connection quality? and (2) Can moderator-led rituals and interventions produce detectable shifts in these indicators over time? This approach draws from Equimundo’s work on men’s connection, belonging, and pathways toward healthier online contexts, as well as Kowert’s Discord moderator research identifying distinct moderator roles and support needs (Equimundo, 2021; Equimundo, 2024; Equimundo, 2025; Kowert & Noel, 2025; Kim et al., 2025).

Zero Latency models connection across five domains: Clear Comms, Tilt Control, Locked In, Clutch, and Respawn. These domains capture behaviors such as welcoming, help-seeking, curiosity, emotional regulation, encouragement, and repair after conflict. Discord messages are classified into behavior categories and aggregated into domain-level indicators; scores are normalized against “healthy community” targets, adjusted for sample size, and penalized for toxicity to avoid masking harm under high activity. We evaluated the framework in live deployments across six Discord communities, pairing dashboard measurement with moderator-designed interventions such as reflection prompts, community nights, and failure-reframing activities, consistent with research emphasizing moderators as community stewards whose functions extend beyond rule enforcement (Kowert & Noel, 2025).

Across a multi-month cohort window from February to May 2026, computed on the complete dataset of captured messages in the measured channels/time windows across participating communities, we observed several promising patterns: toxicity suppression in multiple weeks, emergence of deeper relational behaviors in communities where they had previously been rare or absent, and increases in signals pointing toward growth mindset following interventions designed to normalize emotional risk and recovery. These findings suggest that moderators can use behavioral feedback loops not only to identify problems, but to cultivate desired forms of participation, including the kinds of healthier connection and belonging emphasized in Equimundo’s digital-solutions work (Equimundo, 2024).

Zero Latency offers moderators, esports organizers, and platform stakeholders a practical way to connect community rituals with measurable changes in relational dynamics. Rather than treating moderation as reactive control, the framework positions moderators as designers of social conditions that support belonging, resilience, and psychological safety—a framing aligned with moderator archetype research and Equimundo’s evidence-based approaches to transforming norms and strengthening care-centered forms of masculinity (Equimundo, 2025; Kowert & Noel, 2025).

This work demonstrates a pathway from raw chat data to a moderator-facing, intervention-ready measure of connection quality in esports-adjacent online communities. We address methodological considerations regarding behavior definitions, model validation, and ethical governance, and outline next steps toward a reproducible evaluation across additional servers and platforms (Equimundo, 2021; Equimundo, 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Kowert & Noel, 2025; Lomanowska & Guitton, 2016; Project Moonlight, 2026).

abstracts.title: From Policy to Practice: Implementing Esports Integrity Measures at the 2025 IESF European Esports Championship
abstracts.by: Erika Riedl and Stefano Caneppele, University of Lausanne, Switzerland

sec.t: Integrity threats such as doping, e-doping (technological cheating), and match-fixing have become increasingly prominent in esports. Despite rapid industry growth, governance structures and integrity policies remain fragmented and underdeveloped. Empirical criminological research examining how these policies function in practice is scarce, particularly in live competitive settings.

This study investigates how esports integrity policies are implemented during a major international competition—the 2025 International Esports Federation (IESF) European Esports Championship. It aims to identify regulatory gaps, assess real-world enforcement, and generate evidence-based recommendations using a situational crime prevention (SCP) perspective.

A mixed-methods approach was employed. First, a desktop review analysed approximately 150 pages of IESF regulations, including anti-doping rules, competition rules, and codes of conduct. Second, participant observation was conducted during the championship finals in Pristina, Kosovo (July 2025). The researcher engaged in active observation and informal discussions with key stakeholders, including athletes, coaches, team managers, organisers, and federation officials. Data were analysed using the eSAFE Sport framework and interpreted through SCP theory, focusing on how opportunities for integrity violations are structured and mitigated.

The findings reveal significant gaps in both governance and implementation across all integrity domains. Anti-doping measures showed limited testing activity, a lack of publicly available testing statistics, and sanctions largely confined to IESF competitions, reducing their broader deterrent effect. Stakeholder perceptions suggest that substance use is more prevalent in online competitions than acknowledged by existing controls. E-doping emerged as a major concern, particularly in online settings where cheating was perceived as widespread. While offline safeguards—such as hardware checks, software verification, and device restrictions—reduced opportunities for cheating, the absence of systematic monitoring, continuous control mechanisms, and detection technologies leaves residual risks. Match-fixing risks appeared insufficiently addressed due to regulatory ambiguity, lack of clear definitions, limited stakeholder awareness of betting prohibitions, and the absence of betting market monitoring. Responsibility for detecting and sanctioning match manipulation remains unclear, with an overreliance on referees despite the complexity of such cases. Two criminological conundrums were identified: (1) technological cheating may serve both performance enhancement and betting-related manipulation; and (2) broadcast delays intended to prevent real-time cheating may create informational asymmetries exploitable in betting markets.

The study highlights the need for enhanced testing strategies (including online competitions), greater transparency, harmonised regulations, and systematic anti-cheat and betting monitoring. It also underscores the importance of stakeholder education, clearer allocation of responsibilities, and the development of safeguarding frameworks addressing abuse and harassment.

This study provides the first in situ analysis of esports integrity governance, demonstrating a gap between formal regulations and practical implementation. Addressing these shortcomings requires a coordinated and multi-layered approach that integrates regulatory clarity, technological solutions, and preventive strategies grounded in SCP theory.

abstracts.title: From Regional Scenes to Global Circuits: How Mega-Events Are Reshaping International Esports Ecosystems
abstracts.by: Leandro Francisco Becka and Federico Arteca, Universidad Nacional de La Plata, Argentina
abstracts.aus: Leandro Francisco Becka and Federico Arteca

sec.t: The global consolidation of competitive gaming has traditionally relied on fragmented, publisher-centric regional circuits or localized grassroots community structures. However, the recent emergence of multi-title esports mega-events has triggered a significant paradigm shift in how international ecosystems are structured, governed, and commercialized.

This development highlights a critical tension within the industry: while certain regions lead in game development and heritage, global esports success requires complex cross-regional collaboration and transnational infrastructure. This research examines how centralized mega-events reshape international competitive circuits and redefine the relationship between historical gaming hubs and emerging markets.

Utilizing an organizational ethnography approach backed by a cumulative three-year period of direct operational observation within the Esports World Cup (EWC) framework -covering its initial iterations in Saudi Arabia, and its subsequent strategic relocation to France- this study follows destination management and tourism governance frameworks (Getz, 2008; González Reverté & Morales, 2009). We analyze how destination marketing organizations (DMOs) leverage these multi-title events as strategic tools for city branding and diversification of the tourism offer. Through a comparative multi-regional analysis, this study explores the operational, economic, and cultural friction points across four distinct territories: Asia (the traditional heritage and publisher powerhouse), MENA (the capital-intensive infrastructural catalyst), Europe/North America (the mature, club-driven ecosystem), and LATAM (the high-engagement, resource-constrained regional scene).

The findings indicate that while esports mega-events accelerate internationalization and establish unprecedented global compliance and production standards, they simultaneously challenge localized governance models and underscore the constraints of an incomplete industry structure (Nyström et al., 2022). Furthermore, this research highlights how these centralized multi-title events force regional stakeholders and fanbases to navigate severe geographic and logistical shifts towards non-traditional destinations.

In response to recent calls to examine how cross-cultural and regional variations shape experiential consumption in esports (Brock & Crawford, 2025), this research provides actionable insights for city administrators, tourism boards, and event organizers seeking to integrate competitive gaming into destination value chains (Becka et al., 2024). It provides a roadmap for balancing localized community interests with the demands of global commercial compliance, allowing destination marketing organizations (DMOs) to strategically navigate multi-regional friction points.

Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive, insider-driven framework for understanding the contemporary governance and business management of esports. It illustrates how the convergence of diverse regional practices is forging a new, interconnected matrix for tomorrow’s competitive landscape, forcing a continuous re-evaluation of market development and cultural adaptation.

abstracts.title: From Sentiment to Participation: Topic- and Context-Dependent Danmu Engagement in Esports Match Viewing
abstracts.by: Huawei Sun, Seoul National University, South Korea

sec.t: Danmu comments are time-synchronized on-screen messages that allow esports viewers to react to specific moments in a match. Because each comment is attached to the video timeline, Danmu provides an observable trace of platform-mediated consumer engagement in esports videos (Li et al., 2023). Drawing on emotional contagion theory and interaction ritual chain theory (Collins, 2004; Hatfield et al., 1993), this study examines when emotional expressions in Danmu comments become visible participation during esports match viewing.

The study asks how positive and negative sentiment are associated with minute-level Danmu engagement, whether this association differs across discussion topics, and whether match-level contexts further condition the sentiment-engagement relationship.

The analysis uses 151,814 Danmu comments collected from official Bilibili replay videos of professional League of Legends Pro League matches. These comments were aggregated into 6,094 match-minute observations nested within 34 matches. The outcome variable is minute-level Danmu engagement, measured as the number of comments attached to each match minute. Sentiment was classified as positive, neutral, or negative using a multilingual transformer classifier and validated against 1,500 manually coded comments. Discussion topics were identified with six-topic Latent Dirichlet Allocation. The study then estimates multilevel negative binomial regression models to test sentiment effects, topic moderation, and cross-level moderation by match context.

Positive sentiment is positively associated with minute-level Danmu engagement, whereas negative sentiment is not statistically significant. The positive sentiment-engagement relationship is stronger when comments focus on player performance and broadcast commentary, but weaker in humor-oriented banter. Match context also matters: later games in a series, longer series, and playoff or final-stage matches strengthen the association between positive sentiment and engagement. Star players and popular teams are associated with higher overall engagement, although they do not clearly amplify the sentiment effect in the cross-level models.

The findings suggest that esports platforms, broadcasters, leagues, teams, and sponsors can encourage Danmu participation by foregrounding emotionally resonant player performances, emphasizing high-stakes match narratives, and using commentary or interface cues that support positive collective attention around key moments.

This study shows that time-synchronized Danmu engagement is not simply a reaction to gameplay events. It emerges from the interaction between emotional expression, topical focus, and match context. By clarifying how sentiment becomes observable platform participation, the study extends emotional contagion and interaction ritual theories to esports audience communication and digital consumer engagement research.

abstracts.title: From Traditional Sports Clubs to Esport Organizations: The Development and Challenges of Esport Sections in France
abstracts.by: Philippe Coudert, Université Paris-Saclay, France

sec.t: Over the last ten years, esports has grown significantly and has become an important cultural and economic phenomenon worldwide. In France, many traditional sports and multisport clubs have started to create their own esports sections. This evolution reflects broader changes in the way sports institutions adapt to digital practices, youth culture, and new forms of competition. While most studies on esports focus on publishers, professional organizations, or streaming platforms, fewer works examine the role played by local sports clubs in the development of grassroots esports. The French case is particularly interesting because of the country’s strong fanbase (in both sports and esports) and the increasing recognition of esports by public institutions and sporting actors.

This presentation explores how French esports-clubs, sports-clubs, multisports-clubs, and independent local-esports-organizations create and manage esports-sections, and how these initiatives transform relationships between traditional sport structures, digital practices, and local communities. The aim is to better understand the motivations behind these projects, the organizational models adopted by clubs, and the main opportunities and challenges linked to the development of esports at the local level.

The study is based on a qualitative methodology combining semi-structured interviews, institutional document analysis, and case studies of French clubs that have developed esports activities (this particularly includes GentlesMates, Solary, PSG-Esports, Levallois-Sporting-Club, Courbevoie-Esport-by-Pandore, and Educ-Esport). Interviews were conducted with club managers, coaches, volunteers, players, and local stakeholders involved in these projects. The analysis focuses on several dimensions, including governance, funding, community engagement, relations with federations, and the integration of esports into existing club identities.

The first results show that clubs mainly use esports to attract younger audiences, modernize their image, and diversify their activities. However, the integration of esports into traditional sports organizations remains unequal depending on the club and the local context. Many clubs face financial limitations, governance uncertainties, and a strong dependence on volunteer work. Some tensions also appear between competitive goals and educational or social objectives usually associated with those sports clubs. We will highlight important differences between clubs using esports mainly as a communication tool and those aiming for long-term integration. Local support and territorial dynamics also seem to play a major role in the sustainability of these initiatives.

The findings provide useful insights for sports organizations and educational institutions interested in the extension of esports at grassroots level. The presentation discusses possible approaches regarding governance, volunteer training, youth engagement, and cooperation between public administration and esports stakeholders. In general, it contributes to international discussions about how traditional sports institutions adapt to ongoing digital transformations.

The development of esports sections within French sports clubs illustrates how sport organizations are gradually evolving in the digital era. Rather than replacing traditional sports practices, esports is often seen as a complementary activity that helps clubs expand their identity and reach new communities. However, the long-term sustainability of these projects depends (or will depend) on clearer governance frameworks, stronger local support, and the ability of clubs to balance competitive goals with social and educational values.

abstracts.title: From Viewers to Value Chains: Developing a Sustainable Esports Media Ecosystem Framework for Selected African Contexts
abstracts.by: Gabriel Sikanku, Esports Africa News, United Kingdom; Kenechukwu Okeke, Esports Africa News, Nigeria

sec.t: Esports is one of the fastest-growing sectors of the global digital economy, yet little empirical research examines how esports media organisations in African contexts convert audience engagement into sustainable economic and organisational value. Existing scholarship on streaming, platform economies, and participatory culture centres on North American, European, and East Asian markets, leaving these ecosystems underrepresented.

Avoiding any treatment of “African esports” as a single market, this study focuses on named organisations and platforms in four specified countries — Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa. It asks how selected esports media organisations build and sustain audiences; through what organisational, technological, community-based, and commercial mechanisms engagement is transformed into social, organisational, cultural, and economic value; how infrastructure, platform governance, and digital-payment systems shape sustainability; what similarities and differences exist across cases; and which internationally documented practices are adaptable to these contexts.

The study uses a multiple-case, explanatory, mixed-methods design. For each national case, data comprise semi-structured interviews with organisational stakeholders (founders, managers, and content and community leads), organisational document analysis, and platform/audience analytics drawn from the organisations’ own streaming and social channels. Cross-case analysis compares a common set of indicators — audience-building, value creation and retention, infrastructure, platform governance, monetisation and payment systems, and organisational resilience — to identify shared patterns and context-specific differences, and to surface transferable (rather than universal) best practices.

Findings are organised through the Sustainable Esports Media Ecosystem Framework for Africa (SEMEFA), introduced as a diagnostic and comparative tool for analysing how media content, community participation, digital platforms, infrastructure, governance, and revenue systems interact to support or constrain ecosystem sustainability across national contexts.

As a study in progress, the work is designed to generate context-sensitive evidence rather than a universal model. It is expected to contribute to esports studies, digital-media and platform-governance research, and emerging scholarship on Africa’s digital creative economy, while offering practitioners and policymakers a structured framework for evaluating sustainable esports media ecosystems.

By comparing named organisations across four countries, the study aims to explain how viewers are turned into value chains, and to provide a transferable, evidence-based framework for sustainable esports media ecosystems.

abstracts.title: Generative AI in Rural High School Esports: A Case Study of Coach and Advisor Perceptions, Access, and the Collegiate Pipeline
abstracts.by: Michael Cassens, University of Montana, United States of America

sec.t: The growth of scholastic-to-collegiate (i.e., secondary school to higher education) esports has created unique opportunities for rural high school students to access esports programs, scholarships, and educational pathways previously unattainable (Warnock et al., 2025; Seidmann, 2024). However, generative artificial intelligence (gen AI) adds a new wrinkle to the equation as it becomes increasingly integrated into both the esports game titles students play and the tools developers use. Gen AI, a type of artificial intelligence that generates new content based on training data, has been commonly used in player training, skill development, and game analysis. (Jenny and Pastore, 2025) Therefore, concerns regarding ethical recruiting practices and the same student playing across multiple programs become more complex. There are now also questions about awareness, accessibility, and student readiness, especially for coaches and faculty advisors serving in these rural esports programs.

This pilot study examines how rural high school (i.e., secondary school) esports coaches and advisors perceive and leverage generative AI, the barriers to adopting these tools, and how their attitudes align with or diverge from those of collegiate esports players. In doing so, it examines how coaches should transparently and adequately prepare their students for the programs they join, while balancing the need to educate students with their exposure to gen AI in scholastic competitive gaming contexts.

This pilot case study employs a two-phase sequential survey design, combining a structured Likert-scale instrument (adapted from a parallel study of collegiate esports players) with a written open-ended survey exploring barriers to the adoption of gen AI and usage with coaches and collegiate players alike, along with attitudes toward its integration in esports (College Board, 2025). This pilot study analyzed responses from rural high school esports coaches and advisors (n=10) and a collegiate player dataset (n=26) to uncover emerging comparative patterns between the two demographics. All responses were collected using an anonymous Qualtrics survey consisting of 29 questions for coaches and advisors and 16 questions for players. It took approximately 10-15 minutes for the coach’s survey and 5-10 minutes for the player’s survey. The questions consisted of a mixture of Likert-scale questions assessing literacy, fluency, usage, and perceptions of generative AI, and qualitative questions examining future direction and the influence these tools have on coaches, advisors, and players. For coaches and advisors, the response rate was approximately 58%, while for students it was approximately 32%.

The analysis revealed an intriguing, at times counterintuitive, picture. Although rural coaches often reported slightly lower understanding of gen AI than collegiate players, they reported higher actual usage and greater acceptance of gen AI in esports contexts. In contrast, collegiate players expressed stronger ethical concerns and more negative overall attitudes, resulting in lower usage.

These findings could have essential policy implications for scholastic esports leagues, professional coaching development, and the design of collegiate onboarding for rural recruits. Instead of focusing solely on the accessibility of gen AI in rural programs, administrators and policymakers should first acknowledge that these coaches are informal early adopters whose practical use exceeds their self-reported familiarity with it. Investment in AI literacy resources, ethical-use guidance, and guidance between scholastic and collegiate programs may be more productive than approaches that assume only a deficiency in accessibility.

These discoveries could positively impact the conversation around the digital divide, including the gen AI divide, and open a broader discussion about attitudes toward gen AI in scholastic and collegiate esports. Awareness, attitudes, and accessibility overlap in ways that require additional attention from researchers, educators, and league administrators as they shape AI literacy and the responsible and ethical use of AI (Durak, 2025).

abstracts.title: Implementation of the IPK Esports® Wellness Monitoring Framework in Professional Valorant Players: A Pilot Observational Study
abstracts.by: Juan Carlos Andrade, IPK ACADEMY, Spain

sec.t: Professional esports involves prolonged sitting, repetitive upper-limb movements, extensive screen exposure, irregular schedules, and high psychological demand, all of which can affect player health and readiness (DiFrancisco-Donoghue et al., 2019; Trotter et al., 2020; Zwibel et al., 2019). In traditional sport, repeated subjective wellness monitoring is a practical, low-cost, and ecologically valid way to track readiness, fatigue, and recovery (Hooper & Mackinnon, 1995; Saw et al., 2016), yet structured, routinely implemented monitoring is rarely documented in professional esports.

This pilot study describes the implementation of the IPK Esports® Wellness Monitoring Framework within one professional Valorant team across a competitive season and explores temporal associations between subjective wellness and official performance indicators. No causal or efficacy claims are made.

In a prospective, longitudinal, observational design, five professional Valorant players (Ramboot Club; Spain Rising Challengers League, Split 1, 2024) completed the IPK Wellness Questionnaire (IPK-WQ) weekly. Predefined alert criteria (any domain scored 2 or below) prompted clinical review and individualized, non-standardized interventions. Official performance metrics (K/D, ACS, ADR, KAST) were obtained from the public VLR.gg database. Given the small sample (n = 5), analysis was restricted to descriptive longitudinal observation; no inferential tests, regression, or causal modelling were performed (Saw et al., 2016).

Players with higher average wellness scores tended to show greater stability across official performance indicators. In the two alert-triggered cases with available follow-up, composite scores were higher at the next assessment, describing a favourable short-term trajectory rather than a treatment effect. The team’s 10-match winning streak coincided with no composite scores below the alert threshold. These observations are exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

The framework illustrates how routine, low-cost subjective monitoring can be embedded in professional esports to flag reduced readiness and guide individualized, clinician-led support (Saw et al., 2016; DiFrancisco-Donoghue et al., 2021). Findings should inform hypotheses for adequately powered studies rather than practice recommendations.

Conclusion_ This study documents, transparently and without evaluating efficacy, the real-world implementation of a structured wellness-monitoring framework in professional Valorant. Controlled, larger studies are needed to test the associations observed.
POSITIONALITY AND CONFLICT OF INTEREST

The corresponding author developed the IPK Esports® framework and served as the implementing physiotherapist, and is professionally associated with IPK Academy. The study documents implementation rather than validating the framework; proprietary elements are presented as a practice model, not as evidence of effectiveness.

abstracts.title: Legitimacy, Cultural Entrepreneurship, and Community Fragmentation in Brazilian Esports
abstracts.by: Marco Galo and Sai Kalvapalle, Nova School of Business and Economics, Portugal

sec.t: Prior research shows that new ventures and emerging fields gain legitimacy by aligning with recognizable institutional templates and narratives, signaling professionalism, and becoming intelligible to external stakeholders (Aldrich & Fiol, 1994; Navis & Glynn, 2010, 2011). Similarly, work on cultural entrepreneurship highlights how actors draw in audiences by mobilizing cultural resources, such as symbols and stories, to shape collective meanings and identities (Gehman & Soublière, 2017; Lounsbury & Glynn, 2001; Wry et al., 2011). While prior research has paid significant attention to legitimacy and cultural resonance, it has paid less attention to stakeholder heterogeneity in contexts where organizations must gain legitimacy among new audiences while preserving the identity of their core participants.

This study examines how game developers or publishers build legitimacy for new competitive games without alienating their core players. We investigate the entrepreneurial process through which Riot Games, via League of Legends, helped develop and consolidate esports as a cultural movement in Brazil.

Through purposive sampling, we assembled a dataset comprising more than 1,000 hours of podcasts, documentaries, and secondary interviews, along with hundreds of pages of official announcements, news reports, and industry communications. Sources were selected based on their relevance, coverage of key periods and events, and representation of perspectives from publishers, players, casters, streamers, organizations, journalists, and other stakeholders.

We followed an iterative thematic coding approach. Initial codes remained close to the empirical material and captured specific practices, artifacts, stakeholder perceptions, and forms of interaction. Examples include the use of arenas and formal broadcast formats, perceptions of rigidity, audience migration toward streamer-centered communities, and the gradual opening of co-streaming rights. Through iterative comparison of these codes and engagement with the relevant academic literature, we grouped them into higher-order themes concerning professionalization, legitimization, organizational responses, and community dynamics. We then examined the relationships among these themes to develop a preliminary process model.
At ERNC26, we will present our sampling strategy, coding structure, representative excerpts, and emerging model in detail.

Preliminary findings suggest that, in seeking to legitimize the nascent esports movement, Riot relied heavily on cultural artifacts imported from traditional sports and mainstream media, including broadcast formats, arenas, and competitive structures. These artifacts professionalized esports and built legitimacy among sponsors, mainstream audiences, and external institutions. However, they also produced a countervailing dynamic. As the official product became more formalized and institutionally disciplined, parts of the core audience perceived it as rigid, distant, and misaligned with the language and practices of the gaming community. We conceptualize this dual-sided outcome as non-endemic legitimization and endemic delegitimization.

These legitimacy-building dynamics contributed to community fragmentation, but not to ecosystem exit. A substantial portion of the audience shifted toward streamer-centered subcommunities tied to League of Legends but outside Riot’s official media channels. This redistribution of audience attention and symbolic influence created a strategic challenge for Riot, as streamer-led spaces increasingly competed with the official broadcast for reach, community attachment, and commercial value. Riot initially responded by protecting the official product, restricting access to competition footage, and treating streamers as potential competitors. As these frictions intensified, however, Riot began negotiating with prominent streamers, gradually opening co-streaming rights and incorporating selected practices from streamer-led broadcasts, thereby initiating a process of reconciliation.

Our emerging model connects these successive stages of legitimacy-building, fragmentation, organizational response, and reconciliation. At ERNC26, we will present the model and its supporting evidence to gather feedback before proceeding to a subsequent phase of primary interviews designed to deepen our understanding of the mechanisms connecting these stages.

Our preliminary findings suggest that efforts to legitimize emerging competitive ecosystems may have unintended consequences when the same artifacts that attract external stakeholders also alienate the core audience. Our emerging model identifies practices and conditions through which publishers may manage this duality, retain fragmented audiences, and create conditions for their subsequent reintegration.

This paper contributes to research on legitimation and cultural entrepreneurship by showing how cultural artifacts can produce double-edged outcomes. It also contributes to esports research by offering a process perspective on how publisher-led professionalization and streamer-centered communities may co-evolve. Feedback from ERNC26 will help refine the model and inform the design of a subsequent phase of primary interviews.
