abstracts.title: Mapping the Visual Grammar of Esports Livestreaming: A Cross-Genre Analysis of UI Density and Color Strategy
abstracts.by: Jiayi Xu, Hong Kong Shue Yan University, China; Xiaobo Ke, The Education University of Hong Kong, China

sec.t: Esports livestreaming interfaces are primary mediums for spectator engagement, yet design practices vary substantially across genres. This variation creates a critical tension between real-time data display and spectator cognitive comfort (Korbel et al., 2025). While existing research covers macro engagement metrics, systematic cross-genre analysis regarding visual clutter, overlay density, and chromatic distribution remains limited, leaving production teams insufficient empirical, evidence-based design guidance.

This study asks: What interface design logic and pattern exist in professional esports livestreaming across gaming genres? We aim to establish empirically driven guidelines enabling broadcast production teams to optimize information presentation without compromising spectator satisfaction.

We analyzed eights high-viewership broadcast cases across eight genres: RTS, FPS, MOBA, Fighting, Racing, Sport Simulation, Card Game, and Battle Royale. Interface module area proportions were quantified using Adobe Photoshop, while HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value (or Brightness)) color distribution analysis established empirical baselines of current industry practices.

User Interface (UI) Element Configuration Logic in Esports Livestreaming. The configuration is shaped by two intersecting logics: visual competition and genre identity expectation. Where gameplay saturates the visual field, UI deployment is spatially constrained. Where spectators expect a real-world broadcast aesthetic — as in Sport Simulation and Racing — UI restraint becomes a deliberate authenticity signal rather than a spatial necessity. These logics explain the observed distribution. Fighting, MOBA, and Card Games (31%–35% of total screen area occupied by UI elements) feature static or fixed camera perspectives and slow action pace, carrying no authenticity obligation and enabling maximum UI deployment. RTS, FPS, and Battle Royale titles (22%–26%) involve continuous camera movement, high-tempo action, and broad situational awareness demands, confining UI to fixed peripheral zones to balance informational demand with unobstructed sightlines. Sport Simulation and Racing (9%–12%) are subject to both logics simultaneously, minimizing overlays to preserve spatial immersion and uphold the broadcast aesthetic central to their spectatorial identity. Visual Anchoring and High-Contrast Coloring Pattern. Crucially, a convergent design pattern emerges: while high-tempo titles utilize dark background containers (V ≤ 17%) to anchor attention, certain titles strategically deviate, employing high-value containers (e.g., Fortnite at 93%, Hearthstone at 51%) to sustain genre-specific thematic branding. In two-faction competitive titles (e.g., MOBA, FPS, Fighting), opposing sides are assigned high-contrast color pairs separated by 120°–180° on the color wheel — maximizing chromatic discriminability so that spectators can instantly register critical state changes amid high-motion gameplay.

These findings provide a genre-calibrated diagnostic framework for broadcast teams to benchmark overlay density. Additionally, the validated chromatic patterns offer a replicable template that optimizes information presentation while reconciling cognitive accessibility and color vision inclusivity.

By establishing the UI configuration logic and coloring patterns, this study transforms esports broadcast interface design from convention-driven practice into an empirical, evidence-based discipline.

abstracts.title: Measuring Gender-Based Discrimination in Online Gaming: An Experiment Using Voice and Chat Interactions
abstracts.by: Raphael Prifti and Carlos Gomez-Gonzalez, University of Lausanne, Switzerland; Cornel Nesseler, University of Stavanger, Norway
abstracts.aus: Raphael Prifti, Carlos Gomez-Gonzalez and Cornel Nesseler

sec.t: Online gaming has become one of the largest global entertainment industries and an important social space for younger generations. Despite its rapid growth, concerns about harassment and discrimination - particularly gender-based harassment - remain widespread. Research suggests that female players frequently experience hostile interactions, sexual harassment, and exclusion in online gaming environments. However, much of the existing evidence relies on surveys or interviews, which can suffer from reporting bias and do not provide causal inference. Experimental approaches that observe behavior during actual gameplay remain rare. Understanding whether and under which circumstances gender-based harassment occurs in online games is important for improving the inclusiveness of gaming communities.

This study examines whether players who present as female experience more harassment than players who present as male in online gaming environments. We record chat and audio commentary during gameplay. In addition, we investigate whether negative reactions intensify when players experience a temporary technical problem.

We conduct a field experiment in which 30 adult (aged 18 or older) participants played in team-based online matches. Participants were recruited through a university offered esports minor and gave informed consent before taking part. Participants were randomly assigned to groups of three and played several matches in three popular multiplayer titles that are also established esports games and that support in-game voice and text communication: Fortnite (battle royale), Counter-Strike 2 (tactical shooter), and Rocket League (vehicular soccer). The matches were standard online public matchmaking sessions. The gender each player presented to other players was assigned at random and changed every 20 minutes and was signaled through in-game username; this presented gender is the study’s main independent variable. In some matches, players introduced a scripted technical issue (e.g., “technical problem—trying to rejoin soon”), creating a controlled disruption. During each match, players recorded interactions and categorized them as positive, neutral, negative, or sexually harassing. Additionally, we used AI to categorize voice and chat interactions through an automated pipeline that transcribed in-game audio (OpenAI’s Whisper speech-to-text model), extracted on-screen chat and notifications using optical character recognition, and classified each interaction with a large language model (Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7). The final dataset contains 319 observations, where one observation corresponds to a player participating in a 20-minute match. The experiment involved interactions with other online players who were not enrolled in the study. The protocol was reviewed and approved by the ethical committee of the first author. No personally identifying information about non-participants was collected. We analyze the data using ordinary least squares regression models with multiple controls, and Double Machine Learning to obtain robust estimates of treatment effects.

Results (Key Findings): Results indicate that players presenting as female experience significantly higher levels of sexual harassment compared with male players. Across specifications, the estimated effect ranges from roughly 6 to 9 percentage points. Machine learning estimates confirm these findings. When examining gameplay disruptions, harassment appears more pronounced for female players during glitch conditions compared to normal gameplay. However, the interaction between gender and glitch conditions is not statistically significant in the main specifications.

The findings highlight persistent gender-based harassment in online gaming environments. Game developers and publishers may use these insights to strengthen moderation systems, improve reporting tools, and implement community management strategies that discourage abusive behavior. Interventions aimed at reducing toxicity may be particularly important in situations where gameplay disruptions occur, as frustration can increase hostile responses.

This study provides experimental evidence that female players experience higher levels of sexual harassment in online gaming interactions. While harassment does not occur in the majority of interactions, the gender gap remains meaningful and consistent across analytical approaches. These results contribute to the growing literature on discrimination in digital environments and underline the need for continued efforts to foster more inclusive online gaming communities.

abstracts.title: No Pros in a Pro Tour: Inside a Testing House for Magic: The Gathering
abstracts.by: Matt Knutson, University of North Dakota, United States of America

sec.t: Magic: The Gathering (henceforth MTG) is trading card game played both in person and digitally that earned $1.72B (US) for Hasbro in 2025. Since MTG’s Pro Tour began in 1996, the most accomplished players have each earned hundreds of thousands of US dollars competing in tabletop as well as online tournaments. Nevertheless, MTG remains what the author terms a “peripheral esport,” or one in which there are financial stakes and an audience of spectators, but there are no true full-time professionals in the game. While mainstream esports tend to get the most attention, the mosaic of the esports scene is composed mostly of peripheral esports as varied as MTG, World of Warcraft, Madden, and Forza. This study articulates the precarity of competitive play for little promise of sustainable compensation.

The present study was conducted in a “testing house” in the week before a Pro Tour (henceforth PT) event for MTG. Two research questions guiding interviews were “How do players in a PT testing house reach strategic consensus in their preparations for a tournament?” and “How does MTG fit into these players’ professional goals?”

The researcher was given access to the space of the testing house to conduct observations as a “fly on the wall,” recording handwritten notes about player interactions and communication practices. 10 participants (half the testing house) sat for semi-structured interviews, each about 30 minutes. Afterwards, the researcher attended the Pro Tour tournament and tracked participants’ retrospective observations of team performance.

Players acknowledged that there wasn’t a real path to professionalization in MTG. Instead of a hope for “going pro,” motivations for being there treated it more like an expensive vacation. Despite the demanding cognitive task involved, and despite the time investment entailed in pursuing this goal, the expected value of payoff for all this work was, as the players readily acknowledged, low.

This presentation engages Nieborg and Foxman’s Mainstreaming and Game Journalism (2023) to draw a distinction between what “mainstream” and “periphery” means within the context of esports, itself a cultural niche. The main intervention is a linguistic one: distinguishing between the mainstream and the peripheral helps us better orient ourselves to the material realities of competitive players, even if top-tier players in a given game are colloquially known as “pros.” Often, as is the case with MTG, the “pros” are not truly professional competitors, and both researchers and the broader esports scene can lose sight of that fact. By more carefully observing a distinction between the mainstream and the peripheral, the esports scene can be more clear-eyed about the financial position full-time competitors place themselves in.

Two conclusions emerge from the pair of research questions. To the first question about strategic consensus-building, study participants engaged in animated but collegial interrogation of how best to approach the tournament’s format. One resonating motivation to invest their time and energy on playing high-level competitive MTG was to work on an immensely complex problem with limited information. As to the research question on professional goals, while it is tempting to presume that there is a path to professionalization in most esports, these “pro” level players were clear that there was not really a career in this pursuit. Close examination of a single peripheral esport such as MTG attunes us to the broader picture of an esports scene made up of mostly small peripheral niches of competition, which typically attract dedicated, brilliant players in spite of marginal potential payoff. As it is with so many other games, professionalization for the game’s best players remains out of reach.

abstracts.title: Performance and Perception: How Educational Interventions Shape Esports Doping Attitudes
abstracts.by: Ethan P. Valentine, Coastal Carolina University, United States of America; Elyzia E. Powers, Alexander Engel and Briana Romfo, Minot State University, United States of America; Sarah M. Landen, Anderson Marchetti, Madighan Tracy and Gianna Esposito, Coastal Carolina University, United States of America
abstracts.aus: Ethan P. Valentine, Elyzia E. Powers, Alexander Engel, Briana Romfo, Sarah M. Landen, Anderson Marchetti, Madighan Tracy and Gianna Esposito

sec.t: Esports has expanded rapidly within higher education, with hundreds of institutionally supported collegiate programs in the United States alone and record new investments in 2024-2025 (Postell & Narayan, 2025). As esports spaces continue to grow, questions about governance, ethical standards, and the regulation of competitive play remain. Performance-enhancing drug (PED) use is broadly viewed as unethical in traditional sports (e.g., Jowett et al., 2023) and there is evidence that doping may contribute to reduced acceptance of esports (Gupta et al., 2022). However, prior research indicates collegiate stakeholders view PED use as more acceptable in esports (Valentine et al., 2025). Those findings suggest that this discrepancy may reflect a belief that PEDs do not impact esports performance, raising concerns for competitive integrity.

The present study examines whether providing information about PED efficacy influences collegiate stakeholders’ attitudes toward doping, and whether these effects differ between traditional sports and esports. In addition, the study explores whether perceived effectiveness of PEDs helps explain changes in attitudes toward doping in esports.

A mixed experimental design was used with a between-subjects factor of educational condition (esports PED information, sports PED information, or general esports information [control]) and within-subjects factors of time (pre-, post-intervention) and domain (sports, esports). Collegiate stakeholders (students, faculty, and staff affiliated with collegiate institutions) completed measures of doping attitudes using the Performance Enhancement Attitude Scale (PEAS; Petróczi & Aidman, 2009), with minor wording adaptations for esports, along with brief indices assessing perceived PED effectiveness in each domain. Measures were administered before and after exposure to the assigned intervention. Analyses include a 3x2x2 mixed ANOVA and secondary mediation analyses examining whether changes in perceived effectiveness account for changes in esports doping attitudes.

While data collection is ongoing, preliminary results indicate that exposure to esports-specific PED information appears to increase perceived effectiveness of PEDs in esports while decreasing perceived acceptability of doping in esports. In contrast, attitudes toward doping in traditional sports appear stable across conditions. Initial results also suggest that changes in perceived effectiveness are associated with changes in attitudes toward doping in esports, providing preliminary support for the proposed explanatory mechanism. These patterns will be re-evaluated with the full sample.

These findings have implications for governance and ethics in collegiate esports, particularly in contexts where regulation remains inconsistent. If attitudes toward PED use are shaped in part by beliefs about effectiveness, educational interventions may represent a practical strategy for promoting competitive integrity by shaping competitor and administrator attitudes in ways that reduce willingness to engage in doping and increase support for regulation. Such approaches are especially relevant for organizations seeking to align emerging esports norms with established expectations in traditional sports.

This research builds on prior work by exploring both the malleability of doping attitudes and a potential mechanism underlying those attitudes. The findings suggest that differences in how PED use is evaluated across domains may reflect underlying assumptions about effectiveness, highlighting the role of educational interventions in the ongoing development of esports policy and practice.

abstracts.title: Pieces of Eight Tournament Format: A new tournament format for a new age of competition (WIP)
abstracts.by: Kurtis Homan, St. Cloud State University, United States of America

sec.t: Tournament design research has recently had a renewed focus utilizing operation research techniques to evaluate quantitative metrics in tournament formats. Historically, tournament formats were broken into either elimination or non-elimination formats, and how to run and operate them was the primary focus. Qualitative metrics on how important specific aspects of a tournament ranged from ’not important’ to ’very important’, for example demonstrated in ’Organizing Successful Tournaments’ (Byl, 1990). Recently, Balázs et al. (2022) from operation research utilized Monte Carlos simulations in their research ’The Efficacy of Tournament Design’ and found that Swiss format yielded the best results for final placement of entries and identified that esports current has no standard tournament format that is used across titles. Then Yuan’s (2024) research ’The Impact of Swiss-Style Tournaments of Esports Team Performance: An Examination of the League of Legends World Championships’ analyzed the use of Swiss format tournament for League of Legends competition and identified more unbalanced match up occurred using the tournament format and noted that ’tournament design and is critical in the development and management of esports competition’. By continuing to use operation research and to add to tournament design research for final placement accuracy, a new tournament format was created currently named Pieces of Eight (P8).

P8 is a non-elimination tournament format that utilizes partitioned group play that is used for future pairings and final placements. This new tournament format is compared with existing tournament formats using Monte Carlos simulation and random initial seeding to evaluate the accuracy of the final placement of competitors. Accuracy is primarily evaluated by mean squared error (MSE) to measure the magnitude of error that occurs, lower the better. In addition, a range of sizes of tournament entries are used to further evaluate how scalability of entries affects overall accuracy of the tournament format. Sizes of tournaments that are evaluated are 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512. The 5 data points are used to evaluate how P8 and other tournament formats accuracy adjust with respect to scale of entries. To normalize the comparisons, an accuracy measurement uses the MSE previously calculated and standardizes the number of entries there are in the tournament. The normalization figure is used to determine if there is any form of trend data, or other interesting findings, that emerge as the size of the tournament increases.

The research is still a work in progress, however early findings in a 32 and 64 entry tournament format comparison using random seeding is that the group play of P8 has a 30% or greater reduction of normalized mean squared error for final placement of entries compared to the true rank. Thus, early results show an overall improvement of accuracy to the final placement of entries compared to established tournament formats.

abstracts.title: Playing Without Rules: A Comparative Legal Analysis of Esports Player Contracts in France and South Korea
abstracts.by: Sophie Roman, Trainee Lawyer, France; Pierre-Xavier Chomiac de Sas, PCS Avocat, France
abstracts.aus: Sophie Roman and Pierre-Xavier Chomiac de Sas

sec.t: The starting point of this research was an entry through player–club contracts and the legal issues they raise and key considerations for clubs drafting contracts. To examine these issues meaningfully, it was necessary to identify case studies that would reveal both the diversity of possible legal responses and the persistence of shared problems despite that diversity.
France and South Korea were selected because they represent two radically different trajectories of legal and institutional construction, while nonetheless converging on similar difficulties:

South Korea supported the development of esports very early on (institutionalization, public recognition, structuring of the ecosystem). This support was notably grounded in the Esports Promotion Act, which provides that the Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism shall formulate and implement a plan to promote esports, support and develop competitions and train specialized professionals. However, this support came at the expense of adequate legal protection for the actors involved, particularly players (uncertain status, weak contractual position, etc.).

France, conversely, legislated as early as 2016 with an almost exclusive focus on player protection, without meaningfully addressing the structuring of clubs or the economic development of the industry — an imbalance that has only recently begun to shift, a full ten years later.

This comparison thus makes it possible to challenge the common assumption that South Korea represents the model example of esports regulation. In reality, both countries illustrate a form of partial regulation, but partial in opposite directions (economic/institutional support without legal protection on one side; legal protection without economic consideration on the other). The fact that two such different systems encounter analogous difficulties demonstrates that these problems are not contingent on a particular national legal context, but rather stem from structural tensions inherent to the esports sector itself.

The relevance of this comparison extends beyond the French–Korean framework: the aim is to identify, from two models developed independently of one another, the recurring points of friction in contractual matters. By confronting what has been regulated in one system against what has been overlooked in the other, the analysis helps to draw out directions for a more balanced legal framework governing player–club relations.

Although France and South Korea have each structured their Esports ecosystems differently – the former through belated and imperfect legal recognition, the latter through pioneering institutional frameworks – both share a common shortcoming: the absence of clear and binding rules governing the contractual relationship between players and Esports organizations. France opted for an employment contract specifically tailored to Esports; however, the mismatch between this instrument and industry realities has led clubs to largely disregard it. In fact, industry actors do not make use of the esports-specific fixed-term contract introduced by the 2016 law, which is widely regarded as too costly and poorly adapted to the realities of the sector: the accreditation procedure is time-consuming, esports teams remain financially fragile as they depend primarily on sponsorship revenue, and the high cost of employer social contributions undermines the international competitiveness of French teams.

South Korea, for its part, has seen its Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism introduce three standard contracts, which remain non-binding recommendations. In South Korea, the circumvention of labor law is not specific to esports but is symptomatic of a broader trend in Korean society since the 1997 Asian financial crisis, which led to the development of precarious forms of employment that have since become normalized alongside the standard employment contract.

This resulting precarity, however, is increasingly criticized, and early signs of judicial reclassification of contracts into employment contracts can be observed both in esports and in traditional sport, in both French and Korean law.

Unfortunately, such requalification requires litigation before a judge, and therefore only operates as an ex post remedy — once the harm has already occurred. As a result, clubs remain exposed to the risk of reclassification, with significant financial and reputational consequences.

In parallel, since clubs rely on ill-suited contracts, no common regime can govern the relationship — it is up to the contract itself to spell out each party’s obligations in precise detail. Because these contracts are not reviewed beforehand, there is a real risk that unfair terms may slip in. As a result, both regulatory frameworks lack binding force and oversight, resulting in normative deficiencies, that undermine the stability and security of Esports, as shown in the Kanavi case.

Several categories of sources were mobilized for this research. First, official institutional sources were used, including Korean and French statutory texts and relevant judicial decisions from both jurisdictions. These primary legal materials were selected on the basis of their direct relevance to player–club contractual relationships (labor law provisions, esports-specific regulations, and case law addressing contract requalification).

Second, this primary material was complemented by secondary sources — legal scholarship from both Korean and French researchers, published in academic journals, legal handbooks, and specialized esports-law websites or platforms. These sources were selected for their direct engagement with esports contract law specifically, rather than esports regulation more broadly, in order to keep the analysis focused on the contractual dimension.

Third, in order to move beyond a purely doctrinal reading and verify how these legal frameworks operate in practice, the author consulted directly with Korean lawyers to clarify practical points that were not sufficiently addressed in the available literature

1. The legal characterization of the player-club relationship remains uncertain. Esports player contracts present distinctive features that sit uneasily within established contractual categories, and the absence of a dedicated legal regime has led clubs to resort to ill-suited instruments, generating legal instability and exposure to reclassification risk. 2. Accordingly, the esports player contract cannot delegate the burden of precisely regulating the contractual relationship to an ordinary-law regime. Yet, the diversity of the services expected from the esports player calls for a particularly detailed framework, covering the full range of aspects of the relationship – whether strictly competitive services or ancillary services, notably those related to the promotion of the player’s and the club’s image. These various services may fall within a multitude of distinct regulations, such as the influencer law or regulations specific to social media.

3. Beyond the regulation of the player’s services during the performance of the contract, the end of the contract and the post-contractual period also call for dedicated treatment. The grounds for contractual termination must in particular be provided for in a manner that guarantees the stability of the contractual relationship, which represents a major stake for the parties. Clubs seek to retain players in whom they have invested significantly, while players require protection against abusive clauses, including unilateral renewal provisions, disproportionate non-compete obligations, and punitive transfer terms.

This study provides eSports industry stakeholders with a clear account of the applicable legal framework – identifying mandatory content, lawful and unlawful clauses, and unresolved grey areas – while examining the need for targeted legislative intervention.

Esports player contracts currently lack adequate regulation and a coherent legal regime, undermining the capacity of both parties to enter into stable, legally secure contractual relationships. Clubs may face sanctions or find themselves unable to enforce their contracts effectively, while generating uncertainty for players, who are not always in a position to assess the full extent or the lawfulness of their contracts.

abstracts.title: Psychology Support in Professional Esports: Practitioner Perspectives on Challenges, Opportunities, and Applied Practice
abstracts.by: Oliver Leis and Lara Wunsch, Leipzig University, Germany; Amy Whitehead and Laura D. Swettenham, Liverpool John Moores University, United Kingdom
abstracts.aus: Oliver Leis, Lara Wunsch, Amy Whitehead and Laura D. Swettenham

sec.t: Esports players need to navigate stress in high-performance environments, and tailored psychology support may play a crucial role in promoting their health, performance, and long-term development (e.g., Swettenham et al., 2024). Although more practitioners are entering the field, licensed psychologists may remain hesitant due to esports’ novelty, limited professional recognition, a lack of evidence-based frameworks, and the dominance of traditional sport and clinical settings (e.g., Cottrell et al., 2019; Leis et al., 2021).

This study explores qualified practitioners’ experiences of providing psychology support in professional esports, focusing on perceived challenges, opportunities, and recommendations for applied practice.

Eight qualified psychology practitioners working in high-performance esports (three women, five men) were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling. Participants included licensed or accredited sport and exercise psychology practitioners (n = 6) and licensed clinical psychologists (n = 2), working across different esports titles and countries in Europe, North America, South America, and Australia. Semi-structured online interviews explored their roles, experiences, challenges, opportunities, and recommendations for applied practice. Interviews were analyzed using reflective thematic analysis.

Preliminary findings indicate challenges related to short-term and reactive service provision, limited resources, frequent roster and staff turnover, difficulties gaining buy-in, and uncertainty around role integration. Practitioners also highlighted the need to adapt psychological expertise to esports-specific cultures while maintaining professional boundaries. Female practitioners reported experiences of sexism and additional pressure to establish credibility. Further challenges included demanding schedules, high emotional investment, and difficulties maintaining work–life boundaries. At the same time, practitioners identified opportunities to support player and team development, improve communication and cohesion, foster self-reflection, and promote health-supporting behaviors. They valued meaningful relationships, interdisciplinary and international collaboration, creative freedom, and personal and professional growth. Recommendations centered on openness, patience, perseverance, strategic engagement, and building trust through consistent, context-sensitive work.

The findings suggest that effective psychology support in esports requires patience, contextual understanding, clear role communication, and attention to professional boundaries. Practitioners may benefit from professional exchange and strategies that support their long-term sustainability in a novel and often unstable field. For esports teams and organizations, findings highlight the value of integrating psychology practitioners proactively and sustainably rather than only in response to crises. Role clarity, sufficient access to players and staff, and respectful team cultures may strengthen practitioners’ contributions to player development, performance, and well-being (e.g., Swettenham et al., 2024).

This study provides preliminary insight into psychology practitioners’ experiences in high-performance esports. Findings highlight a demanding but meaningful field shaped by short-term structures, role ambiguity, challenges in building trust, and work–life pressures, alongside opportunities for player, team, and professional development. Clearer role expectations, stronger organizational integration, and sustainable working conditions may support more effective psychological support in esports. Future research may examine differences by gender, professional background, esports title, and competitive context.

abstracts.title: Pupil-Heart Synchronization Characterizes Efficient Cognitive-Sensorimotor Performance in Esports
abstracts.by: Shohei Dobashi, University of Tsukuba, Japan

sec.t: Cognitive–sensorimotor function supports rapid and accurate decision making and behavioral output during esports play; however, the neurophysiological basis of its efficient expression remains unclear. We previously focused on flow as a state of concentration and immersion that facilitates efficient cognitive–sensorimotor function (Gallvan et al., 2021). We then reported that interpersonal pupil synchrony, reflecting central arousal primarily mediated by the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic (LC–NE) system, enhances flow during competitive fighting esports, but is not associated with performance (Harris et al., 2021). Efficient cognitive–sensorimotor performance may require not only rapid central cognitive processing but also coordinated autonomic regulation supporting adaptive motor output. Indeed, previous evidence has shown that intrapersonal brain–heart synchronization is impaired in Parkinson’s disease (Candia-Rivera et al., 2024), suggesting that preserved brain–heart synchronization may serve as a neurophysiological basis for efficient cognitive–sensorimotor performance. Therefore, such brain–heart synchronization may be reflected in pupil-heart temporal coupling.
We aimed to determine whether pupil–heart synchronization, reflecting intra-individual brain–heart coordination, is associated with efficient in-game performance during esports play.

Fourteen healthy young men completed repeated sessions of a one-versus-one fighting esports game under three conditions: passive watching, play against a CPU opponent, and human competition (3 sessions per condition). Pupil diameter and heart rate were continuously recorded. Subjective flow (Sports Flow Scale), workload (NASA-TLX), and in-game performance metrics (the number of knockouts, damage dealt, damage taken, and attacking accuracy) were simultaneously assessed. Gameplay sessions were classified using k-means clustering based on changes in pupil diameter and heart rate relative to the watching baseline. Intra-personal pupil–heart synchronization was quantified using cross-recurrence quantification analysis (CRQA).

Three physiological response profiles were identified. The low-deviation profile, characterized by smaller pupil and heart rate changes relative to baseline, showed selectively sustained pupil–heart synchronization, reflected by smaller recurrence radius and longer maximum diagonal line length. This profile was associated with superior in-game performance and lower subjective workload despite not exhibiting higher subjective flow, suggesting a dissociation between subjective flow and efficient performance states. Mediation analysis revealed that reduction in radius was indirectly associated with enhanced in-game performance through reduced subjective workload.

Joint monitoring of pupil and heart rate dynamics may provide an objective physiological framework for detecting efficient high-performance states and optimizing workload management in competitive esports. Such monitoring may support individualized biofeedback and recovery strategies aimed at preventing overarousal while preserving readiness for rapid adaptive sensorimotor responses. These approaches may help stabilize arousal regulation and maintain composure states during competition, thereby supporting consistent esports performance.

Enhanced pupil–heart synchronization during esports play was associated with superior in-game performance indirectly mediated by reduced subjective workload. These findings suggest that coordinated regulation between pupil-linked central nervous system and heart-linked peripheral autonomic system may support efficient cognitive–sensorimotor performance and underlie zone-like states characterized by regulated arousal, low subjective workload, and high objective performance.

abstracts.title: Relationship Between Esports Performance and Physical Activity Intervention
abstracts.by: Oliver Szabella, Óbuda University, Hungary; Lili Kassay, Eötvös Loránd University, Hungary; György Eigner, Óbuda University, Hungary; Felix Wachholz, University of Innsbruck, Austria
abstracts.aus: Oliver Szabella, Lili Kassay, György Eigner and Felix Wachholz

sec.t: Esports performance relies on sustained cognitive processing, reaction speed, visuomotor coordination, and fine motor control, while prolonged gameplay is associated with sedentary behavior and mental fatigue (Jenny et al., 2016; Ludyga et al., 2020). Although physical activity is increasingly incorporated into esports practice environments, evidence regarding its direct influence on esports-specific performance remains limited (McNulty et al., 2023).

This study examined whether a short-term physical activity intervention could mitigate performance decline during prolonged esports activity. The relationship between physical activity, cardiovascular fitness, cognitive fatigue, EEG activity, and esports-specific mechanical skills was investigated.

Twelve male esports competitors (mean age = 23.75 years), including professional, semi-professional, and retired high-level players from Rainbow Six: Siege, Counter-Strike 2, and League of Legends, participated in a repeated-measures experimental study. Preliminary assessments included demographic and physical activity questionnaires, a VO₂max treadmill test, and a 30-minute STROOP task performed while wearing a portable EEG device. The esports-specific assessment consisted of four consecutive testing blocks measuring reaction time, visual memory, typing speed, mouse control, and mouse accuracy. Between the second and third blocks participants received a passive break, while between the third and fourth blocks they completed a 15-minute high-intensity interval training (HIIT) intervention. EEG Alpha and Theta wave activity was continuously monitored. Statistical analyses included Friedman ANOVA, paired t-tests, and Pearson correlations.

Mechanical performance generally deteriorated during prolonged gameplay but improved following the HIIT intervention. Compared with the third measurement phase, post-intervention improvements were observed in reaction time (75% of participants), typing performance (75%), visual memory (75%), mouse control (75%), and mouse accuracy (66%). Significant differences across repeated measurements were found for typing speed (p =.012), mouse control (p =.003), and mouse accuracy (p =.044). EEG analyses revealed observable alterations in Alpha and Theta wave patterns during esports activity; however, these changes were not statistically significant. Correlations between VO₂max and STROOP performance were weak. Subjective responses strongly supported the intervention, with 11 of 12 participants reporting improved well-being and perceived performance following physical activity.

Short, structured physical activity interventions may represent an effective strategy for maintaining esports performance during extended gaming sessions. Integrating exercise into competitive gaming routines could reduce mental fatigue, sustain mechanical performance, and support healthier behavioral patterns in esports environments.

Acute physical activity appears capable of attenuating performance decline during prolonged esports participation and may positively influence esports-specific mechanical skills. Although EEG findings were inconclusive and the small sample size limits generalizability, the results provide preliminary evidence supporting the integration of physical activity into esports performance optimization models. Larger-scale studies are needed to validate these findings and clarify the underlying physiological mechanisms.

abstracts.title: Sport Psychology Interventions in Esports: A Scoping Review
abstracts.by: Oliver Leis and Jeongeun Shin, Leipzig University, Germany; Matthew Welsh, University of Chichester, United Kingdom; Lara Wunsch, Leipzig University, Germany; Benjamin T. Sharpe, University of Chichester, United Kingdom
abstracts.aus: Oliver Leis, Jeongeun Shin, Matthew Welsh, Lara Wunsch and Benjamin T. Sharpe

sec.t: The growing professionalisation of esports has increased interest in psychological interventions to support player performance and well-being. However, the extent and nature of published intervention research remain unclear. Given the small, heterogeneous, and methodologically diverse evidence base, a scoping review is well suited to map existing research and identify gaps for future work.

This study mapped how sport psychology interventions have been described, delivered, and evaluated in esports research. Specifically, it examined study populations, intervention strategies, delivery formats, assessment approaches, and methodological gaps in the current literature.

The review followed PRISMA-ScR guidance and was pre-registered through the Open Science Framework. Searches were conducted in Web of Science, PubMed, and EBSCOhost databases with no publication date restrictions. Additional reference list screening, citation searching, and hand searching were conducted. Eligibility criteria followed the Population–Concept–Context framework and included peer-reviewed English- or German-language studies describing psychological interventions in competitive esports contexts. Data were extracted descriptively, and methodological features were assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.

Seven studies published between 2022 and 2025 were identified, indicating that published intervention research in esports is still at an early stage. The available evidence was concentrated mainly on League of Legends and Counter-Strike, and samples were predominantly male. Rather than reflecting a coherent intervention literature, the studies varied widely in design, delivery format, target outcomes, and level of ecological validity. Some studies tested brief laboratory-based interventions, such as arousal reappraisal or mindset strategies, whereas others described multi-session applied support involving coping effectiveness training, acceptance-based strategies, psychological skills training, or team-focused workshops. Across studies, interventions primarily targeted stress appraisal, coping, communication, psychological safety, team processes, and performance-related indicators. However, reporting of theoretical grounding, intervention dosage, contextual features, outcome assessment, and follow-up was often inconsistent. Overall, the findings suggest growing interest in psychological interventions in esports, but also highlight a fragmented evidence base that currently limits comparison, replication, and cumulative knowledge development.

The findings provide coaches, support staff, and applied practitioners with an overview of psychological strategies studied in esports to date. However, the limited and heterogeneous evidence base means that findings should not be interpreted as prescriptive best-practice recommendations. Instead, practitioners should apply psychological interventions in a context-sensitive manner, document intervention delivery and outcomes transparently, and evaluate their work over time. Collaboration between researchers and practitioners may help strengthen the evidence base while respecting the applied realities of esports environments.

Published intervention research in esports remains exploratory and limited in scope. Existing studies show growing interest in psychological support, but inconsistent reporting and diverse methodologies constrain comparison and cumulative interpretation. Future research should include clearer reporting of participant and intervention characteristics, broader esports titles and populations, stronger outcome assessment, and greater use of longitudinal, mixed-method, and ecologically valid designs.

abstracts.title: The Challenging Regulation of Esports: the (so) French example
abstracts.by: Geoffray BRUNAUX, University of Reims Champagne-Ardenne, France; Pierre-Xavier CHOMIAC DE SAS and Sophie ROMAN, PCS Avocat, France
abstracts.aus: Geoffray Brunaux, Pierre-Xavier Chomiac de Sas and Sophie Roman

sec.t: Regulating esports is a challenge common to every state: the sector sits at the intersection of intellectual property, labour law, and sports law, with no settled international model. In 2016, France opted for a purpose-built legal regime, creating a specific employment contract for professional players and a dedicated framework for the organization of competitions.

This contribution draws on the French example to illustrate the broader difficulty of regulating esports. It examines the extent to which public regulatory choices have failed to structure the sector, and the consequences of this failure for industry professionals.

The research draws on the 2016 law and its implementing decrees, on subsequent legislative adjustments, and on bill n° 2106 “for a responsible and attractive esports sector” (“pour un esport responsable et attractif”), tabled in November 2025. The absence of published data on these instruments, together with doctrinal writing pointing to the weaknesses and ineffectiveness of the regime among industry actors, is itself revealing of the regime’s inoperability.

The French esports legislative framework has relied, since the minimalist 2016 regime, on marginal corrective measures — whether through referral to implementing decrees or through reforms — rarely, if ever, followed by effect among professionals.
This inoperative regime reveals the inadequacy of a strict, centralized regime for governing a sector as fast-moving as esports.
This ineffectiveness is further illustrated by the scale of contemporary issues facing the sector that the regime has never addressed:
The complexity of the relationship between sport and esports undermines the strict separation envisaged by the legislature in 2016;
The operational protection of players — particularly their physical and mental health — whose risks are now extensively documented;
Persistent discrimination affecting the women’s competitive scene finds no echo across the entire legal framework, left instead to private and associative initiatives;
The status of the esports agent, finally addressed in the bill, reproduces the same structural flaw by deferring its status to a future decree.

The forthcoming text, by focusing on the employment contract, agent status, and the opening-up of online competitions, once again leaves aside a significant share of the contemporary issues identified — further evidence of a partial and inadequate response to the shortcomings of the original regime.

The French situation illustrates the risks of regulation disconnected from sector practice. These dynamics offer a useful comparative lens for debates on esports regulation in Asian systems, where different institutional choices have been made.

Esports constitutes a hybrid legal object whose regulation remains fragmented. Far from being a stabilised model, the French example reveals the universal difficulty of regulating esports practice, and offers a cautionary tale for esports stakeholders hoping that a dedicated, strict regime might serve as a silver bullet.

abstracts.title: The Collegiate-to-Professional Pipeline Revisited: Tier 2 Disruption, Publisher Governance, and Talent Development in North American Esports
abstracts.by: Wil Fisackerly, University of Oklahoma, United States of America

sec.t: Collegiate esports has emerged as a distinctive component of the North American esports ecosystem, shaped by higher education structures, publisher-controlled competition, and uneven connections to professional play (Delello et al., 2021; Fisackerly & Hwang, 2024; Kauweloa & Winter, 2019). Previous research identified a bidirectional talent pipeline between collegiate and professional esports, with collegiate players moving into professional competition and former or current professional players entering collegiate programs (Fisackerly & Hwang, 2024). This differs from dominant North American traditional sport models, where professionalization typically ends collegiate eligibility. The 2024 manuscript called for investigation into the dynamics of these pipelines, particularly as the professional ecosystem continues to evolve. In just the two years since this initial observation of this phenomenon, however, both the professional and collegiate ecosystems have experienced major disruption (LoLEsports Staff, 2024, 2025). In League of Legends, Riot Games replaced the previous Academy and Proving Grounds structure with the North American Challengers League in 2023 and later removed the requirement that LCS organizations field NACL teams, contributing to a major restructuring of North American Tier 2 development pathways and renewed experimentation with hybrid-open and promotion-based systems. At the same time, collegiate programs have become increasingly visible in publisher-linked competitive structures, including Riot-supported collegiate circuits in VALORANT and League of Legends and the participation of collegiate teams in semi-professional Tier 2 contexts (College VALORANT 2024-2025: Championship, 2025).

This exploratory study revisits the conceptual model proposed by Fisackerly and Hwang (2024) to examine how the bidirectional talent pipeline between collegiate and professional esports has changed as collegiate programs have become more visible within semi-professional competition.

Methodologically, the study uses a retrospective longitudinal roster-tracing design, drawing on publicly available archival records from Liquipedia to map player movement before, during, and after collegiate participation in Tier 2 competitions. The analysis focuses on collegiate VALORANT and League of Legends teams competing in these spaces since 2023, identifying directional movement between collegiate and professional ecosystems, prior competitive experience among collegiate competitors, and evidence of collegiate programs functioning as supplemental development infrastructure.

While data collection is still underway, the presentation of this full research at ERNC 2026 will include discussion of observed talent moving between both collegiate and professional ecosystems, as well as the performance of collegiate teams against semi-professional Tier 2 teams. Discussion will connect these roster-tracing findings to broader questions of collegiate esports governance, roster development, and professionalization.

By positioning North American collegiate esports as a case of amateur institutions entering publisher-controlled semi-professional systems, this paper extends earlier work on bidirectional talent pipelines and examines whether collegiate programs are becoming supplemental development infrastructure as professional organizations reduce formal academy investment.

The analysis identifies directional movement between collegiate and professional spaces, prior competitive experience among collegiate Tier 2 participants, and collegiate performance against non-collegiate semi-professional teams. Findings offer implications for collegiate administrators, publishers, and researchers examining esports governance, roster development, and global talent pipelines.

abstracts.title: The Development and Innovation of the Esports Industry Value Chain in Thailand towards the Creative Economy
abstracts.by: Promopan Changkarndee, The University of the Thai Chamber of Commerce, Thailand

sec.t: Driven by the global shift toward a creative economy, understanding esports is crucial for emerging markets facing structural challenges. Although Thailand boasts Southeast Asia’s second-largest gaming market (Asia Sports Tech, 2023), its growth relies heavily on imports (Creative Economy Agency, 2021). Consequently, esports primarily extends the lifecycle of foreign games (Shinnasin Klangthong, 2016), leading to a digital trade deficit (Digital Economy Promotion Agency, 2023).

This research investigates the developmental direction, business management innovations, and strategic promotional mechanisms of Thailand’s esports industry, with a focus on analyzing its value chain structure.

This study integrates a documentary analysis of eight strategic documents from the Digital Economy Promotion Agency (DEPA) and the Creative Economy Agency (CEA) with in-depth interviews of 32 experts across academia (n=7), the business sector (n=22), and civil society (n=3). The interview protocol explores organizational roles within the esports ecosystem; stakeholder communication strategies; learning and adaptation for value creation and process innovation; and communication mechanisms driving the creative economy.

The findings reveal that the private sector is the primary driver of Thailand’s esports industry, spanning creative, production, distribution, and support initiatives. However, Thai-owned intellectual property (IP) accounts for approximately 2% of the industry’s total value (Digital Economy Promotion Agency, 2023), relegating the country to consumer status. This vulnerability stems from shortages in the STEM workforce and English proficiency—fundamental skills required for game development—which directly undermine entrepreneurs’ competitiveness in production timelines, market entry, and operational costs (Sawitree Sutthijakra, 2020). Developing human capital is thus paramount for sustainability (Saowaruj Rattanakhamfu et al., 2021), requiring workforce upgrades in technical hard skills, digital applications, coding, foreign languages, and socio-emotional skills (Sarayoot Ratsamee, 2025). Simultaneously, civil society expresses concerns regarding esports’ official sports designation. This apprehension arises because a significant number of youths, educators, and parents still lack an understanding of the interconnected business opportunities. This is compounded by a lack of systematic youth protection, in contrast to industry leaders such as China and South Korea (Khunlacha Preedasak, 2023).

This study argues that Thailand must urgently establish an integrated Master Plan through public-private-academic collaboration, moving away from fragmented, project-by-project support, including direct IP legal mechanisms, consultation services, and systematic youth protection frameworks to address civil society concerns directly. Furthermore, the higher education sector must co-create specialized curricula with industry experts to enhance STEM, coding, and foreign-language proficiencies systematically. This collaboration is vital for building a local workforce that can drive the creative economy.
The esports industry must transition from a passive consumer base to an active, globally competitive creator by focusing on human capital, R&D, and collaborative innovation.

abstracts.title: The Legislated Athlete: How India’s 2025 Gaming Act Redefines the Coach-Player Dynamic and Duty of Care
abstracts.by: Archit Vyas, Lawyer, India; Tarun Tarun, GNLU Centre for Sports and Entertainment Law (GCSEL), India

sec.t: For decades, the gaming heritage of both the arcade era and the early emergence of esports was shaped by an unregulated culture of endurance commonly described as “the grind,” where prolonged gameplay and intensive training were regarded as indicators of dedication and competitive excellence. However, the continuing professionalisation and institutionalisation of esports have generated increasing concerns regarding player welfare, particularly in relation to burnout, psychological stress, and the health implications of sustained competitive participation. As esports evolve into a structured industry with expanding commercial and legal dimensions, athlete health management is gradually transitioning from a matter of competitive preference to one of regulatory concern and legal obligation.

This paper examines the transformative impact of India’s Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (PROGA) and the establishment of the National Online Gaming Commission (NOGC) on the regulation of player welfare within esports and online gaming environments. It specifically investigates whether the Indian legislative framework represents a shift toward legally enforceable standards of athlete protection and how such regulation redefines the obligations and responsibilities of coaches and other stakeholders.

The study adopts a doctrinal legal research methodology based on a qualitative analysis of statutory provisions, regulatory structures, and comparative legal frameworks. It critically examines PROGA 2025 and analyses its institutional mechanisms through a comparative assessment of two international regulatory models: Japan’s JeSU licensing framework and the predominantly industry-led safeguarding approach like the 2025 British Esports Federation’s International Safeguards for Children in esports. In contrary to the PROGA, which demands statutory enforceability and legal accountability, the British framework relies on voluntary organizational pledges and educational initiatives rather than a binding law.

The analysis demonstrates that PROGA introduces a sophisticated governance framework that extends regulatory authority beyond gaming conduct to the broader physical and mental performance environment of players. The powers granted to the NOGC to mandate responsible gaming measures, including enforced gameplay limits, mental health safeguards, and strict age-verification protocols, establish player well-being as a legally protected interest. Furthermore, the framework significantly redefines the role of coaches from tactical advisors into guardians of player welfare, particularly in relation to minors, thereby creating fiduciary-like obligations that may give rise to administrative and legal consequences in instances of negligence or failure to mitigate burnout and psychological distress.

The findings suggest that esports organisations, coaches, and regulatory bodies may need to adopt structured welfare protocols and compliance mechanisms that prioritise sustainable athlete management.

The paper concludes that although the historical identity of Esports was built upon the culture of the grind, its long-term future will increasingly depend upon enforceable legal frameworks promoting athlete welfare and longevity. While Western models contribute ethical standards of protection and advocacy, the emerging Asian regulatory model, represented by India’s PROGA framework, offers legislative enforceability capable of ensuring sustained institutional stability.

abstracts.title: The Many Ways We Play: Validation of the Gaming Engagement Modes Index (GEMI)
abstracts.by: Kyle Nolla and Justin Bonny, Morgan State University, United States of America

sec.t: The ways in which people engage with games has diversified over time. Modern gaming involves solitary play, cooperative play, and esports across devices from mobile phones to consoles. Yet, most research reduces gaming engagement to estimated hours spent or preferred genre. While existing scales assess motivations or psychological functions of gaming, a gap exists for behavioral measures that capture diverse modes of play.
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the new Gaming Engagement Modes Index (GEMI), an index of gaming engagement that captures heterogenous modes of play.

Participants (n = 1182) from college student, online panel, and gaming tournament samples completed the GEMI. Six items assessed social mode of play (e.g., solitary, cooperative, esports) and four items assessed device use (e.g., mobile phone, desktop). Participants responded on a 7-point behavioral frequency scale (Never to Daily). We computed descriptive statistics, compared two methods of scoring the index (mean and maximum), evaluated criterion validity (AUC, logistic regression) and convergent validity (Pearson correlations, regression), and tested for measurement invariance across sampling context, race/ethnicity, and sex.

Inter-item correlations were low-to-moderate (r=.34-.39), suggesting the GEMI operates as an index of related but non-redundant gaming behaviors. Item means (2.7-5.1), standard deviations (2.0-2.3), and skew (-0.8-0.8) indicated adequate variability, except esports, which had a positive skew consistent with lower prevalence (M=1.9, SD=1.6, skew =1.8). For criterion validity, GEMI scores distinguished between participants recruited at in-person gaming tournaments compared to those in student samples and online panel samples (GEMI mean: t(141.3)=10.9, p<.001, d=0.9, AUC=.75[.70-.79]; GEMI max: t(321.7)=14.5, p<.001, d=0.7; AUC=.71[.68-.75]). GEMI mean remained a significant predictor of tournament status controlling for age and monthly gaming hours (OR=2.27[1.86,2.81], p<.001), and a model including GEMI outperformed a covariates-only model (AUC=.77 vs.53, p<.001). For convergent validity, hours per month of gaming were moderately correlated with GEMI mean (r =.30) and max (r =.28), and the IGDS-SF9 was positively associated with GEMI mean (r =.43) and max (r=.39). GEMI predicted IGDS-SF9 scores beyond monthly gaming hours (ΔR2=.10 for both scoring methods; β=.33 for GEMI mean vs β=.23 for hours). Measurement invariance testing confirmed that the GEMI measures gaming behaviors equivalently across testing contexts, racial/ethnic groups, and sex (all ΔCFIs < 0.01).

Researchers and practitioners can use the GEMI to efficiently assess multimodal gaming behaviors across diverse populations. The index supports flexible scoring approaches to capture both overall engagement and peak modality-specific involvement, making it useful as a summary measure or screening measure in research on social gaming and esports participation.

The GEMI provides a brief index of gaming engagement that captures heterogenous modes of play. Its validity and broad applicability supports its use in behavioral gaming research where it’s crucial to understand how individuals engage beyond how much they play.

abstracts.title: The Private Ownership of Esport? Video Game Intellectual Property and the Emergence of Lex Sportiva Digitalis
abstracts.by: Tomáš Gábriš, Trnava University in Trnava, Slovak Republic

sec.t: Traditional sports law (lex sportiva) operates under the foundational historical assumption that the rules of play, fields of competition, and athletic tools exist within the public domain, meaning no single sovereign state or private corporate entity holds an intellectual property monopoly over them. Conversely, the contemporary landscape of esports represents a radical structural transformation. In professional competitive gaming, every virtual pitch, rule system, digital referee, and broadcast asset is the proprietary, privately owned intellectual property of a game publisher. This tension has created a sovereign regulatory paradigm where End User License Agreements (EULAs) and Terms of Service (ToS) function as private constitutional charters, granting publishers absolute gatekeeping authority that bypasses historic athletic norms, player-union protections, and traditional sports dispute-resolution structures.

The objective of this paper is to analyze the profound friction between traditional sports governance models—which utilize democratic, pyramidal, and non-profit international federations (such as the IESF)—and the highly centralized, profit-driven ecosystems dominated by corporate intellectual property holders.

To analyze this structural friction and propose a novel theoretical framework, this research approach applies algorithmic governance theories and game-theoretic models to the esports ecosystem. Comparison with the co-regulation of technology and co-regulation of traditional sports will be invoked.

The research demonstrates that an absolute publisher monopoly is ultimately unsustainable for long-term commercial, athletic, and cultural evolution. For esports to achieve institutional stability, a behavioral equilibrium must be struck. The paper conceptualizes this equilibrium as the emergence of Lex Sportiva Digitalis—a modern, transnational digital sports law under which publishers, international athletic bodies, and esports athletes engage in a co-regulatory system.

Rather than attempting to force digital competition into obsolete legacy sport legal structures, Lex Sportiva Digitalis utilizes hybrid contractual arrangements, private-public IP licensing pathways, and decentralized arbitration boards to govern the ecosystem.

Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the future of competitive gaming lies not in absolute corporate dominion, but in the collaborative formalization of an agile, borderless, and structurally balanced esports jurisprudence.

abstracts.title: The Relationship Between Heart Rate Variability and Chat Behavior in College-Age Valorant Players
abstracts.by: Nathan Rhea and Robert Calvert, University of the Pacific, United States of America

sec.t: Regulating stress is a common challenge for casual and competitive esports players. Mismanagement of player stress often leads to a psychological state called tilt, in which players become frustrated, play worse, and engage in toxic behavior (McLinton & Pascale, 2024). The chat feature in competitive gaming is one avenue where toxicity is most prevalent, including behaviors like flaming and trolling (Adinolf & Türkay, 2018). Strategic sharing of information within the chat feature is also a critical component of team success and a form of communication often used in team contexts to cope with stress (Beres et al., 2023). Heart rate variability (HRV) is a psychophysiological variable related to autonomic stress regulation (Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017, p. 1). As a potential measure of the player’s physiological stress, HRV could be used to assess the likelihood that the player engages in cooperative chat behavior.
This study aims to explore the relationship between HRV and chat behavior in casual and competitive college-age Valorant players.

Twenty-three university-enrolled players with an average age of 20.1 years played one competitive Valorant match while wearing a Polar H-10 heart rate chest monitor. Fourteen subjects were male (63.6%), eight were female (36.4%), and one declined to share their gender identity. 12.5% of the participants were Iron rank, 12.5% Bronze rank, 8.3% Silver rank, 20.8% Gold rank, 8.3% Platinum rank, 16.7% Diamond rank, 8.3% Ascendant rank, and 4.2% Immortal rank. Each match was screen-recorded using OBS Studio. Text from the game’s chat log was extracted using a Python script to perform optical character recognition and deduplicate. Transcripts of each player’s chat log were manually coded, recording all chat messages by either the player or their teammates, including messages from Valorant’s pinging system that allows players to strategically share information with teammates. Typed chat messages were coded as positive, neutral, or negative based on the content of the message. Coding reliability was not formally assessed. Team ping messages were analyzed separately from typed chat messages. The player’s average root-mean-square of successive differences (RMSSD) and average high-frequency power (HF) were measured for each round of play using the Kubios Scientific software. Time intervals for HRV analysis ranged from thirty seconds to two minutes, depending on the length of the round.

Pearson R correlations show a significant relationship between chat behavior in the first and last three rounds of play, and chat behavior was consistent across rounds. No relationship between chat behavior in the first three rounds and a player’s HRV in the first or last three rounds of a match was found. Similarly, uncooperative chat behavior was not associated with changes in HRV from the first three rounds to the last three rounds of play based on Pearson R correlations, though the data trended toward a positive relationship. Fisher-Z means indicate that the individual player’s chat behavior is associated with their changes in HRV, but with weak effects. Individual player HRV was also related to future chat behavior, with similarly weak effects.

Findings suggest individual players’ changes in physiological stress are weakly associated with future chat behavior. Players and coaches may benefit from monitoring player HRV to assess the likelihood of engaging in toxic or cooperative chat behaviors.

Chat behavior shared a relationship with HRV in Valorant players from this study, but a larger sample size is needed to better understand the dynamic between different types of chat behavior and physiological stress.

abstracts.title: The Role of Social Connection in eSports Mental Health: Differences Between MOBA and FPS Players
abstracts.by: Maria Celina Ferreira Goedert, Universidade Católica Dom Bosco, Brazil; Ana Karla Silva Soares, Universidade Federal de Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil
abstracts.aus: Maria Celina Ferreira Goedert and Ana Karla Silva Soares

sec.t: eSports have become established as important spaces for social interaction in the online context, particularly among young adults (Shan et al. 2023). Beyond competition, online games share psychological features with physical sports, facilitating collective experiences, interpersonal relationships, and feelings of belonging and social connection (Kegelaers et al, 2024; Soares et al., 2022). However, a significant portion of the psychological literature continues to emphasize the potential negative impacts of gaming on mental health, often overlooking meaningful differences between game genres (Marques et al., 2023).

In this context, the present study aimed to examine relationships and group differences between Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) and First-Person Shooter (FPS) players in indicators of social connection within eSports contexts and mental health outcomes.

The study included 146 eSports players (M age = 22.39 years, SD = 3.37), predominantly male (76.03%), distributed between MOBA (n = 82) and FPS players (n = 64). Participants completed the Social Connection Scale, Gaming Behavior Scale, Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS), Positive and Negative Affect Scale, and Satisfaction with Life Scale.

Independent samples t-tests revealed that FPS players reported significantly higher levels of social connection (t(144) = -2.45, M = 4.69, SD = 1.15, d = -0.41) and individual in-game behavior scores (t(144) = -2.41, M = 3.73, SD = 0.82, d = -0.40) compared to MOBA players. In contrast, MOBA players exhibited significantly higher levels of negative affect (t(144) = 2.24, M = 3.78, SD = 1.28, d = 0.37). No significant group differences were observed for stress, anxiety, depression, positive affect, life satisfaction, or collective in-game behavior. Pearson correlation analyses showed that social connection was significantly and negatively associated with stress (r = -0.40), anxiety (r = -0.37), depression (r = -0.44), and negative affect (r = -0.44), and positively associated with positive affect (r = 0.41) and life satisfaction (r = 0.25). Although some variability emerged between MOBA and FPS players, formal comparisons of independent correlations did not reveal statistically significant differences between groups. Logistic regression analysis further indicated that higher levels of social connection and anxiety were associated with a greater likelihood of belonging to the FPS group (β = 0.74), whereas higher levels of negative affect were associated with the MOBA group (β = -0.35, p = 0.04, OR = 0.71). The model explained a modest proportion of variance (McFadden R² = 0.07; Nagelkerke R² = 0.12). Moderation analyses indicated that game genre did not significantly moderate the relationship between social connection and mental health indicators, suggesting that observed associations were consistent across both MOBA and FPS contexts.

Overall, the findings suggest that although MOBA and FPS players exhibit some discrete psychosocial differences, social connection emerges as a key factor associated with better mental health and well-being outcomes across genres, suggesting that fostering positive social interaction in eSports environments may be relevant for player well-being.
These results contribute to a more contextualized and less pathologizing understanding of eSports, emphasizing social processes in competitive online gaming environments.

abstracts.by: François Savard, Université du Québec à Montréal, Canada

sec.t: Esports research has devoted considerable attention to professionalization, high-level performance, and competitive gaming environments (Jin & Besombes, 2024; Savard, 2025). At the same time, emerging research on grassroots esports suggests that community-based environments can provide spaces for inclusion, socialization, belonging, and player support (Baumann et al., 2024). Japan provides a particularly relevant context for exploring these dynamics, as esports cultures across Asia have developed through distinct national and cultural trajectories (Jin & Kim, 2024), while Japan’s developing esports market has received comparatively limited scholarly attention (Meng-Lewis et al., 2026). Its gaming culture also includes distinctive physical and social environments, particularly game centers, that have historically supported interactions and community formation among players (Pelletier-Gagnon, 2019). Exploring these environments may help identify alternative approaches to healthier and more sustainable competitive gaming ecosystems in Canada.

As part of my interdisciplinary PhD in Health and Society, this presentation introduces the preliminary reflections and research design of an exploratory project examining Japanese grassroots esports ecosystems. More specifically, the project seeks to explore how Japanese grassroots esports communities organize player support, community participation, and well-being, and to examine how practices observed in Japan may inform Canadian esports initiatives while contributing to a broader dialogue between Japanese and Canadian esports ecosystems.

Funded by the Tanaka Fund, the project adopts an exploratory qualitative ethnographic approach combining participant and non-participant observation, informal ethnographic conversations, and the collection of relevant public and institutional materials. Fieldwork will be conducted in Japan from September to October 2026 and will include visits to esports organizations, student programs, gaming venues, community spaces, and competitive events. Data collection will focus on how players are supported, how communities are structured, and how physical and social environments shape participation and well-being. Observations will be documented through field notes and, where relevant, photographs and collected materials. The resulting data will be analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2022).

Preliminary findings from the literature review suggest that the Japanese esports landscape differs in several respects from more established international esports markets. Research on esports fans in Japan identifies distinctive preferences in terms of gaming platforms, genres, and motivations, reflecting the influence of Japan’s broader gaming culture and history (Meng-Lewis et al., 2026). The literature also documents a diverse range of contexts, including player health, education, school clubs, gaming facilities, game centers, and regional initiatives. Combined with emerging research on grassroots esports, these findings identify several dimensions to explore during fieldwork, particularly community organization, player support, physical and social environments, and the relationship between competitive gaming and local communities.

The findings may contribute to the development of healthier and more community-oriented esports initiatives in Canada by identifying practices related to player support, community organization, and the use of physical and social environments. For the Japanese esports ecosystem, the study may contribute to documenting and increasing the international visibility of grassroots practices while providing an external perspective on community esports development. More broadly, the project seeks to foster knowledge exchange between Japanese and Canadian esports communities rather than simply transferring practices from one context to another.

By exploring Japanese grassroots esports ecosystems, this project aims to broaden current perspectives on esports beyond highly professionalized models. Through a dialogue between Japanese and Canadian contexts, the study seeks to contribute to ongoing discussions surrounding player well-being, community infrastructures, and culturally situated approaches to competitive gaming environments.
