abstracts.title: Tracing Expert Knowledge and Decision-Making in Gameplay: A Hand-Based Notational Analysis
abstracts.by: Charlie Smith, University of Suffolk, United Kingdom; Peter Howell, Martina Navarro and Brett Stevens, University of Portsmouth, United Kingdom
abstracts.aus: Charlie Smith, Peter Howell, Martina Navarro and Brett Stevens

sec.t: A common methodology in sports science is Performance Analysis (PA) which reviews behaviour naturalistically, encompassing several methods examining behaviour and their determinants (Lames, 2023). One such method is Notational Analysis (NA), the quantifiable recording of critical moments during a task to evaluate contributing factors (Hughes & Bartlett, 2015; Ungvarsky, 2023). Currently both have limited application in esports, despite literature arguing the domain aligns well with PA (Novak et al., 2019; 2020; Smithies et al., 2021). Therefore, there is a justification for further use of PA to analyse player behaviour.

This study aimed to identify behavioural patterns in recurring game contexts within competitive Team Fortress 2, a class-based first-person shooter. Four research questions were asked: can game states predict action efficacy; do actions have prevalence in certain game states; which player and team actions have the highest rate of efficacy; and how frequent are actions in different match contexts? Methodologically, the study seeks to evaluate the efficacy of hand-based NA as a form of analysing video game play.

Data collection was conducted with a bespoke, computerised, hand-based NA system inspired by Lorains et al. (2013). The system has four sections: game details (timestamp & scoreline); game state variables (objectives held, map location, players alive, ‘ultimate ability’ percentage); distinct action (action type, action taken independently, action taken by the team); and action efficacy (effectiveness of independent action & overall team outcome). Twelve public YouTube videos of expert competitive Team Fortress 2 players were analysed; when a distinct action was identified it was recorded alongside match contexts, efficacy was recorded when the action concluded. Chi-squared tests and standardised residuals were used to identify abnormal rates between two variables.

Player behaviour in competitive Team Fortress 2 sees constant adaptation in response to contextual factors, best observed in the oscillation between aggressive actions in advantageous game states, such as greater number of players alive or dominance over game objectives, and the inverse relationship with defensive actions in disadvantageous states. No evidence on consistent predictors of effective actions was found, although collective team actions did have a stronger association with positive outcomes compared to individual actions.

Telemetry, big data, and machine learning have been used to evaluate esports performance at scale (Xenopoulos et al., 2021; Qian et al., 2022; Sifa et al., 2021). While effective, they are expensive to develop, require technical knowledge to operate, and struggle to distinguish between similar actions with different intents or goals. Hand-based NA presents an alternative method of performance analysis in esports that is low-tech, accessible, and can distinguish subtle behaviours and their contributing factors.

Results suggest that expert Team Fortress 2 players exhibit behavioural adaptation in response to dynamic match scenarios, seen with the oscillation between defensive and aggressive actions depending key game state factors. Findings are consistent with the Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model positing that expert decision-making leverages knowledge and experience to recognise a situation and determine the first suitable action, instead of a deliberative process (Klein, 1993).

abstracts.title: Ultra-short High-Intensity Intermittent Exercise Promotes Heart Rate Synchrony and Team Performance in Female Esports Players
abstracts.by: Yukina Tachibana, University of Tsukuba, Japan; Ryonosuke Kasahara, Shion Takahashi, Takafumi Yamaguchi, Ren Takamizawa, Shohei Dobashi and Takashi Matsui, University of Tsukuba, Japan
abstracts.aus: Yukina Tachibana, Ryonosuke Kasahara, Shion Takahashi, Takafumi Yamaguchi, Ren Takamizawa, Shohei Dobashi and Takashi Matsui

sec.t: Team performance in esports requires a balance between individual skill and teamwork. Heart rate (HR) synchrony is a physiological index of interpersonal coordination and team unity; however, excessive synchrony may impair individual performance by reducing autonomous role execution. High-intensity exercise (HIE) enhances inhibitory control, a core executive function supporting individual gaming performance (1). In teams, enhanced inhibitory control may help players regulate self-oriented responses and flexibly coordinate with teammates. We previously found that a 1-minute ultra-short-duration high-intensity intermittent exercise (U-SIE) protocol enhanced inhibitory control and gaming performance in male players, possibly by suppressing excessive HR synchrony. However, its effects on female esports players remain unknown. Females tend to exhibit a “tend-and-befriend” response under stress (2), and team cohesion is more strongly associated with performance success in female teams than in male teams (3). Therefore, U-SIE may adaptively modulate HR synchrony in a sex-specific manner: suppressing excessive synchrony in male players while promoting timely interpersonal synchrony and teamwork in female players.
To elucidate whether a pre-game U-SIE protocol promotes HR synchrony and enhances team performance in female esports players.

A crossover field experiment was conducted during an esports exhibition match. Five female professional players and five male collegiate players participated in both rest and exercise conditions. The 1-minute U-SIE protocol consisted of three sets of 7-second high-knee sprints separated by 20-second rests, followed by 10-minute seated rest. HR was continuously monitored. Ratings of perceived exertion and the Two-Dimensional Mood Scale were assessed before and after the match, and in-game statistics were collected post-match. Cross-correlation analysis quantified HR synchrony, including cross-correlation function and time lag.

U-SIE elevated post-exercise HR to approximately 150 bpm in both sexes, which returned to baseline before the match. During the match, HR was higher under the exercise condition in all players. However, enhanced HR synchrony, characterized by higher cross-correlation function and shorter time lag, was observed only in female players. Concurrently, female players showed an exercise-induced increase in assists per round, which was strongly and negatively correlated with HR synchrony time lag (r = -0.71, p = 0.02). Psychologically, exercise increased vitality and arousal in male players, whereas it increased stability and comfort in female players.

The 1-minute U-SIE protocol may serve as a highly time-efficient pre-game warm-up strategy for esports players. This brief, equipment-free intervention may acutely modulate cognitive control and interpersonal physiological coordination, thereby supporting teamwork-related performance in competitive esports.

A brief 1-minute U-SIE promoted adaptive HR synchrony, characterized by shorter time lag, and was associated with increased assists per round in female esports players. These findings suggest that ultra-short HIE may facilitate timely interpersonal coordination and teamwork-related performance in team-based esports.

abstracts.title: What Do Competitive Players Do With Their Settings? A Multi-Game Esports Configuration Survey
abstracts.by: Ashish Rajpurohit and Arjun Madhusudan, North Carolina State University, United States of America; Josef Spjut, NVIDIA, United States of America; Benjamin Watson, North Carolina State University, United States of America
abstracts.aus: Ashish Rajpurohit, Arjun Madhusudan, Josef Spjut and Benjamin Watson

sec.t: Frame rate and input latency affect competitive performance: Claypool and Claypool (2007) showed this for aiming in first-person shooters, Liu et al. (2021) for local latency in CS:GO, and Watson et al. (2019) for adaptive sync. Yet players must navigate dozens of settings in their games with little guidance. Resources like prosettings.net compile professional configurations, but empirical data on the broader population is missing. Madhusudan and Watson (2021) surveyed 43 Dota 2 players and found that most favored frame rate and disabled VSYNC, though VSYNC is off by default in Dota 2, so this may reflect defaults rather than active choice.

Our ongoing survey pairs self-reported data with actual configuration files from players’ machines to provide the first multi-game empirical account of competitive player configuration behavior, examining how players handle the quality-versus-performance tradeoff, how well they understand their settings, and whether that understanding shapes their choices.

This study (IRB #25527) involves an online Qualtrics survey of esports players recruited from game-specific subreddits, Discord servers, and university communities. Participants reported their in-game rank, hours played, configuration priority, settings understanding, and interface usability. They uploaded configuration files, parsed with custom scripts to extract VSYNC status and other settings.

110 respondents have started the survey so far. The flow moves from demographics to per-game questions to file uploads, so not everyone completed every section: 46 answered questions about specific games, 14 uploaded files. Respondents are serious competitors: 77% play ranked at least several times a week, 59% play to improve their rank, and all reported an in-game rank. Early results from our Qualtrics survey cover 14 PC esports titles across seven genres: tactical shooters, MOBAs, hero shooters, battle royales, sports, strategy, and fighting. Since participants could answer questions about up to three games, 46 respondents provided 44 game responses, each including a visual quality versus frame rate priority. Of those, 75% favored frame rate. Every tactical shooter and battle royale response chose a frame rate. MOBA players were more divided: 56% frame rate, 31% balanced, 13% graphics. Configuration files reinforced the genre pattern: VSYNC was disabled in 12 of 14 parsed files, with both exceptions from genres where respondents indicated weaker performance preference. Even respondents with high-end GPUs (RTX 2060 to 4080 Super) disabled VSYNC. Players with stronger self-rated settings understanding chose frame rate more often (80% Advanced/Expert vs 44% Basic/Novice).

For game developers, the consistency of performance preferences and near-universal VSYNC disabling suggests an opportunity to align competitive defaults with actual player behavior through genre-aware presets. For esports coaches, the apparent relationship between settings understanding and performance choices suggests configuration literacy could support player development.

In our ongoing survey, early results suggest most competitive players choose performance over visuals, but the degree depends on genre and knowledge of settings. The consistency between survey responses and actual configuration files offers further support for these trends and will let us compare player intent to actual action. Future work will seek to confirm these early results, examine within-genre differences, and broaden analysis beyond VSYNC.

abstracts.title: What Do Esports Events Leave Behind? Social Effects and Sponsorship Implications from ASIA esports EXPO 2026
abstracts.by: Takuya Tsukamoto, Chukyo University, Japan; Minoru Toriyama, Osaka Seikei University, Japan

sec.t: In recent years, esports have expanded globally as a form of digital game competition characterized by interactivity, digitality, and competitiveness, and has increasingly been incorporated into international sport events. However, the institutional position of esports within the sport system remains fluid, and its social effects and potential legacy for local communities have not been sufficiently examined. The 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, where esports will be held as an official medal event, provides an important opportunity to explore what effects esports events may generate for local communities, companies, and participants. PURPOSE and METHODS This presentation examines the expected social effects and sponsorship implications of esports events through the case of ASIA esports EXPO 2026, a related event of the 2026 Asian Games. The study consists of two parts. First, semi-structured interviews were conducted with event providers involved in the Asian Games esports competition, including organizations related to game publishing, event management, local media, and esports promotion. These interviews explored the social effects that stakeholders expected from the event. Second, a questionnaire survey was conducted with visitors to ASIA esports EXPO 2026 to examine event satisfaction, perceived social effects, information channels, sponsor recognition, and expectations for future esports policies.

The findings from the provider interviews identified five categories of expected social effects: human resource development and diffusion, legacy formation, marketing promotion, social significance, and community development. These effects were not limited to immediate outcomes such as event excitement or media exposure. Rather, stakeholders expected broader and longer-term impacts, including the development of internationally capable personnel, continuous local esports events, increased corporate participation, enhanced understanding of diversity, and the growth of gaming communities. The visitor survey also examined a 30-item scale consisting of ten factors. In addition to social effects discussed in previous sport event studies, two esports-specific factors were included: promotion of corporate use and legacy formation. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated that the overall model showed an acceptable level of fit, and the factor loadings, construct reliability, and average variance extracted met standard criteria, suggesting a certain level of reliability and convergent validity.

Additional results showed that visitors reported high satisfaction with ASIA esports EXPO 2026. The atmosphere of the venue, live viewing experience, trial-play opportunities, and participatory content were evaluated positively. At the same time, improvements were needed in visitor attraction, publicity, content variety, and the quality of the venue experience. Social media was the main information channel, while sponsor recognition appeared to depend not only on logo exposure but also on experiential touchpoints and visitor flow within the venue.

This presentation argues that esports events should not be understood merely as competitions or entertainment events, but as social platforms connecting local communities, companies, tourism, policy, and community development. It also suggests that sponsorship effects can be enhanced by designing memorable experiential touch points rather than relying only on exposure.

abstracts.title: When the Roster Empties: Sustaining (and Losing) University Esports Teams and Study Programmes in the German-Speaking Region (DACH)
abstracts.by: Aleksander Groth and Susanne Julinek, MCI - The Entrepreneurial School, Austria; Felix Wachholz, University of Innsbruck, Austria; Peter Mirski, MCI - The Entrepreneurial School, Austria
abstracts.aus: Aleksander Groth, Susanne Julinek, Felix Wachholz and Peter Mirski

sec.t: While academic esports expanded rapidly in North America and parts of Asia, in the German-speaking region (DACH) they remain rare and fragile, both as competitive university teams and as study programmes or smaller curricular offerings. As an example, in Austria only two institutions (in the same city) currently commit to and sustain an official university esports team. Many initiatives launch with enthusiasm but stall, contract, or are quietly discontinued, yet the conditions for sustainable academic esports remain poorly understood, especially beyond the dominant North American model. Our study asks which factors and framework conditions enable or undermine the sustainable operation of university esports, teams and study programs alike, in the DACH context. Departing from success-only accounts, we deliberately include dormant, cancelled, and “sunsetting” cases, treating discontinuation as an equally informative outcome.

We read academic esports as a multi-level sustainability problem. At the societal level, participation reflects both individualized forms of engagement and the contested capacity of sport to foster social cohesion beyond individual or small-group outcomes (Moustakas, 2024). At the organizational level, university esports can be understood through the broader collegiate sport club model, where clubs often operate through simple, flexible, and informally coordinated structures. Such arrangements foster autonomy and adaptability but may also make programs vulnerable to leadership turnover and dependent on a small number of committed individuals (Springer & Dixon, 2025). At the cultural level, student commitment is shaped by the still-contested and debated legitimacy of video games: in a cultural context marked by a strong work ethic, gaming is rarely read as career-relevant, dampening students’ investment and institutional support (Gislam et al., 2025). Consequently, our lens foregrounds the people who carry institutional responsibility rather than players alone.

Empirically, we conduct an exploratory qualitative interview study (guided interviews, n = 15-20) with stakeholders who have/had responsibility for university esports in varied roles: athletes and team captains, marketing and communication, university sport and infrastructure units, and departmental or administrative leadership, across both ongoing and discontinued teams and programmes. Interviews are analyzed through qualitative content analysis (Kuckartz & Rädiker, 2023), with categories developed inductively and the framing refined after the first interviews; the findings will inform a subsequent quantitative study phase.
This is an ongoing study and we are looking forward to present our first results in September at ERNC26.

By examining a comparatively under-studied, structurally constrained regional case, and by learning explicitly from teams and programs that did not survive, our study offers a transferable, organizationally and sociologically grounded account of what makes academic esports durable. It speaks to the conference’s focus on collegiate esports development and the governance and management of esports ecosystems and offers an intercultural counterpoint to contrasting successful Asian and North American trajectories.

Drawing on the accounts of those responsible for university esports, including discontinued initiatives, the study identifies the organizational, cultural, and social conditions for sustaining esports, as teams and study programmes, in German-speaking higher education, offering practical guidance for institutions and an international reference point.

text: The Esports Research Network Conference 2025 (ERNC 2025) was held from 12 to 14 November 2025 as a fully online, global conference. Building on previous editions, ERNC25 brought together researchers, practitioners, and students from around the world through a continuous, live digital format designed to support sustained international exchange.

The conference was structured around a hub-based production model, with four regional hubs operating as research and live-streaming nodes. These hubs were hosted by Slippery Rock University of Pennsylvania and Michigan State University (Americas), Staffordshire University (Europe, Middle East and Africa), and UNSW Sydney (Asia-Pacific). Together, the hubs enabled ERNC25 to follow the sun across time zones and remain continuously live throughout the three-day conference.
ERNC 2025 was organised under the theme “Future Realities: Esports as a Global Lab”, positioning esports as both an object of study and a methodological lens for understanding digital transformation.

text: The Esports Research Network Conference 2024 (ERNC 2024) was held from 30 October to 1 November 2024 in London, United Kingdom. ERNC24 once again brought together an international community of researchers, industry professionals, and practitioners to explore critical questions at the intersection of esports, society, and digital culture. The conference was held in a hybrid format, combining in-person participation with online access.

Taking place in the lead-up to the League of Legends World Finals in London, ERNC24 situated esports research within a broader cultural and economic moment, highlighting the growing entanglement of competitive gaming with global media, sport, and urban environments.
ERNC 2024 was organised under the theme “Where Worlds Collide”, capturing the growing intersections between esports and traditional sport, culture, media, technology, education, and governance.

text: The Esports Research Network Conference 2022 (ERNC 2022) was held as an international in-person conference from 21 to 23 November 2022 in Jönköping, Sweden, and was presented by the Media, Management & Transformation Centre (MMTC) at Jönköping International Business School. ERNC 2022 marked the first fully in-person ERN conference and brought together researchers, students, practitioners, and industry stakeholders to engage with pressing questions surrounding sustainability in esports and the digital society.

Hosted in Jönköping, widely recognised as the City of DreamHack, the conference was strategically aligned with DreamHack Winter 2022 (24 to 27 November), enabling participants to connect academic debate with one of the world’s largest digital and esports festivals. Selected key sessions and panels were live-streamed to ensure broader accessibility and international reach.

ERNC 2022 focused on Sustainable Esports in the Digital Society, addressing how esports can continue to develop while maintaining long-term economic viability, social responsibility, and environmental awareness.

about.title: About the Esports Research Network
about.tagline: Connecting researchers, practitioners, and enthusiasts to advance esports research globally.
mission: The Esports Research Network (ERN) is committed to advancing esports research through global collaboration, rigorous scholarship, and meaningful connections between academia and industry.

We strive to create an inclusive, diverse, and supportive community that empowers researchers at all stages of their careers, from emerging scholars to established experts. Our mission is to bridge the gap between research and practice, ensuring that academic insights translate into real-world impact.

Through our conferences, publications, and community initiatives, we aim to tackle the key challenges facing esports and the digital society, driving innovation through interdisciplinary collaboration and fostering the next generation of esports researchers.
history: The Esports Research Network (ERN) was founded to address the growing need for a centralized platform connecting researchers, practitioners, and industry professionals in the rapidly evolving field of esports research.

Since our inception, we have grown into a global community of scholars dedicated to advancing esports research through collaboration, education, and innovation. Our annual conferences have brought together hundreds of researchers from around the world, fostering interdisciplinary dialogue and driving the field forward.

Today, ERN continues to serve as a vital hub for esports research, providing resources, networking opportunities, and a platform for sharing cutting-edge research that shapes the future of esports and digital society.

conduct.lead: The Esports Research Network Conference (ERNC) is dedicated to creating an inclusive, professional, and harassment-free environment for scholars, industry professionals, and students worldwide. This Code of Conduct applies to all participants and encompasses all conference-related activities and platforms.
conduct.version: Version 1.1, in force since 24 August 2026. First published 27 December 2025.
conduct.html:
Scope

This Code of Conduct applies to:

  • All official ERNC activities (talks, workshops, panels, networking, Q&A, etc.)
  • ERN communication platforms, including Discord and Twitch
  • Social media activity related to ERNC (e.g., conference hashtags, posts, or shared media)
  • ERN-supported events and meetings
  • Any use, distribution, or discussion of conference-related media

Expected Behavior

All participants are expected to:

  • Treat all attendees with respect, regardless of race, gender, sexuality, disability, nationality, religion, or other identity factors.
  • Encourage scholarly discussion and constructive feedback in a professional and welcoming tone.
  • Seek consent before capturing or sharing media (e.g., screenshots, videos) of presentations or individuals.
  • Avoid disrupting sessions or conversations in chat, voice, or video settings.
  • Use conference spaces and content responsibly, including proper attribution of work.
  • Handle disagreements constructively and refer concerns to moderators or staff when needed.

Prohibited Conduct

The following are strictly prohibited:

  • Harassment or discrimination of any kind
  • Trolling, spamming, or disruptive behavior in sessions, chats, or voice channels
  • Posting or linking to explicit, violent, or otherwise inappropriate content
  • Sharing media of others without consent, especially for harmful or mocking purposes
  • Unsolicited private messages, especially those of a harassing or invasive nature
  • Retaliation against anyone who reports a concern or cooperates in an investigation

Moderation Policy

To ensure safety and maintain professional standards, ERNC will enforce the following moderation policies on all platforms:

  • Moderators will monitor all active Discord channels and Twitch chats during conference sessions.
  • Messages or content that violate the Code of Conduct will be removed immediately.
  • Timeouts, mutes, or bans will be issued for disruptive participants, with or without warning depending on severity.
  • All moderation decisions are final during the event to ensure smooth operation.
  • If you witness inappropriate behavior, use the /report command in Discord or message a moderator privately.
  • Moderators will be clearly identified (e.g., with a “MOD” or “ERNC Staff” role/tag).

Platform-Specific Rules

Discord

  • Voice Channels: Join voice channels respectfully; do not interrupt or speak over others.
  • Text Channels: Stay on topic and avoid excessive emoji use, spam, or off-topic content.
  • Usernames and Avatars must be appropriate and free of offensive or suggestive material.
  • Direct Messaging (DM): Do not DM other participants unless they have given permission.
  • Screen Sharing and Audio: Only presenters or approved users may share screens or audio in public channels.

Twitch

  • Chat Behavior: Twitch chat will be moderated in real-time. Do not post links, all-caps messages, or repeat content excessively.
  • Emotes and Memes: Keep use respectful. Do not use emotes to mock or harass speakers or other viewers.
  • Usernames and Comments that violate the Code of Conduct will be banned immediately.
  • No Self-Promotion or advertising in chat unless explicitly allowed by moderators.

Reporting a Violation

To report inappropriate behavior:

  • Discord: Use /report or message a moderator directly.
  • Twitch: Use the “Report” option or message a channel moderator.
  • General Reports: Submit concerns via this anonymous form or email ernc@esportsresearch.net.

Reports may be made during or after the event. Anonymous reporting is supported.

In serious cases, ERNC organizers may contact local law enforcement.

Non-responsive Presenters

Individuals whose abstract submissions are accepted for presentation are required to confirm their participation and to maintain timely communication with conference organizers. Presenters are expected to attend their scheduled session or provide notice if circumstances arise that prevent participation as soon as they become aware. Failure to respond to repeated communication attempts, failure to confirm acceptance, or absence from a scheduled presentation without prior notice is considered a breach of professional conduct and may result in a sanction.

Presenters who do not fulfill these obligations may be prohibited from presenting at ERN-sponsored conferences for a period of two years. Exceptions will be made in cases of medical emergencies or other serious, documented circumstances beyond the presenter’s control. The intent of this policy is to support a respectful, dependable, and academically professional conference environment.

Consequences of Violations

Violations may result in:

  • Warnings (verbal or written)
  • Muting or banning from Discord/Twitch
  • Removal from the conference
  • Exclusion from ERNC content or proceedings
  • Reporting to employer or academic institution
  • Referral to law enforcement in severe cases

Anti-Retaliation Policy

ERNC prohibits retaliation against any participant who reports a violation or participates in an investigation. We will take all appropriate steps to protect and support those individuals.

Version history

1.1, 24 August 2026. Scope extended: the code now applies to ERN communication platforms (Discord, Twitch) at all times rather than only to conference communication platforms, and ERN-supported events and meetings were added.

pages.cfa:
About the conference

Esports research still often lives within disciplines that rarely meet: management and sport science, media and cultural studies, psychology, law, computer science, education, and more. Each discipline studies esports with its own questions and its own methods. The Esports Research Network Conference (ERNC) exists to bring these perspectives into one room with a deliberately international, interdisciplinary approach to understanding esports. The previous ERNC in 2026 at the University of Tsukuba (Japan) gathered 163 participants from 29 countries. For the first time, the ERNC moves to North America in 2027. NC State University will host three conference days from 9 to 11 November 2027, preceded by pre-conference workshops on the afternoon of 8 November.

Theme: Think & Do: Where Research, Competition & Community Converge

Esports has always lived in three worlds at once, especially in education. It is a field of research that has produced its own handbooks, journals, and degree programs in little more than a decade; it is a competitive practice that spans from the scholastic leagues to world championships; and it is a community of players, fans, organizers, clubs, universities, and cities. These three worlds, however, meet less often than they should. Research tends to study competition from the outside, organizers rarely draw on what research already knows, and communities appear as the object of a study more often than as its partner. Still, there are places where the three converge, and NC State is one of them: a university with an esports program, an esports arena, esports academic coursework, and an esports research community, in a city that treats esports as part of its event economy.

NC State’s motto, Think & Do, describes the task ERNC27 sets itself. We invite contributions that think about esports, contributions that do something with it, and, above all, those that do both. Three questions run through the conference:

  • What can research learn from esports competition and community, and what does it owe them in return?
  • How do esports competitive structures, from collegiate programs to professional circuits, shape the communities around them?
  • When esports research, competition, and community converge, what makes that convergence last?

Topics

The program is organized in three strands that follow the theme. However, as is our tradition at every ERNC, work on any aspect of esports is welcome; the conference theme and listed topics are an invitation, not a filter.

Esports Research

  • Theory building and the place of esports in the wider social sciences
  • Research methods, data, and measurement in esports research
  • Technology, data, and artificial intelligence in esports
  • Academic esports education and curriculum
  • History, heritage, and culture of competitive gaming

Esports Competition

  • Performance, expertise, and sport science
  • Health, psychology, and wellbeing of players
  • Collegiate and scholastic esports
  • Events, formats, and tournament design
  • Governance, integrity, regulation, and law
  • Business, management, and economics: sponsorship, media rights and business models

Esports Community

Abstract requirements

Abstracts that do not follow these requirements will not be accepted.

  1. Length: at most 500 words, including references.
  2. Language: English.
  3. Structure: the six headings Introduction, Purpose, Methods, Results, Practical Implications, and Conclusion. Work in progress may report anticipated results; conceptual papers use Methods for the approach and Results for the argument.
  4. Keywords: three to five.
  5. References: in-text citations that match a short reference list (APA 7th edition).
  6. Fit: the abstract makes its contribution to esports explicit. Work on games or gamification in general belongs at other venues unless the link to esports is clear.

Conference Overview

The Esports Research Network Conference 2026 (ERNC26) took place from 15 to 17 September 2026 at the University of Tsukuba, in the University's 30th Anniversary Hall (Daigaku Kaikan). After the fully online edition of 2025, ERNC26 brought the network back into one room, and it did so in a country that shaped the history of games like few others. Japan is a gaming powerhouse with an unparalleled heritage in console and arcade gaming; its esports ecosystem, however, has only recently started to grow, helped by the relaxation of prize money regulations in 2018 and the rise of professional leagues. Consequently, Tsukuba was a fitting place to ask what gaming heritage means for the future of esports.

The conference was hosted by the University of Tsukuba, funded by the KDDI Foundation and the Tsukuba Tourism and Convention Association, and co-organised by GAKU.

Theme and Contributions

ERNC26 was organised under the theme “Bridging Gaming Heritage and Esports Futures: Transformations, Traditions, and Tomorrow”, with a particular focus on intercultural perspectives and on the relationship between Asia and other regions. The programme reflected the breadth of the field. Health and performance science was strongly represented, from physical conditioning and cardiovascular reactivity to exercise adherence and the menstrual cycle in training and competition. Governance and integrity formed a second cluster, with work on legal frameworks, e-doping, AI ethics and the role of the state. Further sessions examined fandom across borders, collegiate esports, inclusion, older adults as players, and esports tourism.

Three keynotes framed the programme: Hideki Okamura (SEGA, JESU and GAKU) on the esports journey in Japan, Brian McCauley (Jönköping International Business School) on gaming heritage as infrastructure for esports and the digital society, and Michael Murray (Bandai Namco Entertainment) on keeping community at the heart of esports. An opening panel with SEGA, KONAMI Esports Academy and the Japan Esports Union discussed how publishers and public authorities shape Japan's esports scene.

Format and Participation

ERNC26 brought together 163 participants from 29 countries and more than 40 institutions. The Book of Abstracts contains 64 peer-reviewed presentations and one panel, held in four parallel session rooms alongside the keynotes and industry panels. In line with ERN practice, the plenary sessions were streamed on the ERN Twitch channel and the recordings are published on the ERN YouTube channel.
